A religious system that tells husbands they may strike disobedient wives, even “lightly,” gives male violence a sacred framework. It makes a woman’s physical safety conditional on her obedience and on her husband’s judgment. That is why the proposition stands: in its authoritative texts and classical legal tradition, Islam encourages — or at minimum legitimizes — violence toward women.
steps.conclusion_against:
## Concluding statement against the proposition

The proposition before us is that **Islam encourages violence towards women**. That claim has not been proven.

What has been shown is that there is a difficult and debated text — Qur’an 4:34 — which some classical jurists interpreted as allowing a highly restricted, non-injurious, last-resort disciplinary measure in a specific marital crisis. But even if one accepts that classical interpretation, it still does not establish that Islam **encourages** violence toward women.

Encouragement means approval, promotion, or moral endorsement. Yet the overwhelming direction of Islamic teaching is the opposite.

The Qur’an describes marriage as a bond of:

> “affection and mercy” — **Qur’an 30:21**

It commands:

> “Live with them in kindness” — **Qur’an 4:19**

It forbids using harm as a means of control:

> “Do not retain them to harm them and transgress against them” — **Qur’an 2:231**

And:

> “Do not harm them in order to make things difficult for them” — **Qur’an 65:6**

These are not incidental statements. They form the ethical framework through which Islamic family life is to be understood.

The Prophet Muhammad’s example is even more decisive. He never struck a woman:

> “The Messenger of Allah never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant…” — **Sahih Muslim 2328**

He said:

> “The best of you are those who are best to their wives” — **Tirmidhi 3895; Ibn Majah 1977**

He said:

> “Do not beat the female servants of Allah” — **Sunan Abi Dawud 2146**

And when women complained that their husbands had beaten them, he did not praise those men. He condemned their conduct morally, saying:

> “Those men are not the best among you” — **Sunan Abi Dawud 2146**

That is not encouragement. That is disapproval.

The opponent’s argument depends on turning restricted toleration into endorsement. But Islamic ethics clearly distinguishes between what may have been regulated in a particular social context and what is morally ideal. The Prophet’s own conduct establishes the ideal: he did not strike women, and he made kindness to wives a measure of a man’s excellence.

Nor can one ignore Islam’s broader treatment of women. Islam condemned female infanticide, gave women inheritance rights, recognized their spiritual equality, required consent in marriage, and prohibited the killing of women in war. That wider framework is inconsistent with the claim that women are treated as legitimate targets of violence.

The strongest fair version of the opponent’s case is this: some traditional jurists allowed a limited, non-injurious physical measure under strict conditions in cases of serious marital breakdown. But that is very different from saying Islam encourages violence towards women.

The proposition overstates the evidence. It takes a contested and restricted issue, isolates it from the Qur’an’s commands of mercy and non-harm, minimizes the Prophet’s non-violent example, and then presents the result as if it represents Islam’s moral teaching as a whole.

It does not.

Islam’s core message regarding women in family life is kindness, mercy, restraint, justice, and accountability before God. The Prophet’s model was not violence but compassion. Therefore, the proposition fails: **Islam does not encourage violence towards women.**

debates.topic: Islam permits Muslims to eat any beef sold in Christian countries

steps.opening_for:
## Opening argument for the proposition

Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us is that **Islam permits Muslims to eat beef sold in Christian countries**. I affirm that proposition because the Qur’an, the Sunnah, and the practice of classical jurists establish a clear rule: **the food—especially the slaughtered meat—of the People of the Book is lawful for Muslims, and Muslims are not required to investigate hidden details of slaughter in order to eat it.**

The starting point is the Qur’an itself. Allah says:

> “This day all good things have been made lawful for you. **The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them**.”  
> —Qur’an 5:5

Classical Muslim exegetes understood “their food” here to include their slaughtered animals. Ibn ʿAbbās, the great Companion and Qur’anic commentator, explained the phrase “the food of those given the Scripture” as meaning **“their slaughtered animals.”** This is cited by al-Bukhārī in his chapter on the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book.

That verse is decisive. It was revealed while Christians already held doctrines the Qur’an criticizes elsewhere, such as the Trinity and the divinity of Christ. Yet Allah still permitted their food. So the permission is not conditional on Christians having perfect theology, nor on their slaughter being identical to Muslim dhabīḥah. If Allah intended Muslims to eat only meat slaughtered by Muslims, Qur’an 5:5 would have no practical meaning.

The Sunnah confirms this practical understanding. The Prophet ﷺ ate meat prepared by Jews, who are also People of the Book. At Khaybar, a Jewish woman offered him a roasted sheep, and he ate from it. The report is found in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. The Prophet ﷺ did not first demand a ritual audit of the slaughter.

Even more directly, ʿĀ’ishah reported that some people said to the Prophet ﷺ:

> “Some people bring us meat, and we do not know whether they mentioned the name of Allah over it or not.”  
> The Prophet ﷺ replied:  
> **“Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat.”**  
> —Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 5507

This hadith establishes an important legal principle: **ordinary Muslims are not required to investigate uncertain or hidden matters before eating meat that comes to them as lawful food.** If the meat is presented as beef, and it comes from a society whose food is covered by the Qur’anic permission for the People of the Book, the Muslim may eat it unless there is specific knowledge that it is forbidden.

Classical jurists stated this broadly. Ibn Qudāmah wrote in *al-Mughnī* that the scholars agreed on the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book. Ibn Rushd likewise notes in *Bidāyat al-Mujtahid* that the basic permissibility of their slaughter is grounded in Qur’an 5:5.

Therefore, the argument is simple:

1. **Beef is a lawful animal in Islam.**
2. **The Qur’an explicitly permits the food of Christians and Jews.**
3. **The Sunnah shows the Prophet ﷺ ate such meat without investigating its slaughter.**
4. **Doubt alone does not overturn a revealed permission.**
5. Therefore, beef sold in Christian countries is permissible for Muslims to eat, unless one has definite knowledge that a particular item is carrion, pork, blood, or dedicated to another deity.

This position is not a relaxation of Islam; it is fidelity to the Qur’an. To forbid ordinary beef in Christian countries without clear proof is to make unlawful what Allah expressly made lawful.

## Key citations

- Qur’an 5:5 — “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you.”
- Qur’an 5:3 — Lists specifically forbidden meats: carrion, blood, pork, and what is dedicated to other than Allah.
- Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 5507 — “Mention the name of Allah over it and eat.”
- Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 2617; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, no. 2190 — The Prophet ﷺ ate from a sheep prepared by a Jewish woman at Khaybar.
- Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, *Kitāb al-Dhabā’iḥ wa’l-Ṣayd*, chapter on the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book — Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation that “their food” means “their slaughtered animals.”
- Ibn Qudāmah, *al-Mughnī*, Book of Slaughter — Reports scholarly agreement on the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book.
- Ibn Rushd, *Bidāyat al-Mujtahid*, Book of Foods/Slaughter — Discusses the permissibility of the slaughter of the People of the Book based on Qur’an 5:5.
steps.opening_against:
Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us is not that *some* beef in Christian countries may be halal. That would be a serious discussion. The proposition is much stronger: that Islam permits Muslims to eat **any** beef sold in Christian countries. That claim is religiously indefensible.

Islam does not make meat halal by geography. It makes meat halal by **the animal**, **the slaughterer**, and **the method of slaughter**. The Qur’an certainly says: “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you” — referring, according to classical tafsir, to the slaughtered animals of Jews and Christians. But that verse is not a blank cheque. The same Qur’an also forbids carrion, blood, animals killed by strangling or beating, and animals dedicated to other than Allah.

Allah says:

> “Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which any name other than Allah has been invoked, and animals killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a fall, by goring…”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

And:

> “Do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned.”  
> **Qur’an 6:121**

And:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you…”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

These verses must be read together. Verse 5:5 permits the lawful slaughter of the People of the Book; it does not legalize every dead cow sold under a supermarket label in a historically Christian country.

The Prophet ﷺ also tied permissibility to proper slaughter. He said:

> “Whatever causes the blood to flow and Allah’s name is mentioned over it, eat from it…”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 2488; Sahih Muslim 1968**

So if an animal dies before slaughter by stunning, strangulation, a blow, or another prohibited method, it is not halal beef simply because it is sold in London, Paris, Toronto, or Texas. If the slaughterer is not Muslim, Jewish, or Christian, the Qur’anic concession for Ahl al-Kitab does not apply. If the meat is dedicated to other than Allah, it is expressly forbidden. If the process is unknown and industrialized, one cannot turn uncertainty into a universal rule that “any beef” is permissible.

Classical scholars also understood the verse about the People of the Book as conditional, not absolute. Ibn Kathir explains under Qur’an 5:5 that “their food” refers to their slaughtered animals, because ordinary foods like grains and fruits were already permissible. The issue is slaughter. Likewise, jurists such as Ibn Qudamah in *al-Mughni* discuss the permissibility of meat from Jews and Christians in the context of proper slaughter, not as permission to eat carrion or improperly killed animals.

Even the hadith sometimes cited for leniency does not prove the proposition. Aisha رضي الله عنها reported that some people said to the Prophet ﷺ: “People bring us meat and we do not know whether they mentioned Allah’s name over it.” He replied:

> “Mention Allah’s name over it yourselves and eat.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5507**

But this was about uncertainty regarding meat brought by people associated with Islam; it was not permission to eat meat known to be carrion, improperly slaughtered, or produced by a non-qualifying slaughterer.

Therefore, the correct Islamic position is balanced: Muslims may eat beef in Christian countries **when it meets the requirements of halal slaughter**, including the valid slaughterer and method. But Islam does **not** permit Muslims to eat **any** beef sold there. The proposition replaces divine law with supermarket geography, and that is not a sound Islamic argument.
steps.response_for:
## Rebuttal for the proposition

My opponent’s argument depends on changing the proposition into a caricature. No serious Muslim says that **known carrion**, **pork mislabeled as beef**, or an animal **explicitly sacrificed to another deity** becomes halal because it is sold in a Western supermarket. The real question is this:

> When ordinary beef is sold in a Christian / People-of-the-Book country, must a Muslim investigate the slaughterer, the method, the words said at slaughter, and the plant procedure before eating it?

The answer from the Qur’an, Sunnah, and juristic practice is: **No. It is permitted unless one has definite knowledge of a specific prohibition.**

---

## 1. Qur’an 5:5 is a real legal permission, not an empty slogan

Allah says:

> “This day all good things have been made lawful for you. **The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you**, and your food is lawful for them.”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

The classical explanation is that “their food” means their slaughtered animals. Al-Bukhārī records from Ibn ʿAbbās:

> “The food of the People of the Book means **their slaughtered animals**.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Kitāb al-Dhabā’iḥ wa’l-Ṣayd, chapter on the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book**

This verse was revealed in the same sūrah that lists the forbidden meats in Qur’an 5:3. So Allah first mentions forbidden categories, then explicitly permits the food of Jews and Christians. That means 5:5 is not cancelled by 5:3; rather, they are read together:

- carrion, blood, pork, and sacrifices to other than Allah are forbidden;
- but the slaughtered food of the People of the Book is lawful.

If every Christian slaughter had to be inspected to verify that it resembled Muslim slaughter in every detail, Qur’an 5:5 would lose its practical meaning.

---

## 2. Doubt does not make lawful meat unlawful

My opponent repeatedly says: “What if the animal died before slaughter? What if the slaughterer was not Christian? What if the method was wrong?”

But Islamic law distinguishes between **knowledge** and **speculation**. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about meat whose slaughter details were unknown:

> ʿĀ’ishah reported that people said:  
> “Some people bring us meat, and we do not know whether they mentioned Allah’s name over it or not.”  
> The Prophet ﷺ replied:  
> **“Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat.”**  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 5507**

This hadith establishes a principle: when meat comes from people whose slaughter is legally acceptable, Muslims are not required to investigate hidden details.

Even if the immediate case involved people recently connected to Islam, the legal principle is broader: **where the source is a lawful source, uncertainty about unseen slaughter details is not enough to prohibit the meat.** The People of the Book are explicitly a lawful source by Qur’an 5:5.

---

## 3. The Prophet ﷺ ate meat from the People of the Book without investigation

At Khaybar, a Jewish woman offered the Prophet ﷺ a roasted sheep, and he ate from it.

> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 2617; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, no. 2190**

The Prophet ﷺ did not ask:

- Who exactly slaughtered it?
- Was the name of Allah mentioned?
- Was the slaughterer personally observant?
- Was the method identical to Muslim practice?

The relevance is obvious: if the meat comes as food from the People of the Book, the Muslim may eat unless a specific prohibiting fact is known.

---

## 4. Qur’an 6:121 does not erase Qur’an 5:5

My opponent cites:

> “Do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned…”  
> **Qur’an 6:121**

But classical jurists did not understand this as cancelling the permission of the People of the Book. Otherwise Qur’an 5:5 would become meaningless.

The People of the Book did not generally perform slaughter exactly like Muslims, and Allah knew that when He revealed 5:5. Yet He still said their food is lawful.

Many jurists therefore held that the slaughter of Jews and Christians is lawful even if we do not know whether they mentioned Allah’s name. Ibn Qudāmah writes:

> “The scholars are in agreement in general regarding the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book, because Allah says: ‘The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you.’”  
> **Ibn Qudāmah, al-Mughnī, Book of Slaughter**

Ibn Rushd likewise states that the permissibility of their slaughter is founded on Qur’an 5:5.

> **Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Book of Foods / Slaughter**

So 6:121 cannot be used to create a duty of investigation that the Prophet ﷺ himself did not impose.

---

## 5. Modern “industrial slaughter” does not automatically equal carrion

My opponent says that if an animal dies from stunning, strangulation, or a blow, it is forbidden. In principle, yes: if one knows the animal died before slaughter, then it would fall under Qur’an 5:3.

But that does not prove that ordinary supermarket beef is haram. Stunning is not automatically death. In many slaughter systems the animal is stunned, then killed by cutting and bleeding while still alive. Even stricter scholars who object to some stunning methods usually distinguish between:

- an animal killed before slaughter — prohibited;
- an animal stunned but alive at slaughter — a separate juristic question.

The burden of proof is on the one declaring the meat haram. Suspicion about industrial processes does not override the Qur’anic permission of the food of the People of the Book.

---

## 6. The religion of the individual factory worker is not something Muslims are commanded to audit

My opponent also argues: “What if the slaughterer is not Christian?”

Again, this turns Islam into an impossible bureaucracy. Qur’an 5:5 speaks of the food of the People of the Book as a social and legal category. It does not require every Muslim consumer to trace the personal creed of every slaughterhouse employee.

If meat is sold as ordinary beef in a Christian / People-of-the-Book society, it falls under the apparent category of their food unless one has specific knowledge otherwise. This is exactly the kind of uncertainty the hadith of ʿĀ’ishah addresses: do not investigate hidden matters; say bismillah and eat.

---

## 7. The opponent’s rule effectively forbids what Allah permitted

The opponent says: “Muslims may eat beef in Christian countries only when it meets halal slaughter requirements.”

But if by “halal slaughter requirements” he means Muslim dhabīḥah rules in full, then he has effectively erased Qur’an 5:5. The whole point of the verse is that Jews and Christians have a distinct legal permission. Their slaughter is not treated as Muslim slaughter, yet Allah made it lawful.

The correct rule is:

1. Beef is a lawful animal.
2. The food/slaughter of the People of the Book is lawful by Qur’an 5:5.
3. Muslims are not required to investigate unknown slaughter details.
4. Therefore, beef sold as ordinary beef in Christian countries is permissible.
5. It becomes impermissible only with definite knowledge of a specific forbidden factor, such as carrion, pork contamination, or dedication to another deity.

That is not “supermarket geography.” It is the Qur’anic concession for the People of the Book applied in real life.

---

## Conclusion

The opponent’s case proves only that **known haram meat is haram**. We agree. But it does not prove that Muslims must treat ordinary beef in Christian countries as forbidden until audited.

The Qur’an says:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you.”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

The Prophet ﷺ ate meat from the People of the Book. He also instructed Muslims, when uncertain about slaughter details, to say Allah’s name and eat.

Therefore, Islam permits Muslims to eat beef sold in Christian countries unless they have definite knowledge that a particular item falls into a prohibited category. Doubt, speculation, and modern anxiety do not overturn a clear Qur’anic permission.
steps.response_against:
## Rebuttal: The proposition still fails

My opponent has wisely retreated from the literal proposition. The motion says:

> “Islam permits Muslims to eat **any beef sold in Christian countries**.”

But my opponent now says: “ordinary beef is permitted **unless** one knows a specific prohibition.” That is already a major qualification. If there are real categories of beef sold in Christian countries that are not halal — carrion, animals killed before slaughter, meat slaughtered by non-eligible slaughterers, meat dedicated to other than Allah — then the word **“any”** is false.

The Islamic rule is not “Christian-country beef is halal.” The rule is: **the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book are lawful when they are actually slaughtered by eligible people and do not fall into Qur’anic prohibitions.**

---

## 1. Qur’an 5:5 permits Ahl al-Kitab slaughter — not every meat product in their lands

Allah says:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you…”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

Yes, classical tafsir explains “their food” here as their slaughtered animals. Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنهما said:

> “Their food means their slaughtered animals.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Kitāb al-Dhabā’iḥ**

But that actually hurts the proposition. The verse is about **their slaughtered animals** — not meat merely sold in a country with Christian history, not beef processed by anyone of any religion, and not animals killed by any industrial method.

The same sūrah says:

> “Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which any name other than Allah has been invoked, and animals killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a fall, by goring… except what you slaughter…”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

So Qur’an 5:5 cannot mean: “Any beef in a Christian country is lawful regardless of how it died.” It means: lawful animals slaughtered by Jews or Christians are permissible, while the prohibitions of 5:3 remain in force.

---

## 2. “Do not investigate” is not an absolute Islamic principle

My opponent uses the hadith of ʿĀ’ishah رضي الله عنها:

> Some people said: “People bring us meat and we do not know whether they mentioned Allah’s name over it.” The Prophet ﷺ said:  
> “Mention Allah’s name over it yourselves and eat.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5507**

But the narration itself states that those people were **new Muslims** — “حديثو عهد بالكفر” — recently converted from disbelief. So the meat was coming from people under the apparent legal category of Muslims. The question was not: “Was the animal strangled?” or “Was the slaughterer Hindu, atheist, or unknown?” or “Was the animal already dead before cutting?” The question was specifically about whether the tasmiyah had been said.

That hadith cannot be expanded into a blanket permission to eat all industrial beef in all Christian countries.

In fact, other authentic hadiths show the opposite: when the cause of death is uncertain between a lawful and unlawful cause, one may not eat.

ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim رضي الله عنه reported that the Prophet ﷺ said regarding hunting:

> “If you send your dog and mention Allah’s name, then eat. But if you find with it another dog, do not eat, for you mentioned Allah’s name over your dog and not over the other.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**

And he ﷺ said regarding hunted game:

> “If you find it drowned in water, do not eat, for you do not know whether the water killed it or your arrow.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**

These narrations are extremely relevant. They prove that uncertainty about the **cause of death** is not dismissed by simply saying “bismillah and eat.” If there is a serious possibility that the animal died through an unlawful cause — drowning, another dog, strangulation, stunning before slaughter, violent blow — then the permissibility is not automatically established.

---

## 3. The slaughterer matters; the country does not slaughter the cow

Qur’an 5:5 speaks about the food of **the People of the Book**. It does not say “the food of countries that are culturally Christian,” nor “the food of corporations registered in the West.”

A modern slaughterhouse in a “Christian country” may employ Christians, atheists, Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Muslims, Jews, or people of no religion. The legal status of the slaughterer is not determined by the flag over the factory.

Classical jurists discussed the permissibility of meat from Jews and Christians because the slaughterer’s religious eligibility mattered.

Ibn Qudāmah wrote:

> “The scholars are agreed in general regarding the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book…”  
> **Ibn Qudāmah, al-Mughnī, Kitāb al-Dhabā’iḥ**

But this is precisely about **their slaughtered animals** — not animals slaughtered by anyone in their lands. Ibn Qudāmah also discusses that if a slaughtered animal is known to have been dedicated to other than Allah, it is not lawful.

Likewise, Ibn Rushd says the permissibility is based on Qur’an 5:5, but he treats it under the chapter of slaughter, meaning the question is the legal validity of the slaughter, not geography.

> **Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Kitāb al-Aṭʿimah / al-Dhabā’iḥ**

So the proposition “any beef sold in Christian countries” erases the actual juristic category: **valid slaughter by an eligible slaughterer**.

---

## 4. The method of killing remains essential

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “Whatever causes the blood to flow and Allah’s name is mentioned over it, eat…”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2488; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1968**

This shows that slaughter is not merely a label. The animal must be killed by a valid slaughtering act, not by a prohibited cause.

Allah specifically forbids animals killed by:

- strangling,
- a violent blow,
- a fall,
- goring,
- carrion/death before slaughter.

> **Qur’an 5:3**

Therefore, if a cow is killed by stunning, captive bolt, gas, electrocution, or another method before the valid cut, it is not halal merely because the package says “beef” and the country has churches.

Even contemporary fiqh bodies that allow some forms of stunning do so only conditionally. The International Islamic Fiqh Academy allowed stunning only where the animal remains alive and then dies by proper slaughter; if it dies from stunning before slaughter, it is not lawful.

> **International Islamic Fiqh Academy, Resolution on slaughter and stunning, Resolution no. 95 (3/10)**

That alone refutes “any beef.”

---

## 5. Khaybar does not prove supermarket permissibility

My opponent cites the incident in which the Prophet ﷺ ate from a roasted sheep given by a Jewish woman at Khaybar.

> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2617; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2190**

But this proves only that meat prepared by Jews may be eaten without interrogating every detail when it comes from an identifiable People-of-the-Book source. It does not prove that meat sold in a secular industrial market, slaughtered by unknown workers using unknown or potentially impermissible methods, is automatically halal.

At Khaybar, the food was directly from a Jewish person in a Jewish community. That is very different from a modern supply chain where the slaughterer may not be Jewish or Christian at all, and the animal may not have been slaughtered in a Qur’anically valid way.

---

## 6. Qur’an 6:121 cannot be ignored

Allah says:

> “Do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned…”  
> **Qur’an 6:121**

Scholars differed over the details of tasmiyah, especially regarding forgetfulness or the slaughter of Ahl al-Kitab. But no mainstream position says Qur’an 5:5 permits carrion, animals beaten to death, or slaughter by non-eligible slaughterers.

The verses must be harmonized:

- Qur’an 5:5 permits the slaughtered animals of Jews and Christians.
- Qur’an 5:3 forbids carrion and animals killed by invalid causes.
- Qur’an 6:121 emphasizes that slaughter is a religious act, not merely meat production.

So the permission is real, but it is not unlimited.

---

## 7. The opponent’s standard is too broad

My opponent says:

> “Beef sold as ordinary beef in Christian countries is permissible unless definite knowledge of prohibition exists.”

But this smuggles in a false presumption: that ordinary beef in a Christian country is presumptively the slaughter of the People of the Book by a valid method.

That may have been more plausible in a society where butchers were actually Jews or Christians and slaughter was done manually. It is far less obvious in modern secular, religiously mixed, industrial supply chains.

At minimum, one cannot say **“any beef”** is permissible.

A more defensible position would be:

> If the beef is from a lawful animal, slaughtered by a Muslim, Jew, or Christian, by a valid slaughtering method, and not dedicated to other than Allah, then it is halal. If those conditions are not met, or if one knows the process violates them, it is not halal.

That is the balanced Islamic position. But it is not the proposition.

---

## Conclusion

The Qur’an permits the food of the People of the Book:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you.”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

But this means their validly slaughtered animals, not every piece of beef sold in a country called Christian.

Islamic law still requires that:

1. the animal itself be lawful;
2. it not be carrion;
3. it not be killed by strangling, beating, or another prohibited cause;
4. the slaughterer be legally eligible;
5. it not be dedicated to other than Allah.

The opponent has proven only that some beef from Jews and Christians may be eaten without obsessive investigation. He has not proven that Islam permits Muslims to eat **any beef sold in Christian countries**.

Therefore, the proposition remains false.
steps.conclusion_for:
## Concluding statement for the proposition

Ladies and gentlemen, the issue in this debate is not whether known carrion, pork, blood, or meat explicitly sacrificed to another deity is halal. Islam clearly forbids those things. The real issue is whether a Muslim, seeing ordinary beef sold in a Christian or People-of-the-Book country, must investigate the slaughterhouse, the religion of the worker, the exact method, and the words said at slaughter before eating.

My position has been clear: **Islam permits such beef unless there is definite knowledge of a specific prohibition.**

The foundation is the Qur’an:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them.”  
> — Qur’an 5:5

Classical authorities explained that “their food” means their slaughtered animals. Ibn ʿAbbās said this explicitly, and jurists such as Ibn Qudāmah and Ibn Rushd recognized the general permissibility of the slaughter of Jews and Christians.

This Qur’anic permission would be meaningless if Muslims were still required to treat every piece of Christian meat as suspect until proven halal by Muslim standards. Allah revealed Qur’an 5:5 while fully knowing the beliefs and practices of the People of the Book. Yet He still permitted their food.

The Sunnah confirms this practical approach. The Prophet ﷺ ate from meat prepared by a Jewish woman at Khaybar without first conducting an investigation into the slaughter. And when people asked him about meat whose slaughter details were unknown, he said:

> “Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat.”  
> — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5507

That hadith establishes the principle that uncertainty about hidden slaughter details does not by itself make meat forbidden.

My opponent’s argument repeatedly relies on hypotheticals: what if the animal died before slaughter, what if the slaughterer was not Christian, what if the method was invalid? But Islamic law does not operate by turning every possibility into prohibition. **Certainty is not removed by doubt**, and a clear Qur’anic permission is not cancelled by speculation.

Yes, if a Muslim knows that a particular animal was carrion, killed before slaughter, dedicated to another deity, or otherwise falls into a forbidden category, then it is haram. But absent such knowledge, ordinary beef sold as beef in Christian lands falls under the Qur’anic permission of the food of the People of the Book.

So the proposition stands:

1. Beef is a lawful animal.
2. The Qur’an permits the food and slaughtered animals of the People of the Book.
3. The Prophet ﷺ did not require Muslims to investigate hidden slaughter details.
4. Doubt and suspicion do not overturn a revealed allowance.
5. Therefore, Islam permits Muslims to eat beef sold in Christian countries unless there is definite knowledge that a specific item is forbidden.

To forbid ordinary beef in Christian countries as a general rule is not caution; it is to restrict what Allah expressly allowed. The safer religious position is not to invent prohibitions, but to follow the text:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you.”

For these reasons, I affirm the proposition.
steps.conclusion_against:
## Concluding Statement Against the Proposition

The proposition says:

> **“Islam permits Muslims to eat any beef sold in Christian countries.”**

That claim is too broad, and it cannot be defended from the Qur’an, Sunnah, or classical fiqh.

Islam does not make meat halal merely because it is sold in a country with a Christian background. The relevant Islamic questions are not geographical; they are legal and religious:

1. **What animal is it?**  
2. **How did it die?**  
3. **Who slaughtered it?**  
4. **Was it valid slaughter or carrion?**  
5. **Was it dedicated to other than Allah?**

The Qur’an is clear:

> “Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which any name other than Allah has been invoked, and animals killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a fall, by goring…”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

And the Qur’an also says:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you…”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

These verses must be read together. Qur’an 5:5 gives a real concession regarding the slaughtered animals of Jews and Christians. But it does not cancel Qur’an 5:3. It does not make carrion halal. It does not make animals killed by invalid methods halal. It does not make slaughter by any person of any religion halal. And it does not make every supermarket beef product automatically permissible.

My opponent’s strongest argument is that Muslims are not required to investigate every hidden detail when meat comes from a lawful source. In principle, that is true. But it does not prove the proposition. The hadith of ʿĀ’ishah رضي الله عنها — “Mention Allah’s name over it yourselves and eat” — concerned uncertainty about tasmiyah from people apparently within a lawful category. It was not a blanket permission to eat meat known or reasonably established to have been killed by prohibited means, or slaughtered by an ineligible slaughterer.

Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ eating from the food of Jews at Khaybar proves that the food of the People of the Book may be lawful. It does not prove that every piece of beef in a modern secular industrial supply chain is automatically halal simply because the country contains Christians.

The core problem is the word **“any.”** If even one category of beef sold in Christian countries is not halal — beef from an animal that died before slaughter, beef killed by a prohibited method, beef slaughtered by someone outside the eligible categories, or beef dedicated to other than Allah — then the proposition is false.

And Islamic law clearly recognizes such categories.

The correct position is balanced:

- Muslims may eat beef slaughtered by Muslims, Jews, or Christians when the animal is lawful and the slaughter is valid.
- Muslims are not required to engage in obsessive investigation without reason.
- But Islam does not permit **any and all** beef merely because it is sold in a Christian country.

The permission of Qur’an 5:5 is not “supermarket geography.” It is a permission for the valid food of the People of the Book, within the limits set by the rest of the Qur’an and Sunnah.

Therefore, the proposition as stated is false. Islam permits some beef in Christian countries, under proper conditions. It does not permit Muslims to eat **any beef** sold there.

debates.topic: Islam permits Muslims to take mortgages with interest

steps.opening_for:
Ladies and gentlemen, my position is not that Islam treats interest lightly, nor that Muslims should prefer interest-based finance when lawful Islamic alternatives are genuinely available. The Qur’an’s condemnation of *riba* is serious and foundational. My argument is more precise: **Islamic law can permit a Muslim to take an interest-based mortgage in cases of genuine need—especially for a primary residence where no viable Sharia-compliant alternative exists—because the Sharia contains recognized principles of necessity, hardship removal, and public need.**

### Opening argument

Islamic law is not a rigid system that ignores human realities. It is a moral-legal tradition whose objectives include the preservation of religion, life, family, dignity, wealth, and social stability. Housing is not a luxury. A safe and stable home is central to family life, privacy, children’s upbringing, community belonging, and protection from exploitation. In many countries, especially where Muslims are minorities, long-term rental markets can be insecure, expensive, and unstable, while Islamic finance may be unavailable, unaffordable, or merely nominal. In such circumstances, a conventional mortgage may be the only realistic way for a family to secure a modest primary home.

The Qur’an itself establishes that even prohibited matters may become permitted under compulsion or necessity. Allah says:

> “He has explained to you in detail what He has forbidden you, excepting that to which you are compelled.”  
> **Qur’an 6:119**

And regarding prohibited foods, the Qur’an states:

> “But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him.”  
> **Qur’an 2:173; see also 5:3**

This is not a loophole; it is a core principle of Islamic jurisprudence. The classical legal maxims derived from the Qur’an and Sunnah include:

> **“Necessities permit prohibited matters”** — *al-darūrāt tubīḥ al-maḥẓūrāt*  
> **“Hardship brings facilitation”** — *al-mashaqqah tajlib al-taysīr*  
> **“Need, whether public or private, may be treated like necessity”** — *al-ḥājah tanzil manzilat al-ḍarūrah*

These maxims are discussed in standard works of Islamic legal theory, including al-Suyūṭī’s *al-Ashbāh wa’l-Naẓāʾir* and Ibn Nujaym’s *al-Ashbāh wa’l-Naẓāʾir*. They are not modern inventions; they are part of the inherited juristic toolkit.

The Qur’an repeatedly emphasizes that Allah does not intend unbearable hardship:

> “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 2:185**

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

> “Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.”  
> **Qur’an 2:286**

The Prophet ﷺ likewise said:

> “When I command you to do something, do of it as much as you are able.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7288; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1337**

And the well-known legal principle from the Sunnah states:

> “There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm.”  
> **Sunan Ibn Mājah 2340; al-Muwaṭṭaʾ of Mālik**

So the question is not: “Is *riba* normally prohibited?” Yes, it is. The question is: **Can an otherwise prohibited contract become permitted when the alternative is serious hardship and no reasonable lawful alternative exists?** Islamic law answers: yes, under conditions.

This is why a number of contemporary juristic bodies and scholars have permitted conventional mortgages for Muslims in non-Muslim-majority countries when needed for a primary residence. The **European Council for Fatwa and Research**, in its 1999 resolution on purchasing homes through conventional mortgages, allowed Muslims in the West to use such mortgages where necessary to obtain a family home and where no viable Islamic alternative is available. The Council relied on the principles of necessity, need, and removal of hardship. This view was also supported by scholars such as **Shaykh Yusuf al-Qaradawi**, who argued that the need for stable housing in Western contexts can rise to the level that permits an exception.

Similarly, some North American fatwa discussions have recognized that while interest-based mortgages are normally forbidden, exceptions may apply in cases of necessity or pressing need, particularly for a primary residence and not for investment or luxury. Even more restrictive bodies often concede the general legal rule that necessity can create an exception.

Therefore, the proposition is defensible: **Islam can permit Muslims to take mortgages with interest—not as a general indulgence, not for speculation, not for luxury homes, but as a conditional concession for real housing need when no practical halal alternative exists.**

The conditions matter. Such permission should generally be limited to:

1. A primary residence, not investment property.  
2. Genuine need, not convenience or luxury.  
3. Absence of a viable Sharia-compliant alternative.  
4. A mortgage within one’s means, avoiding excessive debt.  
5. Intention to minimize the interest burden where possible.

In conclusion, Islam’s prohibition of *riba* is real, but so is Islam’s mercy, flexibility, and concern for human welfare. A family seeking shelter, stability, and dignity is not the same as a financier exploiting the needy. Under the established principles of necessity and hardship removal, Islam can permit an interest-based mortgage in genuine cases of need.

### Key citations

- Qur’an 2:173 — necessity exception for prohibited matters.  
- Qur’an 5:3 — necessity exception.  
- Qur’an 6:119 — forbidden matters except under compulsion.  
- Qur’an 2:185 — Allah intends ease, not hardship.  
- Qur’an 22:78 — no undue hardship in religion.  
- Qur’an 2:286 — no soul burdened beyond capacity.  
- Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7288; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1337 — obey commands as much as able.  
- Sunan Ibn Mājah 2340; Mālik’s *al-Muwaṭṭaʾ* — “no harm and no reciprocating harm.”  
- Al-Suyūṭī, *al-Ashbāh wa’l-Naẓāʾir* — legal maxims: necessity permits prohibitions; hardship brings ease.  
- Ibn Nujaym, *al-Ashbāh wa’l-Naẓāʾir* — same juristic maxims.  
- European Council for Fatwa and Research, Resolution on purchasing houses through conventional mortgages, 4th Ordinary Session, Dublin, 1999.  
- Yusuf al-Qaradawi, fatwas and discussions supporting the ECFR position on home mortgages for Muslims in the West under need/necessity.
steps.opening_against:
Honourable judges, respected opponents, and audience:

The proposition before us is not “Do Muslims need housing?” nor “Should Muslims seek stability for their families?” Of course they should. The question is narrower and more serious: **Does Islam permit Muslims to take mortgages with interest?** My position is that it does not.

A conventional mortgage is, in substance, a loan in which the borrower repays the principal plus a stipulated increase over time. That stipulated increase is interest. In Islamic law, this is **riba**, and riba is not a marginal issue—it is one of the clearest financial prohibitions in the Qur’an and Sunnah.

Allah says:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

And He commands believers:

> “O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of riba, if you are believers. And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger. But if you repent, you may have your principal—neither wronging nor being wronged.”  
> **Qur’an 2:278–279**

This verse is decisive. It does not say, “You may take moderate interest,” or “Interest is allowed if the rate is affordable,” or “Interest is allowed for housing.” It says: take back your **principal**, and no more. That is precisely what an interest-based mortgage violates.

The Sunnah is equally explicit. Jabir ibn Abdullah reported:

> “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it, and he said: They are all the same.”  
> **Sahih Muslim, 1598**

This matters because some argue, “The bank is the one taking interest, not the Muslim homeowner.” But the hadith explicitly includes **the one who pays riba**. In an interest-based mortgage, the borrower is contractually agreeing to pay interest for decades. That is not a minor technicality; it is the core of the contract.

Classical jurists also treated this as a matter of consensus. Ibn al-Mundhir wrote that scholars agreed that if a lender stipulates an increase over the loan, that increase is riba. Similarly, Ibn Qudamah states:

> “Every loan in which it is stipulated that more be paid back is haram, without disagreement.”  
> **Ibn Qudamah, al-Mughni, Kitab al-Qard**

Modern collective fiqh bodies have reaffirmed the same principle. The International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC declared that bank interest on loans is prohibited riba.  
**International Islamic Fiqh Academy, Resolution No. 10, 1985**

Now, our opponents may say, “But a house is a necessity.” We must be careful here. Islamic law does recognize necessity, but necessity is not the same as convenience, investment, social pressure, or the desire to own rather than rent. If lawful shelter is available through renting, family support, saving, cooperative models, or genuinely Sharia-compliant financing, then the threshold of necessity has not been met. The exception cannot swallow the rule.

They may also say, “But the interest is not exploitative.” Yet the Qur’an did not prohibit only “excessive” riba. Allah says, “You may have your principal.” The excess over principal is the problem. Whether the rate is 3%, 7%, or 15%, the contract remains a loan with a guaranteed stipulated increase.

Islam is not against home ownership. Islam is not against commerce. Islam is not against financial planning. But Islam insists that our means must be lawful. A Muslim may rent, save, enter a genuine partnership, use a properly structured murabahah, ijara, or diminishing musharakah arrangement—provided it is real and not a disguise for interest. But a conventional interest-bearing mortgage is not made halal because the asset is a house.

So the issue is simple: if Allah has forbidden riba, if the Prophet ﷺ cursed the payer of riba, if jurists have agreed that a stipulated increase on a loan is riba, and if conventional mortgages are built precisely on that stipulated increase, then Islam does not permit Muslims to take interest-based mortgages as a general rule.

For that reason, the proposition must be rejected.
steps.response_for:
Honourable judges and respected opponent,

My opponent has proved something I already accept: **riba is normally forbidden** and a conventional mortgage is normally an interest-bearing loan. But that does **not** defeat the proposition. The proposition is not “riba is generally halal.” It is: **Islam permits Muslims to take mortgages with interest** — and my case is that Islam can permit this **as a limited concession in genuine need**, particularly for a primary residence where no viable halal alternative exists.

So the real question is: **Can a normally prohibited transaction become permitted because of necessity, hardship, or pressing need?** Islamic law’s answer is yes.

---

## 1. The opponent proves the general rule, not the absence of exceptions

The opponent cites:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

And:

> “Give up what remains of riba…”  
> **Qur’an 2:278–279**

And the hadith:

> “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it.”  
> **Sahih Muslim 1598**

These texts establish the **default prohibition**. I do not deny that. But Islamic law is not built only on default rules; it also contains rules for exceptional circumstances.

The Qur’an itself repeatedly says that prohibitions may be relaxed under compulsion or necessity:

> “He has explained to you in detail what He has forbidden you, excepting that to which you are compelled.”  
> **Qur’an 6:119**

> “Whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him.”  
> **Qur’an 2:173**

> “But whoever is forced by severe hunger with no inclination to sin, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

And Allah says:

> “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 2:185**

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

Therefore, citing the prohibition of riba does not answer the legal question. The question is whether **a necessity or pressing need can create a concession**. The juristic answer is yes.

---

## 2. Necessity and hardship are recognized legal principles

Classical Islamic jurisprudence contains well-known legal maxims:

> **الضرورات تبيح المحظورات**  
> “Necessities permit prohibited matters.”

> **المشقة تجلب التيسير**  
> “Hardship brings facilitation.”

> **الحاجة تنزل منزلة الضرورة عامة كانت أو خاصة**  
> “Need may be treated like necessity, whether public or private.”

These maxims are discussed in major works such as:

- al-Suyuti, **al-Ashbah wa’l-Naza’ir**
- Ibn Nujaym, **al-Ashbah wa’l-Naza’ir**
- al-Zarkashi, **al-Manthur fi’l-Qawa’id**
- The Ottoman **Majallah al-Ahkam al-‘Adliyyah**, legal maxims including “Hardship brings ease” and “Need is treated as necessity”

These principles are not modern excuses. They are part of the classical architecture of Islamic law.

The Prophet ﷺ also said:

> “When I command you to do something, do of it as much as you are able.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 7288; Sahih Muslim 1337**

And:

> “There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm.”  
> **Sunan Ibn Majah 2340; al-Muwatta’ of Malik**

So when the opponent says, “The hadith curses the payer of riba,” the response is: yes, under normal voluntary circumstances. But Islamic law has always recognized that legal rulings can change under necessity, compulsion, or serious hardship.

---

## 3. Even severe prohibitions can be relaxed under necessity

The opponent speaks as if riba is too serious ever to admit an exception. But Islamic law allows exceptions even in extremely serious matters.

For example, the Qur’an permits a person under compulsion to utter words of disbelief while faith remains firm in the heart:

> “Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief — except one who is compelled while his heart is secure in faith…”  
> **Qur’an 16:106**

If compulsion can excuse even outward words of kufr, then it is not legally impossible that compulsion, necessity, or pressing need can excuse involvement in an otherwise prohibited financial contract.

Likewise, eating pork and carrion is explicitly forbidden, but the Qur’an permits it under necessity:

> “Whoever is compelled by necessity… there is no sin upon him.”  
> **Qur’an 2:173**

Therefore, the mere seriousness of a prohibition does not prove that no exception can exist.

---

## 4. The Sunnah itself shows exceptions in financial law because of need

Islamic commercial law is strict, but it is not blind to real human needs.

For example, the sale of fresh dates on trees for dried dates is generally problematic because of uncertainty and potential riba-related concerns. Yet the Prophet ﷺ allowed **bay‘ al-‘araya** as a concession for need.

This is reported in:

- **Sahih al-Bukhari**, Kitab al-Buyu‘
- **Sahih Muslim 1540**

Similarly, the Prophet ﷺ allowed **salam** — advance payment for goods delivered later — even though it is an exception to the normal rule against selling what one does not yet possess, because farmers and traders needed it.

Ibn Abbas reported that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah, people used to pay in advance for fruits, so he said:

> “Whoever pays in advance, let him do so for a specified measure, specified weight, and specified time.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 2240; Sahih Muslim 1604**

These examples matter because they show that Islamic financial law includes **structured concessions** when genuine need exists. The concession is not lawlessness; it is regulated mercy.

---

## 5. Housing can be a genuine need, not merely a luxury

My opponent says Muslims can simply rent. Sometimes that is true. If safe, stable, affordable rental housing is realistically available, and if halal financing is genuinely available, then the concession may not apply.

But in many places, especially for Muslim minorities, the situation is not so simple. Renting may involve:

- repeated eviction or instability;
- unaffordable rent increases;
- inability to house a large family properly;
- insecurity for children’s schooling;
- lack of privacy or religious accommodation;
- dependence on exploitative landlords;
- inability to remain near mosque, work, or community;
- severe long-term financial harm, especially in old age.

A primary home is not like buying a luxury car or an investment property. Housing relates directly to family stability, dignity, privacy, and protection from harm. These are recognized interests of the Sharia.

The Sharia’s objectives include preservation of life, family, wealth, dignity, and religion. Stable housing can serve all of these.

---

## 6. Contemporary jurists have recognized this concession

This is not merely my personal reasoning. A number of contemporary scholars and juristic bodies have permitted conventional mortgages in restricted circumstances.

The **European Council for Fatwa and Research**, in its 1999 Dublin resolution on purchasing homes through conventional mortgages, permitted Muslims in the West to use conventional mortgages where there is genuine need, no viable Islamic alternative, and the purchase is for a primary residence.

The Council relied on principles including:

- necessity;
- general need treated as necessity;
- removal of hardship;
- protection of Muslim family life in minority contexts.

Shaykh **Yusuf al-Qaradawi** also supported this position, arguing that the need for a stable family home in Western societies can rise to the level of a legally recognized need, especially where Islamic alternatives are absent or impractical.

Even many scholars who are stricter on the issue still acknowledge the underlying legal principle: **necessity can permit what is otherwise prohibited**, though they may disagree over whether a specific case reaches that threshold.

That means the opponent’s absolute claim — “Islam does not permit this” — is too broad. The more accurate position is: **interest-based mortgages are normally prohibited, but may be permitted in genuine necessity or pressing need under strict conditions.**

---

## 7. The concession is limited and does not swallow the rule

I am not arguing that Muslims may casually take interest-bearing mortgages. The permission is conditional.

It should be limited to cases where:

1. The property is a **primary residence**, not an investment or holiday home.  
2. The family has a **genuine need**, not mere preference or luxury.  
3. Renting is not a reasonable long-term solution in that person’s circumstances.  
4. No viable Sharia-compliant alternative exists.  
5. The home is modest and within one’s means.  
6. The borrower minimizes the interest burden where possible.  
7. The concession is used only to the extent of need, according to the maxim:  
   > **الضرورة تقدر بقدرها**  
   > “Necessity is measured according to its extent.”

This last maxim is important. It prevents abuse. It means necessity does not permit buying a mansion, taking multiple mortgages, or entering debt recklessly.

---

## 8. Direct response to the opponent’s central claim

The opponent says: “Allah says you may have your principal, and no more. Therefore any mortgage interest is haram.”

But those verses address the default rule and the creditor’s entitlement. They do not say that a desperate debtor or a family under serious housing hardship can never receive a legal concession. The Qur’an’s prohibitions must be read alongside the Qur’an’s own principles of necessity, ease, and removal of hardship.

The opponent says: “The hadith curses the payer of riba.”

Again, yes — normally. But the hadith does not discuss a case of genuine necessity. Islamic law does not apply texts in isolation from other established principles such as compulsion, hardship, and necessity.

The opponent says: “Renting means there is no necessity.”

That is too simplistic. Renting may remove necessity in some cases, but not in all. If renting is stable, affordable, and adequate, then the mortgage concession may not apply. But if renting creates serious hardship or insecurity, then a juristic need may exist.

The opponent says: “Interest is still interest, whether 3% or 15%.”

Agreed. My argument is not that low interest becomes halal by being low. My argument is that an otherwise prohibited contract may become temporarily permitted due to need or necessity.

---

## Conclusion

The opponent has defended the general prohibition of riba, but I never denied that. The debate is about whether Islam can permit an interest-based mortgage in exceptional circumstances.

The Qur’an, Sunnah, legal maxims, classical juristic principles, and contemporary fatwas all show that Islamic law recognizes concessions in cases of necessity and serious need.

Therefore, the balanced Islamic position is:

**Interest-based mortgages are normally prohibited, but Islam can permit them for Muslims in genuine need, especially for a modest primary residence where no viable Sharia-compliant alternative exists and where renting or other options cause serious hardship.**

That is why the proposition stands.
steps.response_against:
Honourable judges, respected opponent:

My opponent’s case rests on a true principle applied in the wrong place. Yes, Islamic law recognizes necessity. Yes, hardship can bring facilitation. But it does **not** follow that a Muslim may take a conventional interest-bearing mortgage merely because home ownership is beneficial, financially sensible, or emotionally stabilizing.

The question is not whether necessity exists in Islamic law. The question is whether the ordinary need to buy a primary residence through an interest loan reaches the level that suspends one of the clearest prohibitions in the Qur’an and Sunnah. It does not.

---

## 1. Necessity is an exception, not a new rule

The opponent repeatedly cites the maxim:

> **الضرورات تبيح المحظورات**  
> “Necessities permit prohibited matters.”

But the same juristic tradition immediately limits that maxim:

> **الضرورة تقدر بقدرها**  
> “Necessity is measured according to its extent.”

This is recorded in the classical legal maxims and in the **Majallah al-Ahkam al-‘Adliyyah**, articles 21–22.

So even where necessity exists, it permits only the minimum required to remove the necessity. It does not turn a prohibited contract into a normal financing tool for 20 or 30 years.

The Qur’anic necessity verses themselves contain limits:

> “Whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him.”  
> **Qur’an 2:173**

The words **“neither desiring nor transgressing”** matter. Necessity is not desire. It is not convenience. It is not wealth preservation. It is not the wish to own rather than rent.

A person starving may eat enough prohibited food to survive. That does not mean pork becomes a lawful meal plan. Likewise, if a Muslim were literally facing homelessness with no lawful alternative, that would be an individual emergency question. But that does not prove that Islam permits Muslims generally to enter interest mortgages for home ownership.

---

## 2. Shelter is necessary; ownership is not

My opponent’s strongest emotional point is housing stability. But Islam requires that a person have shelter, privacy, and family protection. It does not require that this shelter be owned through an interest-bearing loan.

There is a crucial distinction between:

- needing **a place to live**, and  
- needing **to own property through riba**.

The first is a legitimate human need. The second does not automatically follow.

If renting is available, even if imperfect, then the claimed necessity normally collapses. Many lawful things in life are inconvenient, costly, or unstable. That does not make the prohibited lawful.

The opponent lists difficulties in renting: rent increases, instability, landlords, schooling, community, old age planning. These may be real hardships, but they are not automatically **darurah**. They are not equivalent to starvation, nakedness, homelessness, or immediate danger.

Classical jurists defined necessity narrowly. Al-Suyuti explains in **al-Ashbah wa’l-Naza’ir** that necessity is when a person reaches a point where, if he does not take the prohibited thing, he will perish or come close to perishing. That is far beyond the normal case of wanting a mortgage to secure long-term ownership.

---

## 3. “Need treated as necessity” cannot override explicit riba texts so broadly

The opponent cites another maxim:

> **الحاجة تنزل منزلة الضرورة عامة كانت أو خاصة**  
> “Need may be treated like necessity, whether public or private.”

But this maxim is not a blank cheque. It does not mean every serious financial difficulty permits riba. If that were true, the prohibition of riba would become practically meaningless, because almost every borrower can claim some need: business need, education need, medical need, debt consolidation, family need, retirement need, and so on.

The Qur’an’s language about riba is unusually severe:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

And:

> “If you do not give up riba, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger.”  
> **Qur’an 2:279**

The Prophet ﷺ did not only curse the one who receives riba. He cursed:

> “The one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it.”  
> **Sahih Muslim, 1598**

So the borrower in a conventional mortgage is directly included in the warning. He is not a passive victim of the bank; he voluntarily signs a contract promising to pay interest.

---

## 4. The opponent’s examples actually weaken his case

My opponent mentions eating pork under necessity, uttering disbelief under compulsion, salam, and bay‘ al-‘araya. But these examples do not prove that conventional mortgages are permitted.

### Pork under necessity

Eating carrion or pork is allowed only when a person is compelled, such as by starvation, and only to the extent necessary.

That supports my position: necessity is narrow and temporary. A 25-year interest mortgage for asset ownership is not comparable to eating enough food to avoid death.

### Uttering kufr under compulsion

The Qur’an says:

> “Except one who is compelled while his heart is secure in faith…”  
> **Qur’an 16:106**

This concerns coercion under threat. Again, this is not comparable to voluntarily entering a mortgage contract because ownership is more stable than renting.

### Salam and ‘araya

Salam and ‘araya were not invented by jurists as broad exceptions to riba. They were specific, textually recognized transactions regulated by the Prophet ﷺ.

Regarding salam, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> “Whoever pays in advance, let him do so for a specified measure, specified weight, and specified time.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 2240; Sahih Muslim 1604**

Regarding ‘araya, the concession was limited and regulated. It was not a general permission to bypass riba rules.

So these examples show that Islamic finance can contain lawful alternatives and structured concessions. They do **not** show that a clearly interest-based loan becomes permissible whenever people feel housing pressure.

---

## 5. Contemporary fatwas are disputed, and major fiqh bodies reject the mortgage concession

My opponent cites the European Council for Fatwa and Research. But that is not consensus, and its view has been strongly disputed.

Major international fiqh bodies have reaffirmed the prohibition of conventional interest-bearing loans.

The **International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC** declared that bank interest on loans is prohibited riba.  
**OIC Islamic Fiqh Academy, Resolution No. 10, 1985**

The **Islamic Fiqh Council of the Muslim World League** also addressed buying homes in non-Muslim countries through interest-based loans and did not accept the broad mortgage concession, emphasizing that the availability of renting prevents the claim of necessity.  
**Muslim World League Islamic Fiqh Council, 18th session, Makkah, 1427 AH / 2006**

Likewise, the long-standing juristic principle remains:

> “Every loan in which it is stipulated that more be paid back is haram, without disagreement.”  
> **Ibn Qudamah, al-Mughni, Kitab al-Qard**

A conventional mortgage is exactly that: a loan with a stipulated increase.

---

## 6. The concession argument risks making riba ordinary

If the opponent’s standard is accepted, then riba becomes permissible for almost every major life need:

- education loans because education is important;
- business loans because livelihood is important;
- car loans because transportation is important;
- credit cards because emergencies occur;
- investment loans because wealth preservation matters.

But the Sharia did not prohibit riba only in unnecessary situations. Riba is usually taken precisely because people have needs. The Qur’an prohibited it despite the fact that people used it for real economic purposes.

Allah says:

> “But if you repent, you may have your principal — neither wronging nor being wronged.”  
> **Qur’an 2:279**

The permitted entitlement is the principal. The stipulated increase is the forbidden element. That is the essence of the mortgage contract.

---

## 7. A real emergency may excuse an individual; it does not prove the proposition

Let us be precise.

If a Muslim family were genuinely facing homelessness, danger, or severe unavoidable harm, with no rental option, no family support, no Islamic financing, no cooperative solution, and no other lawful path, then that would be a specific emergency to present to qualified scholars.

But that is not the proposition. The proposition says:

> “Islam permits Muslims to take mortgages with interest.”

That statement is too broad. Islam does not generally permit interest mortgages. At most, one may discuss rare individual cases of genuine compulsion. But a rare emergency excuse does not transform an interest mortgage into an Islamically permitted financial product.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent has proven that Islamic law contains the concept of necessity. I agree.

But he has not proven that ordinary home ownership through a conventional mortgage qualifies as necessity. Shelter is necessary; ownership through riba is not. Renting, saving, family support, cooperative arrangements, and genuine Sharia-compliant financing remain lawful alternatives.

The Qur’an forbids riba. The Prophet ﷺ cursed the one who pays it. The jurists agreed that a stipulated increase on a loan is riba. Major fiqh bodies have reaffirmed that bank interest is prohibited.

Therefore, the correct ruling remains:

**Conventional interest-bearing mortgages are haram as a general rule. Necessity is a narrow individual exception, not a general permission for Muslims to buy homes through riba.**

For that reason, the proposition must still be rejected.
steps.conclusion_for:
Honourable judges, respected opponent, and audience,

This debate has never been about denying the prohibition of *riba*. I have repeatedly acknowledged that interest is normally forbidden, that the Qur’an strongly condemns *riba*, and that Muslims should seek lawful alternatives wherever they are genuinely available. The real question is narrower: **Can Islam permit an interest-based mortgage in exceptional circumstances of genuine need?** My answer is yes.

My opponent has argued the general rule: that *riba* is prohibited, that the Prophet ﷺ cursed those involved in it, and that a conventional mortgage contains stipulated interest. But proving the general rule does not prove that no exception can ever exist. Islamic law is not only a law of prohibitions; it is also a law of mercy, necessity, hardship removal, and practical human welfare.

The Qur’an itself establishes that prohibited matters may become permitted under compulsion or necessity:

> “Excepting that to which you are compelled.”  
> **Qur’an 6:119**

> “Whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him.”  
> **Qur’an 2:173**

And Allah says:

> “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 2:185**

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

From these texts, jurists derived the well-known legal maxims:

- **Necessities permit prohibited matters.**
- **Hardship brings facilitation.**
- **Need may be treated like necessity.**
- **Necessity is measured according to its extent.**

These are not modern inventions. They are classical principles found in works of Islamic legal theory and applied across many areas of law.

We also saw that the Sunnah itself recognizes financial concessions in cases of need, such as *salam* and *‘araya*. These examples show that Islamic commercial law is principled, but not blind to hardship.

Housing is not a luxury. A secure primary residence protects family life, privacy, dignity, children’s stability, religious practice, and long-term welfare. In many contexts, especially for Muslims living as minorities, renting may be unstable, unaffordable, or seriously harmful, while Islamic finance may be unavailable, excessively costly, or only Islamic in name. In such circumstances, a modest conventional mortgage may become the only realistic path to securing basic family housing.

That is why contemporary juristic bodies such as the **European Council for Fatwa and Research** and scholars such as **Shaykh Yusuf al-Qaradawi** have permitted conventional mortgages in restricted cases: not for investment, not for luxury, not out of convenience, but for a genuine primary housing need where no viable halal alternative exists.

So my position is not careless permissiveness. It is a conditional concession:

1. The home must be a primary residence.  
2. The need must be genuine.  
3. No viable Sharia-compliant alternative should exist.  
4. Renting must not be a reasonable solution in the person’s circumstances.  
5. The home must be modest and within one’s means.  
6. The interest burden should be minimized as far as possible.  
7. The concession must not be expanded beyond the need.

My opponent’s position treats the prohibition as though it operates without the wider framework of Islamic legal mercy. But the Sharia does not work that way. The same Lawgiver who prohibited *riba* also revealed the principles of necessity, ease, and removal of hardship.

Therefore, the balanced conclusion is this:

**Interest-based mortgages are normally prohibited. But Islam can permit them in genuine cases of necessity or pressing need, especially for a modest primary residence where no practical halal alternative exists.**

For that reason, the proposition stands.
steps.conclusion_against:
Honourable judges, respected opponent, and audience:

This debate has not been about whether Muslims need housing, stability, privacy, or dignity. We all agree that they do. The question has been whether Islam permits Muslims to take **conventional mortgages with interest**. My answer remains: **No, not as a general ruling.**

A conventional mortgage is a loan with a stipulated increase. That is the very definition of riba. The Qur’an states plainly:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

And Allah commands believers to give up riba, saying:

> “If you repent, you may have your principal — neither wronging nor being wronged.”  
> **Qur’an 2:279**

The Sunnah is equally explicit. The Prophet ﷺ cursed not only the one who consumes riba, but also:

> “the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it.”  
> **Sahih Muslim 1598**

So the borrower in an interest-based mortgage is not outside the prohibition. He is contractually agreeing to pay riba.

My opponent’s main argument has been necessity. But necessity in Islamic law is a narrow exception, not a broad financial policy. The maxim says, “Necessities permit prohibited matters,” but it also says, “Necessity is measured according to its extent.” It permits only what is required to remove unavoidable harm. It does not turn a 20- or 30-year interest-bearing contract into a normal halal path to property ownership.

The central distinction is this: **shelter is necessary; owning a house through riba is not.** If lawful shelter exists through renting, family support, saving, cooperative arrangements, or genuine Sharia-compliant financing, then the claim of necessity normally fails. Renting may be inconvenient, expensive, or imperfect, but inconvenience is not the same as darurah.

My opponent cited contemporary opinions that allow mortgages in some minority contexts. But those opinions are disputed, not consensus. Major fiqh bodies, including the OIC International Islamic Fiqh Academy and the Muslim World League Islamic Fiqh Council, have reaffirmed the prohibition of bank interest and rejected broad mortgage concessions where alternatives like renting exist.

And this matters because if “need” is expanded too loosely, the prohibition of riba becomes hollow. People could justify interest loans for education, cars, businesses, investments, retirement, or debt consolidation — all on the grounds of hardship or benefit. But riba was prohibited precisely because people use it for real needs. Need alone does not make riba halal.

To be clear: if a person faces a genuine, unavoidable emergency — actual homelessness, danger, severe harm, and no lawful alternative — that is a specific case for qualified scholars. But rare emergency dispensation does not prove the proposition that Islam permits Muslims to take interest mortgages generally.

The Islamic position is therefore balanced but firm:

- Riba is clearly prohibited.
- A conventional mortgage is riba-based.
- The payer of riba is included in the prophetic warning.
- Necessity is narrow and exceptional.
- Home ownership is not itself a necessity when lawful shelter is available.
- Disputed minority fatwas cannot overturn the general rule.

Islam encourages Muslims to seek housing through lawful means: renting, saving, partnerships, cooperative models, or genuinely Sharia-compliant financing. But it does not permit us to achieve a good end through a prohibited contract.

For these reasons, the proposition must be rejected.

debates.topic: Islam permits homosexuality

steps.opening_for:
## Opening argument for the proposition: “Islam permits homosexuality”

The proposition before us is not whether every Muslim jurist in history has approved of same-sex relationships. Many have not. The question is deeper: **does Islam itself—through the Qur’an’s moral principles and its standards for declaring something forbidden—clearly prohibit homosexuality?** I argue that it does not. Properly understood, Islam permits homosexuality: an innate same-sex orientation, and by extension ethical, consensual, faithful same-sex love.

First, in Islam, **only God has the authority to declare something haram**. The Qur’an warns believers not to invent prohibitions in God’s name: “Do not say, falsely, ‘This is lawful and this is forbidden,’ so as to fabricate lies against God” (Qur’an 16:116). It also says that God has “explained in detail what He has forbidden” (Qur’an 6:119). Therefore, if homosexuality is to be declared categorically haram, the burden of proof is high. There must be clear, decisive evidence.

But the Qur’an never condemns “homosexuality” as we understand it today: a stable same-sex orientation or a loving, consensual relationship. The verses usually cited are the story of the people of Lot. Yet those passages are not about mutual love between two adults. They describe a violent, predatory society that humiliates strangers, threatens guests, commits public indecency, and attempts sexual assault. In Qur’an 29:29, Lot condemns his people not only for approaching men, but also for “cutting off the road” and committing evil in their gatherings—language associated with banditry, coercion, and social corruption. In Qur’an 54:37, the people “demanded his guests,” again pointing to attempted assault, not consensual partnership. The sin of Lot’s people is not love; it is domination, violence, inhospitality, and sexual aggression.

Second, the Qur’an’s broader ethical vision supports inclusion rather than exclusion. The Qur’an teaches that human diversity is among God’s signs: “Among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the diversity of your languages and colors” (Qur’an 30:22). It declares that all human beings possess dignity: “We have honored the children of Adam” (Qur’an 17:70). It says the most honored before God are not those who fit a social majority, but those most conscious of God: “The most noble of you in the sight of God is the most righteous of you” (Qur’an 49:13). Nothing in these verses makes heterosexuality a condition of dignity, piety, or belonging.

Third, Islam’s sexual ethic is not based on disgust or stigma; it is based on justice, responsibility, consent, fidelity, and avoidance of harm. The Qur’an condemns zina, exploitation, coercion, adultery, and sexual injustice. A faithful same-sex relationship between consenting adults does not fall under the moral logic of rape, adultery, or exploitation. If the core purposes of Islamic relationship ethics are tranquility, affection, mercy, and moral responsibility—“He placed between you love and mercy” (Qur’an 30:21)—then same-sex couples are capable of embodying those same Islamic values.

Finally, the tradition itself shows that the issue is not as simple as opponents claim. The harsh hadith reports often quoted against same-sex acts are not found in Sahih al-Bukhari or Sahih Muslim, and classical jurists disagreed over their legal force and punishment. That disagreement matters: it shows that the prohibition was not established with the kind of clear, uncontested Qur’anic certainty required to condemn an entire class of people. Modern Muslim scholars such as Scott Siraj al-Haqq Kugle, Kecia Ali, and Junaid Jahangir and Hussein Abdullatif have argued that the Qur’anic evidence does not justify a blanket condemnation of homosexuality and that Islamic ethics can support same-sex unions grounded in justice and compassion.

So the proposition stands: **Islam does not prohibit homosexuality as such. It prohibits coercion, lust without responsibility, exploitation, and injustice. But same-sex love, lived ethically and faithfully, is not condemned by the Qur’an. To declare it haram without decisive evidence is to risk doing exactly what the Qur’an warns against: attributing to God a prohibition God did not clearly make.**

## Relevant citations

- Qur’an 16:116 — warning against falsely declaring things lawful or unlawful in God’s name.  
- Qur’an 6:119 — God has explained what is forbidden.  
- Qur’an 17:70 — human dignity: “We have honored the children of Adam.”  
- Qur’an 30:22 — human diversity as a sign of God.  
- Qur’an 49:13 — moral worth based on righteousness, not identity.  
- Qur’an 30:21 — love, mercy, and tranquility as purposes of intimate partnership.  
- Qur’an 7:80–84; 11:77–83; 15:67–77; 26:160–175; 27:54–58; 29:28–35; 54:33–39 — Qur’anic accounts of Lot’s people.
