> “If any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah. Then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> **Qur’an 9:6**

That is decisive. If Qur’an 9:5 meant “kill all polytheists everywhere simply because they are polytheists,” verse 9:6 would make no sense. The passage is about hostile groups who broke treaties, attacked the Muslim community, and violated peace agreements. Qur’an 9:13 makes this explicit:

> “Would you not fight a people who broke their oaths and determined to expel the Messenger, and they began against you the first time?”  
> **Qur’an 9:13**

So Qur’an 9:5 is not a general license for violence. It is part of a specific wartime context involving treaty-breaking aggression.

## 2. Qur’an 9:29 concerns political conflict, not forced conversion

My opponent also cited Qur’an 9:29, which commands fighting certain People of the Book until they pay jizya. But again, this does not prove that Islam promotes coercion in religion.

First, the Qur’an’s general rule remains:

> “There shall be no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

Second, the Qur’an explicitly permits peaceful relations with non-Muslims who are not fighting Muslims:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.”  
> **Qur’an 60:8**

The next verse clarifies that hostility is directed toward those who engage in aggression:

> “Allah only forbids you from those who fight you because of religion and expel you from your homes and aid in your expulsion…”  
> **Qur’an 60:9**

So the Qur’anic framework is not “fight people because they are different.” It is “do not aggress, but resist aggression and oppression.”

As for jizya, historically it functioned as a tax on non-Muslim subjects in exchange for protection and exemption from military service. One may debate whether that system matches modern liberal equality, but it is not the same as forced conversion. In fact, if Islam’s goal were simply forced conversion, jizya would make no sense; non-Muslims would not have been allowed to remain Jews, Christians, Zoroastrians, and others under Muslim rule.

## 3. Qur’an 8:12 is a battlefield verse, not a doctrine of terrorism

The opponent cited Qur’an 8:12: “I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve.” But this verse refers to the Battle of Badr, a specific military confrontation in which the early Muslim community faced an armed enemy.

It is not a general command to terrorize civilians. The Qur’an elsewhere sets clear limits:

> “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”  
> **Qur’an 2:190**

And:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and trust in Allah.”  
> **Qur’an 8:61**

Islamic law did not understand warfare as unlimited violence. The Prophet Muhammad forbade the killing of noncombatants:

> “Do not kill women and children.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**

He also prohibited treachery and mutilation:

> “Do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, and do not kill children.”  
> **Sahih Muslim 1731**

These are not the teachings of a tradition that glorifies indiscriminate violence.

## 4. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” must be read with the Qur’an and the Prophet’s practice

My opponent cited the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

But this hadith cannot be interpreted as a universal command to force all humanity into Islam, because that would contradict explicit Qur’anic teachings:

> “There shall be no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

> “If your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them entirely. Then would you compel people until they become believers?”  
> **Qur’an 10:99**

> “So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller.”  
> **Qur’an 88:21–22**

The Arabic word used in the hadith is **uqatil**, meaning “to fight,” not “to murder” or “to kill indiscriminately.” It refers to combat against hostile forces, not forced conversion of peaceful civilians.

This is supported by the Prophet’s own conduct. When a man pronounced the testimony of faith during battle and was killed by Usama ibn Zayd, the Prophet strongly condemned it, asking:

> “Did you kill him after he said ‘There is no god but Allah’?”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 4269; Sahih Muslim 96**

That shows that even in war, the Prophet rejected violence once the person ceased hostility and claimed peace.

## 5. Apostasy law is debated and cannot override the Qur’an’s broader principle of religious accountability before God

The opponent cited:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3017**

This is one of the most debated legal texts in Islamic law. Classical jurists often treated apostasy as a capital crime, but many scholars—classical and modern—have connected the punishment to political treason and rebellion, not mere private belief. Another hadith describes the punishable case as one who leaves religion and separates from the community:

> “The one who abandons his religion and separates from the community.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676**

That wording matters because in the Prophet’s context, apostasy was often tied to joining enemy forces, betrayal, or armed rebellion.

More importantly, the Qur’an repeatedly mentions people believing, disbelieving, and even returning to disbelief—yet it does not prescribe a worldly death penalty for mere change of belief:

> “Indeed, those who believed then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, and then increased in disbelief—Allah will not forgive them…”  
> **Qur’an 4:137**

If mere apostasy automatically required execution, this verse’s repeated sequence—belief, disbelief, belief, disbelief—would be impossible in practice.

The Qur’an locates ultimate judgment of belief with God:

> “The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.”  
> **Qur’an 18:29**

So the existence of a contested legal tradition on apostasy does not erase Islam’s broader teaching that faith cannot be coerced.

## 6. Islamic history includes conquest, but history must be distinguished from principle

My opponent points to early Muslim conquests. Yes, Muslim empires expanded militarily. But this does not prove that Islam itself promotes violence any more than European imperialism proves Christianity’s essence is colonialism, or Buddhist nationalist violence proves Buddhism’s essence is violence.

All major civilizations in late antiquity and the medieval world engaged in warfare and empire-building. The fair question is: **What moral constraints did the religion place on power?**

Islamic sources placed significant constraints on war:

- no aggression: **Qur’an 2:190**
- accept peace when offered: **Qur’an 8:61**
- protect noncombatants: **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**
- honor treaties: **Qur’an 9:4; 16:91**
- protect even enemy asylum-seekers: **Qur’an 9:6**
- act justly even toward enemies: **Qur’an 5:8**

The Prophet’s own life also shows preference for reconciliation. The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was a peace treaty that many Muslims initially saw as unfavorable, yet the Qur’an described it as a “clear victory”:

> “Indeed, We have given you a clear victory.”  
> **Qur’an 48:1**

That “victory” was not a massacre; it was a peace agreement.

At the conquest of Mecca, when the Prophet had power over former persecutors, he did not order mass revenge. The traditional biographies record that he granted broad amnesty, saying in effect: “Go, for you are free.” This prophetic model is one of restraint, mercy, and reconciliation after conflict.

## 7. Islam’s central moral vocabulary is peace, mercy, and justice

The Qur’an repeatedly presents peace as the better path:

> “Reconciliation is best.”  
> **Qur’an 4:128**

> “If they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a cause against them.”  
> **Qur’an 4:90**

> “The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth humbly, and when the ignorant address them harshly, they say: peace.”  
> **Qur’an 25:63**

The Prophet defined a Muslim in terms of the safety others experience from him:

> “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40**

He also said:

> “Allah is gentle and loves gentleness.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6927; Sahih Muslim 2593**

And:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant shall not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166**

These are not marginal teachings. They are central to Islamic ethics.

## Conclusion

My opponent is correct that Islam, like Judaism, Christianity, and most serious legal-moral traditions, contains teachings on war. But the existence of wartime rules does not mean Islam does not promote peace. It means Islam is not naïve about human conflict.

The Qur’anic pattern is clear:

- peace is preferred;
- aggression is forbidden;
- treaties must be honored;
- noncombatants must be protected;
- religious compulsion is rejected;
- justice must be upheld even toward enemies;
- mercy is central to the character of God and the mission of the Prophet.

So the proposition stands. Islam does not teach peace as passive surrender to injustice, but as a moral order built on mercy, restraint, justice, and reconciliation. Therefore, **Islam promotes peace**.
steps.response_against:
## Rebuttal against the proposition: “Islam promotes peace”

My opponent’s response is thoughtful, but it depends on redefining the proposition into something much weaker: “Islam contains rules limiting violence” or “Islam sometimes prefers peace.” I do not deny that. My argument is that Islam cannot fairly be described, without qualification, as promoting peace when its authoritative texts and classical legal tradition also promote religiously sanctioned warfare, subordination of non-Muslims, and punishment for apostasy.

A tradition that regulates war is not necessarily a peace-promoting tradition. Empires regulate war too. The key question is whether Islam’s normative sources make peace the overriding principle, or whether peace is often conditional on submission to Islamic authority. The evidence points to the latter.

---

## 1. Context does not remove the militancy of Qur’an 9

My opponent says Qur’an 9:5 is only about treaty-breaking polytheists. Context matters, yes. But context does not make the verse peaceful.

Qur’an 9 is one of the latest and most politically assertive chapters of the Qur’an. It does not merely say, “Defend yourselves if attacked.” It announces the end of certain treaties, commands fighting, and establishes Muslim supremacy over hostile religious communities.

Qur’an 9:5 states:

> “Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush…”  
> **Qur’an 9:5**

Even if one grants that some treaty-keeping groups were exempted, the verse still authorizes aggressive military action after a grace period. The options given are not modern religious liberty; they are repentance, submission, or war.

Then Qur’an 9:29 expands the issue beyond Arabian polytheists:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day… from among those who were given the Scripture until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.”  
> **Qur’an 9:29**

Notice the stated reasons: they “do not believe” correctly and do not follow “the religion of truth.” The endpoint is not merely “until they stop attacking you,” but “until they pay jizya… while humbled.” That is not simply defensive war. It is the political subordination of non-Muslims under Islamic rule.

---

## 2. “No compulsion in religion” does not erase coercive structures

My opponent relies heavily on:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

But this verse does not cancel the coercive elements of the tradition. Classical Islamic law often allowed non-Muslims to retain their religion, but under inferior legal status. That is not full religious freedom; it is tolerated subordination.

Qur’an 9:29 does not say, “Let Jews and Christians live as equal citizens.” It says to fight them until they pay jizya “while humbled.” Historically, this became the basis for the **dhimmi** system, under which Jews, Christians, and some other groups could live under Muslim rule but with special taxes and legal disabilities.

So the issue is not forced conversion alone. A system can avoid forced conversion while still being coercive. If non-Muslims must either accept Islamic political dominance, pay a religiously marked tax, and live in a lower legal status, then Islam cannot straightforwardly be described as promoting peace in the modern moral sense.

Classical legal manuals reflect this. For example, the Shafi‘i manual *Reliance of the Traveller* states that jihad is a communal obligation and describes fighting non-Muslims until they become Muslim or pay jizya. See:

- *Reliance of the Traveller*, o9.0–o9.8, “Jihad”
- Al-Mawardi, *Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya*, chapters on jihad and jizya

Scholars of Islamic law have also recognized that classical jihad doctrine included offensive war. Majid Khadduri wrote that jihad functioned as an instrument for expanding the domain of Islamic rule. Rudolph Peters likewise notes that classical jurists developed jihad as a collective duty that could include expansionist warfare.

Relevant secondary sources:

- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*
- Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*

---

## 3. Qur’an 8:12 may be battlefield language, but battlefield violence is still religiously sacralized

My opponent says Qur’an 8:12 refers to the Battle of Badr. That may be true, but it still matters that the Qur’an presents God as inspiring terror in unbelievers during battle:

> “I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip.”  
> **Qur’an 8:12**

The point is not that this verse commands modern terrorism against civilians. The point is that Islamic scripture sacralizes violence against unbelieving enemies in war. That complicates any simple claim that Islam promotes peace.

Other verses are also broader than mere self-defense:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and the religion is entirely for Allah.”  
> **Qur’an 8:39**

Similarly:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah.”  
> **Qur’an 2:193**

Those are not merely police-style restrictions on violence. They envision fighting until religious-political opposition is overcome.

---

## 4. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” remains deeply problematic

My opponent argues that the hadith uses the word “fight,” not “kill,” and therefore should be read as combat against hostile forces. But that does not solve the problem.

The hadith says:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

The endpoint of fighting is religious confession. That is precisely why the hadith has been central in legal discussions of jihad.

It was also used by Abu Bakr during the Ridda wars against Arab tribes who refused zakat after Muhammad’s death. Abu Bakr said:

> “By Allah, I will fight whoever differentiates between prayer and zakat…”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6924; Sahih Muslim 20**

This is important because it shows that the earliest Muslim leadership did not interpret “fight the people” as only defensive warfare against outside aggressors. It was used to enforce religious-political submission within the Muslim community itself.

So the opponent’s interpretation is possible as a modern apologetic reading, but it is not the only historically authoritative reading, and it is not the dominant classical one.

---

## 5. Limits on war do not prove that Islam promotes peace

My opponent cites rules against killing women and children:

> “Do not kill women and children.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**

And:

> “Do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, and do not kill children.”  
> **Sahih Muslim 1731**

These are real restrictions, and they matter. But they prove only that Islam regulates warfare, not that Islam promotes peace as its overriding principle.

A legal tradition can forbid killing noncombatants while still authorizing offensive war, conquest, enslavement, jizya, and religiously motivated expansion. Medieval Christian just-war theory also regulated war; that would not prove medieval Christendom was simply “a religion of peace.”

The proposition is not “Islam places some moral limits on war.” If that were the proposition, I could agree. The proposition is “Islam promotes peace.” The evidence is far more mixed.

---

## 6. Apostasy law is not a marginal issue

My opponent says apostasy punishment is debated and may refer to treason. But historically, the mainstream classical position was that adult sane apostates could be executed.

The hadith is blunt:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3017**

Another hadith says the blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in three cases, including:

> “The one who abandons his religion and separates from the community.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676**

My opponent emphasizes the phrase “separates from the community” to argue that this means treason. But classical jurists did not usually limit apostasy punishment only to armed rebellion. Many treated apostasy itself as a capital offense after the person was asked to repent.

For example:

- *Reliance of the Traveller*, o8.1–o8.4, discusses execution for apostasy after refusal to repent.
- Ibn Rushd, *Bidayat al-Mujtahid*, discusses juristic disagreement over details, but not over the seriousness of apostasy as a punishable legal offense.
- The four Sunni schools historically affirmed capital punishment for at least male apostates, with disagreement over women and procedural details.

A tradition that threatens death for leaving the religion cannot be described as simply promoting peace. Even if some modern scholars reinterpret apostasy as treason, that does not erase centuries of mainstream Islamic law.

---

## 7. Islamic history is not irrelevant because it was shaped by Islamic legal ideas

My opponent says Islamic conquests do not prove Islam itself promotes violence, just as Christian imperialism does not prove Christianity is essentially violent. That comparison is fair up to a point. But there is an important difference: early Islamic expansion was closely tied to the formation of Islamic law, governance, taxation, and jihad doctrine.

Within a century of Muhammad’s death, Muslim armies conquered Syria, Egypt, Persia, North Africa, and beyond. These were not merely defensive wars. They produced a religious-political order in which Muslims ruled and non-Muslims were subordinated as dhimmis.

Relevant historical studies include:

- Hugh Kennedy, *The Great Arab Conquests*
- Fred Donner, *The Early Islamic Conquests*
- Patricia Crone, *God’s Rule: Government and Islam*

The point is not that Muslims were uniquely violent by ancient standards. The point is that Islamic civilization’s formative period included conquest as a central mechanism of expansion, and this conquest was later normalized in legal doctrines of jihad.

---

## 8. “Peace” in Islamic sources is often conditional peace under Islamic dominance

My opponent cites verses such as:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> **Qur’an 8:61**

That is a peaceful verse. But it exists alongside verses commanding fighting until religion belongs to Allah, or until non-Muslims pay jizya in humiliation.

Similarly, Qur’an 9:33 says:

> “It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion…”  
> **Qur’an 9:33**

Also:

> “He has sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion…”  
> **Qur’an 61:9**

This is not a vision of neutral pluralism. It is a vision of Islam’s supremacy. Peace, in this framework, often means peace after resistance to Islamic authority has ended.

That is why “Islam promotes peace” is too vague and too generous. More accurately, Islam promotes order, submission to God, and justice as Islam defines it. Sometimes that includes peace. Sometimes it includes war.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent has shown that Islam contains peaceful teachings, restrictions on war, and traditions of mercy. I accept that. But he has not shown that peace is Islam’s clear, consistent, overriding message.

The evidence shows something more complicated:

- Qur’an 9:5 authorizes fighting against polytheists after a grace period.
- Qur’an 9:29 commands fighting People of the Book until they pay jizya in a humbled state.
- Qur’an 8:39 and 2:193 command fighting until religion is for Allah.
- Sahih hadith command fighting people until they testify to Islam.
- Sahih hadith prescribe death for apostasy.
- Classical Islamic law developed doctrines of jihad, dhimmi status, and apostasy punishment.
- Early Islamic history involved rapid imperial conquest justified through religious-political authority.

Therefore, the proposition “Islam promotes peace” is misleading. A more accurate statement would be:

**Islam contains teachings that can support peace, and many Muslims sincerely promote peace. But Islam also contains authoritative texts and legal traditions that sanction religiously justified violence, conquest, coercive hierarchy, and punishment for apostasy.**

For that reason, the proposition should be rejected.
steps.conclusion_for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

In conclusion, the proposition before us is not that Islam is pacifist, nor that Muslims have never fought wars, nor that every Muslim ruler throughout history has lived up to Islamic ideals. The proposition is that **Islam promotes peace**—and the evidence shows that it does.

Islam promotes peace first through its core moral vision. The Qur’an calls believers to “enter into peace completely” and commands reconciliation when peace is offered: **“If they incline to peace, then incline to it also”**. It teaches that human life is sacred, declaring that killing one innocent soul is like killing all humanity, while saving one life is like saving all humanity. It commands justice even against oneself and even toward enemies, saying: **“Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just.”**

Islam also promotes peace through the example and teachings of the Prophet Muhammad. He defined a true Muslim as one **“from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”** He forbade the killing of women, children, and noncombatants. He prohibited treachery and mutilation. He accepted peace treaties, forgave former enemies, and embodied mercy when he had the power to take revenge. The Qur’an itself describes him as **“a mercy to the worlds.”**

My opponent has argued that certain verses and hadiths prove Islam does not promote peace. But those texts were cited without their full legal, historical, and textual context. Qur’an 9:5, for example, is not a universal order to kill non-Muslims; the same passage exempts treaty-keepers and commands Muslims to protect enemy polytheists who seek safety. Qur’an 9:29 concerns political conflict and governance, not forced conversion. The Qur’an’s broader framework remains clear: **“There is no compulsion in religion.”**

Yes, Islam discusses war. But regulating war is not the same as glorifying war. Modern legal systems also regulate warfare, policing, and self-defense, yet we do not say they promote violence simply because they recognize that aggression sometimes exists. Islam’s teaching is that force must be limited, defensive, restrained, and governed by justice. The Qur’an says: **“Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”**

History also must be judged carefully. Muslim empires, like Christian, Buddhist, Hindu, and secular empires, sometimes engaged in conquest and injustice. But the failures of rulers do not erase the ethical teachings of a faith. The proper question is: what does Islam command as an ideal? The answer is mercy, justice, restraint, protection of life, honoring treaties, accepting peace, and refusing religious compulsion.

So the final picture is clear. Islam does not teach peace as weakness or silence in the face of oppression. It teaches peace as a moral order rooted in justice. It teaches that human beings must be safe from one another’s hands and tongues. It teaches that mercy is central to God’s nature and must be reflected in human conduct. It teaches that even enemies have rights, treaties must be honored, and peace must be accepted when offered.

Therefore, the proposition stands: **Islam promotes peace—not by denying conflict exists, but by commanding justice, mercy, restraint, reconciliation, and respect for human life.**
steps.conclusion_against:
## Concluding statement against the proposition: “Islam promotes peace”

Ladies and gentlemen,

Throughout this debate, I have not argued that Muslims are inherently violent, nor have I denied that many Muslims live peaceful, compassionate, and admirable lives. I have also not denied that Islamic scripture and tradition contain teachings about mercy, reconciliation, justice, treaty-keeping, and limits on warfare. They do.

But that is not enough to prove the proposition.

The proposition before us is not “many Muslims promote peace,” or “Islam contains peaceful teachings,” or “Islam regulates war.” Those statements are true. The proposition is stronger: **“Islam promotes peace.”** And my argument has been that this claim is too broad, too simple, and ultimately misleading.

The evidence shows that Islam is not a purely peace-centered tradition. It contains both peaceful and militant elements, and some of the militant elements are not marginal. They appear in the Qur’an, in canonical hadith, in classical jurisprudence, and in early Islamic history.

We have seen that Qur’an 9:5 commands fighting against polytheists after a period of warning. Even if one emphasizes its historical context, it remains a text authorizing religiously framed violence. Qur’an 9:29 goes further, commanding fighting against People of the Book until they pay jizya “while humbled.” That is not merely self-defense. It establishes a system in which non-Muslims may be tolerated, but under Islamic political dominance and legal inferiority.

We have also seen that Qur’an 8:39 and 2:193 speak of fighting until “religion is for Allah,” and that hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim say Muhammad was commanded to fight people until they testify to Islam. These texts have not merely been misused by extremists; they have been taken seriously by mainstream jurists across Islamic history.

The same is true of apostasy. The hadith “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” became the basis for a classical legal doctrine under which apostasy could be punished by death. Modern reinterpretations may soften that teaching, but they do not erase the fact that for centuries major Islamic legal schools treated leaving Islam as a punishable offense. A religious system that historically threatens death for apostasy cannot be described, without qualification, as promoting peace.

Nor can history be ignored. Early Islamic expansion was not simply a series of defensive wars. Muslim armies rapidly conquered vast territories, and those conquests helped shape Islamic doctrines of jihad, governance, jizya, and the status of non-Muslims. Again, this does not mean Islam was uniquely violent by medieval standards. But it does mean that conquest and religious-political domination were part of Islam’s formative historical development.

My opponent has pointed to verses such as “There is no compulsion in religion,” “If they incline to peace, incline to it,” and prophetic instructions not to kill women and children. These are important texts. But they prove only that Islam contains restraints and peaceful strands. They do not cancel the other texts. They do not erase jihad doctrine. They do not erase dhimmi status. They do not erase apostasy law. They do not erase the historical reality of expansion under Islamic rule.

So the central issue is this: **Does Islam promote peace as its clear, consistent, overriding principle?** The answer is no.

A more accurate conclusion is this:

**Islam contains teachings that can support peace, and many Muslims sincerely interpret and practice their faith peacefully. But Islam also contains authoritative texts and legal traditions that sanction religious warfare, coercive hierarchy, conquest, and punishment for apostasy.**

Therefore, the proposition “Islam promotes peace” is too simplistic. It overlooks the complexity of the tradition and selectively emphasizes only one side of the evidence.

For that reason, I urge you to reject the proposition.

debates.topic: Islam promotes violence towards non Muslims

steps.opening_for:
I can help frame this as a debate argument about **texts, doctrine, and legal tradition**, not as an attack on Muslims as people. A responsible opening should make clear that many Muslims interpret Islam peacefully, while arguing that certain authoritative sources have also been used to justify violence toward non-Muslims.

## Opening Argument: For the Proposition

Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us is not that every Muslim is violent, nor that Muslims as individuals are morally suspect. That would be both false and unfair. The question is whether Islam, as found in some of its authoritative scriptures, hadith, and classical legal traditions, contains teachings that promote or legitimize violence against non-Muslims. I will argue that it does.

Islamic scripture contains passages that do not merely permit self-defense, but command fighting against unbelievers under religiously defined conditions. The Qur’an’s so-called “Sword Verse” states: “kill the polytheists wherever you find them” unless they repent and accept Islamic obligations. Another passage commands Muslims to “fight those who do not believe in Allah” from among the People of the Book “until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.” These are not simply vague spiritual metaphors; they are legal and political instructions that were historically read as authorizing military domination over non-Muslim communities.

This interpretation is reinforced by hadith literature. In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Muhammad is reported to have said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.” Another hadith in Sahih Muslim describes a process in which non-Muslims are invited to accept Islam, pay the jizya, or face battle. That is not merely defensive warfare; it is a religiously structured ultimatum.

Nor were these passages ignored by classical Islamic jurists. Major works of Islamic law developed the doctrine of jihad not only as personal spiritual struggle, but as armed struggle against non-Muslim political communities. Classical jurists commonly held that the ruler had a duty to wage jihad to expand or defend Islamic rule, and that non-Muslims could be fought until they accepted Islam, submitted to Muslim rule, or paid tribute. This became embedded in the legal distinction between Muslims, protected non-Muslim dhimmis, and enemy unbelievers.

Of course, there are peaceful passages in Islamic scripture, and many Muslims today emphasize them sincerely. But the existence of peaceful interpretations does not erase the violent ones. A religion can contain multiple strands, and the question here is whether Islam contains an authoritative strand that promotes violence toward non-Muslims. The textual and legal record shows that it does.

Therefore, while it would be wrong to claim that all Muslims are violent, it is historically and textually defensible to argue that Islam has promoted violence against non-Muslims in important parts of its scripture, prophetic tradition, and classical jurisprudence.

## Relevant Citations

- **Qur’an 9:5**: “Then, when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them…”  
- **Qur’an 9:29**: “Fight those who do not believe in Allah… among the People of the Book until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.”  
- **Qur’an 8:12**: “I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve, so strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip.”  
- **Qur’an 47:4**: “So when you meet those who disbelieve, strike their necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, then secure their bonds…”

- **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**: Muhammad is reported to have said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
- **Sahih Muslim 1731a**: Instructions attributed to Muhammad tell Muslim commanders to invite enemies to Islam; if they refuse, invite them to pay jizya; if they refuse that, then fight them.  
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 3017**: “Whoever changes his religion, kill him,” often cited in classical law regarding apostasy.

- **Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*:** Discusses classical Islamic legal theory of jihad and the division between the realm of Islam and the realm of war.  
- **Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*:** Surveys classical juristic understandings of jihad as armed struggle and its legal role in relations with non-Muslims.  
- **Michael Bonner, *Jihad in Islamic History: Doctrines and Practice*:** Explains the historical development of jihad doctrine from early Islam through later legal traditions.
steps.opening_against:
**Opening argument (against the proposition):**

Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition says: *“Islam promotes violence towards non-Muslims.”* That claim is not only sweeping; it is contradicted by Islam’s core texts, its legal-ethical principles, and the conduct it demands even in conflict.

Islam does not teach violence against people simply because they are non-Muslim. The Qur’an explicitly states: **“There is no compulsion in religion”** — a foundational rejection of forced conversion. It also commands Muslims to treat peaceful non-Muslims with justice and kindness: **“Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just to those who have not fought you because of religion or driven you from your homes.”** That is not a call to violence; it is a call to coexistence.

Where the Qur’an discusses fighting, it is overwhelmingly in the context of persecution, aggression, treaty-breaking, or self-defense. The Qur’an says: **“Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”** The limiting phrase is crucial: *those who fight you*. It is not a blank cheque for violence against non-Muslims. In fact, the Qur’an commands Muslims to accept peace when the enemy inclines to peace: **“If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”**

Islamic ethics also place strict limits on warfare. The Prophet Muhammad forbade the killing of non-combatants, including women and children. He warned that whoever kills a protected non-Muslim under treaty would not “smell the fragrance of Paradise.” These teachings are incompatible with the claim that Islam promotes indiscriminate violence toward non-Muslims.

Of course, Muslims, like members of every major civilization and religion, have at times committed violence and injustice. But the debate is not whether some Muslims have been violent. The debate is whether Islam itself promotes violence against non-Muslims as a principle. The evidence says no. Islam permits fighting in limited circumstances — defense, protection from persecution, and response to aggression — but it forbids coercion in religion, commands justice toward outsiders, protects peaceful non-Muslims, and restricts warfare.

Extremists promote violence by tearing verses from their historical and textual context. But a fair reading of Islam’s sources shows a religion that distinguishes between combatants and civilians, aggression and defense, justice and revenge. Therefore, the proposition is false: Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims; it promotes justice, restraint, and peaceful coexistence with those who do not wage war.

### Relevant citations

- **Qur’an 2:256** — “There is no compulsion in religion.”
- **Qur’an 60:8–9** — Muslims are not forbidden from showing kindness and justice to those who do not fight them because of religion or expel them from their homes.
- **Qur’an 2:190** — “Fight… those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”
- **Qur’an 8:61** — “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”
- **Qur’an 5:8** — Do not let hatred of a people lead you away from justice.
- **Qur’an 5:32** — Killing one innocent person is likened to killing all humanity.
- **Qur’an 22:39–40** — Fighting is permitted to those who have been wronged and expelled; the verse mentions protection of monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques.
- **Qur’an 16:125** — Invite to the way of God with wisdom and good instruction.
- **Qur’an 29:46** — Argue with the People of the Book “in the best manner.”
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015** — The Prophet forbade killing women and children in war.
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166** — The Prophet said whoever kills a protected non-Muslim under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.
- **Sahih Muslim 1731** — The Prophet instructed armies not to act treacherously, mutilate, or kill children.
steps.response_for:
## Rebuttal: For the Proposition

The opposition’s argument depends on narrowing the proposition into something easier to deny: that Islam commands indiscriminate violence against every non-Muslim in every circumstance. But that is not the claim I need to prove. The proposition is that Islam **promotes or legitimizes violence toward non-Muslims** in important parts of its scripture and legal tradition. A system can condemn some forms of violence — such as killing women, children, or treaty-protected people — while still authorizing religiously defined warfare against non-Muslim communities.

The opponent cites peaceful and restrictive passages, but those do not erase the passages that explicitly command fighting unbelievers until they convert, submit, or pay tribute.

### 1. “No compulsion in religion” does not negate military coercion

The opponent relies heavily on Qur’an 2:256: “There is no compulsion in religion.” But even if forced conversion is prohibited, that does not mean Islamic sources prohibit coercive religious-political domination.

Qur’an 9:29 commands:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah… from among the People of the Book until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.”

That verse does not say, “Fight only those currently attacking you.” It identifies the targets by religious category — those who do not believe — and gives the condition for ending the fighting: payment of jizya in submission. That is not simple self-defense.

Similarly, **Sahih Muslim 1731a** reports Muhammad instructing commanders to invite enemies to Islam; if they refuse, invite them to pay jizya; if they refuse, then fight them. Again, this is not merely “fight those who fight you.” It is an ultimatum: Islam, tribute/submission, or war.

So “no compulsion in religion” may mean non-Muslims are not always forced to convert, but Islamic sources still authorize fighting them until they submit to Islamic rule.

### 2. The opponent’s defensive verses are not the whole Qur’anic picture

The opposition cites Qur’an 2:190: “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.” But the Qur’an contains later and broader commands that classical jurists did not interpret as purely defensive.

For example:

- **Qur’an 9:5**:  
  > “Kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them…”

- **Qur’an 9:29**:  
  > “Fight those who do not believe in Allah… until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.”

- **Qur’an 9:123**:  
  > “O you who believe, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers and let them find in you harshness.”

- **Qur’an 8:39**:  
  > “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”

Whatever peaceful or defensive verses exist, these passages were historically read by many classical authorities as authorizing offensive jihad against non-Muslim political communities.

Indeed, many classical exegetes treated Qur’an 9 as a later, more forceful revelation. Ibn Kathir, commenting on Qur’an 9:5, refers to it as the “Sword Verse” and records the view that it superseded earlier permissions of patience or treaty with polytheists. Whether or not all Muslims accept abrogation today, the point remains: influential Islamic scholarship did read these verses as authorizing aggressive warfare against unbelievers.

### 3. Rules against killing civilians do not disprove religiously sanctioned violence

The opponent cites hadith forbidding the killing of women and children. But that only proves Islamic law sometimes distinguishes combatants from non-combatants. It does not prove that Islam rejects violence against non-Muslims as such.

Many military systems have rules of war while still authorizing aggressive or expansionist war. The fact that Muhammad reportedly forbade killing women and children does not cancel the hadith saying:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

Nor does it cancel **Sahih Muslim 1731a**, where non-Muslim enemies are offered Islam, jizya, or battle.

So the issue is not whether Islamic law has limits. It does. The issue is whether Islamic law also authorizes religious warfare against non-Muslims. It does.

### 4. Protected non-Muslims are protected because they submit to Islamic rule

The opponent cites the hadith warning against killing a protected non-Muslim under covenant:

> “Whoever kills a mu‘ahid will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166**

But this actually supports the proposition when understood legally. A “protected” non-Muslim is protected because he has a covenant, often as a **dhimmi** or treaty-holder. The protection is conditional upon submission to Islamic political authority or treaty terms.

That is exactly the structure of Qur’an 9:29: fight the People of the Book until they pay jizya “while humbled.” In other words, non-Muslims are safe when they accept subordinate status under Muslim rule. If they refuse Islam and refuse submission, classical doctrine allowed fighting them.

That is not equal peaceful coexistence. It is coercive hierarchy backed by violence.

### 5. Classical Islamic jurisprudence confirms this was not merely extremist distortion

The opposition says extremists take verses out of context. But the doctrine of armed jihad against non-Muslim polities was not invented by modern extremists. It appears in mainstream classical jurisprudence.

Majid Khadduri, in *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, explains that classical Islamic law often viewed jihad as a collective duty of the Muslim community and divided the world into the realm of Islam and the realm of war.

Rudolph Peters, in *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, similarly notes that classical jurists understood jihad primarily as armed struggle against unbelievers, not merely as inner spiritual effort.

Michael Bonner, in *Jihad in Islamic History*, also shows that jihad developed as both a spiritual and military concept, with armed struggle playing a central role in Islamic legal and political thought.

Classical manuals of Islamic law likewise present jihad as warfare against non-Muslims. For example, *Reliance of the Traveller*, a later Shafi‘i legal manual, defines jihad in legal terms as warfare against non-Muslims and treats it as a communal obligation.

So this is not a fringe reading. It is part of the inherited legal tradition.

### 6. Peaceful verses prove diversity within Islam, not absence of violent doctrine

I fully accept that Islam contains peaceful teachings. Qur’an 60:8 speaks of kindness toward those who do not fight Muslims. Qur’an 8:61 permits peace if the enemy inclines to peace. Qur’an 16:125 says to invite with wisdom. These passages matter.

But the existence of peaceful teachings does not refute the existence of violent ones. A tradition can contain both restraint and aggression. The proposition does not require proving that Islam is only violent. It requires proving that Islam contains authoritative teachings that promote violence toward non-Muslims under religiously defined conditions.

And the evidence is clear: the Qur’an, hadith, and classical legal tradition include commands to fight unbelievers, impose jizya, subdue non-Muslim communities, and punish apostasy.

## Conclusion

The opposition is correct that Islam contains teachings about mercy, justice, and restraint. But those teachings do not erase the other side of the record. Authoritative Islamic sources also command fighting non-Muslims until they convert, submit, or pay tribute. Classical jurists developed those texts into doctrines of armed jihad and dhimmi subordination.

Therefore, the proposition stands: not that all Muslims are violent, and not that Islam contains no peaceful teachings, but that Islam has promoted and legitimized violence toward non-Muslims in significant parts of its scripture, hadith, and legal tradition.

### Key Citations

- **Qur’an 9:5** — “Kill the polytheists wherever you find them…”
- **Qur’an 9:29** — “Fight those who do not believe… until they give the jizya willingly while humbled.”
- **Qur’an 9:123** — “Fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers…”
- **Qur’an 8:39** — “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22** — “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify…”
- **Sahih Muslim 1731a** — Commanders instructed to invite enemies to Islam, then jizya, then battle.
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 3017** — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”
- **Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam***
- **Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam***
- **Michael Bonner, *Jihad in Islamic History***
steps.response_against:
## Rebuttal against the proposition

My opponent’s case depends on treating every Qur’anic command to “fight” as a general religious command to attack non-Muslims *because they are non-Muslims*. But that reading ignores the immediate context of the verses, the Qur’an’s own limiting clauses, and the way Islamic law distinguishes between peaceful non-Muslims, treaty partners, civilians, and active enemies.

The real question is not: “Does Islam ever permit fighting?” Of course it does, as virtually every legal and moral tradition does. The question is: **Does Islam promote violence toward non-Muslims as such?** The evidence still says no.

---

## 1. Qur’an 9:5 is not a command to kill all polytheists

My opponent cites Qur’an 9:5:

> “Kill the polytheists wherever you find them…”

But he omits the surrounding verses, which radically change the meaning.

The same passage says:

> “Excepted are those polytheists with whom you made a treaty and who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term.”  
> — **Qur’an 9:4**

And immediately after the so-called “Sword Verse,” the Qur’an says:

> “If any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the word of Allah, then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> — **Qur’an 9:6**

So Qur’an 9:5 cannot mean “kill non-Muslims wherever they exist.” The text itself excludes peaceful treaty-holders and even commands Muslims to protect and safely escort a pagan seeking asylum.

The same chapter explains the reason for fighting:

> “Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, intended to expel the Messenger, and attacked you first?”  
> — **Qur’an 9:13**

That is not violence promoted against people merely for disbelief. It is armed conflict against groups who broke treaties, aided aggression, and attacked the Muslim community.

---

## 2. Qur’an 9:29 does not prove forced religious violence

My opponent also relies on Qur’an 9:29:

> “Fight those who do not believe… from among the People of the Book until they give the jizya…”

But again, this must be read alongside the Qur’an’s broader rules: no compulsion in religion, treaty protection, and peace when the other side ceases hostility.

The Qur’an says:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:256**

It also says:

> “If they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them.”  
> — **Qur’an 4:90**

That verse is especially important: if non-Muslims do not fight and offer peace, Muslims are given “no way” against them. That directly contradicts the claim that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims simply because they are non-Muslim.

As for **jizya**, it was a tax imposed on non-Muslim subjects in exchange for protection and exemption from military service, while Muslims paid zakat and were liable for military defense. One may criticize pre-modern unequal taxation by modern standards, but it is not the same as saying Islam promotes violence against non-Muslims. In fact, the jizya system presupposed that non-Muslims could remain non-Muslim, retain communal life, and receive legal protection.

This is why the Prophet said:

> “Whoever kills a mu‘ahid — a non-Muslim under covenant — will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166**

That is a severe religious warning against harming protected non-Muslims.

---

## 3. “Fight them until there is no fitnah” refers to persecution, not forced conversion

My opponent cites Qur’an 8:39:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”

But the Qur’an uses similar language in Qur’an 2:193, and there the limiting condition is explicit:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah. But if they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:193**

“Fitnah” in this context refers to persecution, oppression, and religious coercion — the very conditions early Muslims suffered in Mecca. The verse does not say, “Fight until everyone becomes Muslim.” It says that if the enemy ceases, aggression must cease.

This matches Qur’an 2:190:

> “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:190**

So the Qur’anic rule is not unrestricted violence. It is restricted fighting against aggression and oppression.

---

## 4. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” cannot mean all non-Muslims

My opponent cites the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

But if this meant “fight every non-Muslim until conversion,” it would contradict the Qur’an’s permission for People of the Book to remain non-Muslim under covenant, the Prophet’s treaties with non-Muslims, and the hadith protecting the mu‘ahid.

Therefore “the people” in this hadith cannot mean every human being or every non-Muslim. It refers to the hostile pagan opponents of the Prophet in that specific conflict-context — those waging war against the Muslim community.

This is not special pleading. The Qur’an itself uses general language in context-specific ways. For example, when the Qur’an says “people said to them…” it does not mean every human being on earth; it means particular people in that situation. The same applies here.

---

## 5. Sahih Muslim 1731 is a rule for conduct during war, not a command to attack peaceful non-Muslims

My opponent cites **Sahih Muslim 1731a**, where commanders are instructed to invite enemies to Islam, then jizya, then battle.

But that hadith is addressed to military commanders already engaged in a campaign. It is a rule of engagement, not a universal command to attack all peaceful non-Muslim communities. The same narration also includes restrictions: do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, and do not kill children.

So the hadith shows that when war occurs, Islam regulates it and seeks alternatives before combat. It does not prove that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims in general.

---

## 6. Classical jurists were not unanimous that unbelief itself is the cause of war

My opponent presents classical Islamic law as if it had one simple doctrine: fight non-Muslims because they are non-Muslims. That is not accurate.

There were juristic debates over the cause of jihad. Many jurists, especially in the Hanafi tradition, argued that the legal cause of fighting is not mere unbelief but hostile aggression or combatant status. This is why Islamic law prohibited killing women, children, monks, the elderly, and other non-combatants.

The Prophet forbade killing women and children:

> “A woman was found killed in one of the battles, and the Messenger of Allah disapproved of killing women and children.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**

And in military instructions:

> “Do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, and do not kill children.”  
> — **Sahih Muslim 1731**

If disbelief itself were the reason for killing, these categories would not be protected. Their protection shows that the relevant distinction is not simply Muslim vs non-Muslim, but combatant vs non-combatant, aggressor vs peaceful person, treaty-breaker vs treaty-holder.

---

## 7. The Qur’an explicitly commands justice and kindness toward peaceful non-Muslims

The opponent admits peaceful verses exist but treats them as secondary. They are not secondary; they are direct moral commands.

The Qur’an says:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion and have not expelled you from your homes. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.”  
> — **Qur’an 60:8**

It continues:

> “Allah only forbids you from taking as allies those who fought you because of religion, expelled you from your homes, or supported your expulsion.”  
> — **Qur’an 60:9**

This passage makes the distinction perfectly clear: peaceful non-Muslims are to be treated with justice and kindness; hostility is directed against those who wage persecution and aggression.

The Qur’an also says:

> “Do not let hatred of a people cause you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> — **Qur’an 5:8**

That is not the language of a religion promoting violence toward outsiders.

---

## 8. Apostasy is not evidence of violence toward non-Muslims

My opponent also mentions apostasy. But apostasy concerns people who leave Islam, not non-Muslims as such, so it is not directly relevant to the proposition.

Even then, the Qur’an repeatedly mentions apostasy without prescribing a worldly death penalty:

> “Whoever among you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever…”  
> — **Qur’an 2:217**

> “Those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved…”  
> — **Qur’an 4:137**

The second verse describes people moving in and out of belief more than once, which would make no sense if mere private apostasy automatically required immediate execution. Many modern Muslim scholars therefore understand the harsh hadith reports on apostasy in the context of treason, rebellion, or joining wartime enemies, not mere change of conscience.

In any case, apostasy law cannot prove that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims generally.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent’s argument proves only that Islam, like other pre-modern legal traditions, contains laws of war. It does not prove that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims as non-Muslims.

The Qur’an commands:

- no compulsion in religion — **Qur’an 2:256**
- kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims — **Qur’an 60:8**
- fighting only those who fight Muslims — **Qur’an 2:190**
- cessation of hostilities when the enemy ceases — **Qur’an 2:193**
- acceptance of peace when offered — **Qur’an 8:61**
- protection for treaty-holders — **Qur’an 9:4**
- asylum and safe passage even for polytheists — **Qur’an 9:6**
- no aggression against those who withdraw and offer peace — **Qur’an 4:90**

Yes, Islam permits warfare under defined conditions. But permission for regulated warfare is not the same as promotion of violence against non-Muslims. The stronger reading of the Qur’an and Prophetic practice is that Islam forbids religious coercion, protects peaceful non-Muslims, restricts warfare, and condemns transgression.

Therefore, the proposition remains false: **Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims; it permits limited, regulated fighting against aggression, persecution, and treaty-breaking while commanding justice and protection for peaceful outsiders.**
steps.conclusion_for:
## Concluding Statement: For the Proposition

Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us has never required proving that all Muslims are violent, or that Islam contains no teachings of mercy, justice, or restraint. It clearly does contain such teachings, and many Muslims today sincerely interpret their faith in peaceful ways. But that is not the question. The question is whether Islam, in its authoritative texts and classical legal tradition, has promoted or legitimized violence toward non-Muslims under religiously defined conditions. The evidence shows that it has.

We have seen that the Qur’an includes passages commanding Muslims to fight unbelievers, not merely in immediate self-defense, but until they submit to Islamic authority. Qur’an 9:29 explicitly commands fighting the People of the Book “until they give the jizya willingly while humbled.” Qur’an 9:5 commands violence against polytheists after the sacred months. Qur’an 9:123 calls on believers to fight nearby disbelievers and show harshness. These are not simply abstract moral teachings; they became part of legal and political doctrine.

The hadith literature reinforces this pattern. In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Muhammad is reported to have said, “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify” to Islam. Sahih Muslim 1731 describes a military procedure in which non-Muslims are invited to accept Islam, pay jizya, or face battle. That structure is not merely defensive. It presents religious submission, political subordination, or war.

The opposition has cited important peaceful verses: “There is no compulsion in religion,” “Fight those who fight you,” and “If they incline to peace, incline to it.” But those verses do not erase the other passages. At most, they prove that Islamic sources contain multiple strands — some peaceful, some restrictive, and some coercive. A tradition can forbid indiscriminate killing while still authorizing religiously justified warfare. Rules against killing women, children, or treaty-protected people do not disprove the existence of doctrines allowing war against non-Muslim communities that refuse Islamic rule.

Most importantly, this was not merely a modern extremist invention. Classical Islamic jurists developed doctrines of armed jihad, jizya, dhimmi status, apostasy punishment, and the political subordination of non-Muslims. Scholars such as Majid Khadduri, Rudolph Peters, and Michael Bonner have shown that armed struggle against non-Muslim polities was a major component of classical Islamic legal thought.

So the opposition’s central mistake is to treat peaceful Islamic teachings as though they cancel the violent ones. They do not. The existence of peaceful interpretations does not negate the fact that influential scriptures, hadith, and legal traditions have authorized violence toward non-Muslims when they refused conversion, tribute, or submission.

Therefore, the proposition stands: Islam should not be reduced to violence, and Muslims as people should not be maligned. But historically and textually, Islam has contained authoritative doctrines that promote or legitimize violence against non-Muslims in significant contexts. That is the claim we set out to prove, and that is what the evidence demonstrates.
steps.conclusion_against:
## Concluding statement against the proposition

The proposition before us is: **“Islam promotes violence towards non-Muslims.”** That is a broad claim, and it has not been proven.

What has been shown is that Islam, like virtually every major religious and legal civilization, contains rules about warfare. But **permission for regulated fighting in specific circumstances is not the same as promoting violence against non-Muslims as non-Muslims**.

The Qur’an repeatedly places limits on fighting. It says:

- **“Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress”** — Qur’an 2:190  
- **“If they incline to peace, then incline to it also”** — Qur’an 8:61  
- **“If they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer peace, then Allah has not made for you a way against them”** — Qur’an 4:90  
- **“There is no compulsion in religion”** — Qur’an 2:256  
- **“Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just to those who have not fought you because of religion”** — Qur’an 60:8  

These are not marginal verses. They establish a consistent moral framework: peaceful non-Muslims are not to be attacked; they are to be treated with justice and kindness.

My opponent relied heavily on verses such as Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29, but those verses were presented as though they exist in isolation. They do not. Qur’an 9 itself excludes treaty-holding polytheists, commands Muslims to honour treaties, and even orders Muslims to grant asylum and safe passage to a pagan who seeks protection. Qur’an 9:13 explains the conflict context: people had broken oaths, supported aggression, and attacked the Muslim community first. That is not a blanket command to kill non-Muslims.

The same applies to hadith about fighting. They cannot reasonably be interpreted as commands to fight every non-Muslim until conversion, because that would contradict the Qur’an’s ban on religious compulsion, the Prophet’s treaties with non-Muslims, the protection of Jewish and Christian communities, and the severe warning that whoever kills a protected non-Muslim will not even smell the fragrance of Paradise.

Islamic law also forbids transgression in war. The Prophet prohibited killing women, children, and other non-combatants. He forbade treachery and mutilation. These rules show that Islam distinguishes between combatants and civilians, aggression and peace, treaty-breakers and treaty-holders. If mere disbelief were the reason for violence, such protections would make no sense.

Nor does the existence of jizya prove that Islam promotes violence. One may debate pre-modern political systems by modern standards, but the jizya system itself meant that non-Muslims could remain non-Muslim, retain their communities, and receive protection under law. That is not forced conversion, nor is it indiscriminate violence.

The strongest evidence in this debate remains clear: Islam commands justice even toward those outside the faith. It forbids compulsion in religion. It commands kindness toward peaceful non-Muslims. It restricts fighting to contexts of hostility, persecution, aggression, or treaty violation. And it commands peace when the other side seeks peace.

So yes, Islam permits fighting under defined circumstances. But that is very different from saying Islam **promotes violence toward non-Muslims**. The proposition confuses regulated warfare with religious hatred, and contextual conflict with universal aggression.

For these reasons, the proposition fails. Islam does not promote violence against non-Muslims as a principle. Its core teaching is that violence is restricted, transgression is forbidden, peaceful outsiders are to be treated justly, and religion cannot be forced. Therefore, I stand firmly against the proposition.

debates.topic: Islam promotes women's rights

steps.opening_for:
Madam Chair, honorable judges, and respected opponents:

I rise to affirm the motion: **Islam promotes women’s rights.**

To judge this proposition fairly, we must distinguish Islam’s foundational teachings from cultural practices that sometimes contradict them. The question is not whether every Muslim society has always treated women perfectly—no civilization can make that claim. The question is whether Islam, in its core sources, advances women’s dignity, agency, and rights. The answer is yes.

First, Islam establishes the **equal spiritual and moral worth** of women and men. The Qur’an declares that men and women come from a single human origin: “He created you from one soul” (Qur’an 4:1). It repeatedly states that women and men are equally accountable before God and equally rewarded for faith and good works: “For Muslim men and Muslim women, believing men and believing women… God has prepared forgiveness and a great reward” (Qur’an 33:35). It also says, “Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while believing, We will surely grant them a good life” (Qur’an 16:97). This is a powerful foundation: women are not spiritually secondary, morally inferior, or less human.

Second, Islam gave women **legal and economic rights** in a context where women were often treated as property. The Qur’an explicitly grants women inheritance: “For men is a share of what parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share” (Qur’an 4:7). It affirms women’s right to their own earnings: “For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned” (Qur’an 4:32). It commands that women receive their marriage gift directly: “Give women their bridal gifts graciously” (Qur’an 4:4). These are not symbolic gestures; they establish women as independent legal and financial persons.

Third, Islam protects women’s **consent and dignity in marriage**. The Qur’an forbids inheriting women against their will and commands men to live with wives honorably (Qur’an 4:19). The Prophet Muhammad taught that a woman cannot be married without her consent: “A previously married woman should not be married until she is consulted, and a virgin should not be married until her permission is sought” (Sahih al-Bukhari 5136; Sahih Muslim 1419). In another case, when a woman complained that her father had married her off against her will, the Prophet annulled the marriage (Sahih al-Bukhari 5138). That is a clear recognition of women’s agency.

Fourth, Islam promotes women’s **right to education and participation in religious and public life**. Women directly asked the Prophet for dedicated time to learn, and he set aside a day to teach them (Sahih al-Bukhari 101). The Qur’an describes believing men and believing women as mutual allies who promote good and oppose wrong (Qur’an 9:71). Women pledged allegiance directly to the Prophet, showing their independent civic and religious responsibility (Qur’an 60:12). Islam did not imagine women as silent or invisible; it recognized them as moral actors in society.

Fifth, Islam challenged abusive practices against women. The Qur’an condemned female infanticide in devastating moral language: “When the girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed” (Qur’an 81:8–9). It criticized the shame some men felt at the birth of daughters (Qur’an 16:58–59). The Prophet elevated treatment of women as a measure of character, saying, “The best of you are those who are best to their wives” (Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3895). In his Farewell Sermon, he reminded men to fear God concerning women and treat them well (Sahih Muslim 1218).

Sixth, Islam recognizes women’s rights even in divorce. The Qur’an commands that divorce must not be used to harm or trap women (Qur’an 2:231). It also recognizes separation procedures, including return of marital gift in cases of khulʿ, as illustrated when the Prophet allowed the wife of Thabit ibn Qays to end her marriage (Sahih al-Bukhari 5273). This matters because a right to marry without a right to leave an unbearable marriage is incomplete.

So the proposition stands on strong ground. Islam promotes women’s rights by affirming women’s equal spiritual worth, legal personhood, property ownership, inheritance, consent in marriage, access to education, moral agency, and protection from abuse. Where Muslims have failed to honor these principles, the failure lies not in Islam’s ideals but in human practice falling short of them.

In a world where women were often denied property, consent, dignity, and public voice, Islam declared that women are servants of God, possessors of rights, moral agents, and partners in building a just society. For that reason, I proudly affirm: **Islam promotes women’s rights.**

**Key citations:** Qur’an 4:1; 33:35; 16:97; 4:7; 4:32; 4:4; 4:19; 9:71; 60:12; 81:8–9; 16:58–59; 2:231. Sahih al-Bukhari 101, 5136, 5138, 5273; Sahih Muslim 1218, 1419; Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3895.
steps.opening_against:
## Opening argument against the proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights”

Ladies and gentlemen, I oppose the proposition not by attacking Muslims, nor by denying that many Muslim women are strong advocates for equality, but by examining the claim itself: **Does Islam, in its canonical texts and traditional legal structures, promote women’s rights as equal, individual human rights?** My answer is no.

A system that promotes women’s rights should affirm women’s equal legal status, equal autonomy, equal credibility, and equal freedom within marriage and society. But the Qur’an and major hadith sources repeatedly place women in a legally and socially subordinate position to men.

First, **Islamic scripture gives men authority over women within the family**. Qur’an 4:34 states that “men are in charge of women” because of what God has given one over the other and because men spend from their wealth. The same verse instructs husbands, in cases of marital disobedience, to admonish wives, separate from them in bed, and then “strike” them, depending on translation. Even where modern interpreters soften this meaning, the traditional reading has been used for centuries to justify male disciplinary authority over wives. That is not a rights-based framework; it is a hierarchy.

Second, **women’s legal value is not treated as equal to men’s**. In inheritance, Qur’an 4:11 gives a son the share of two daughters. In financial testimony, Qur’an 2:282 calls for two women in place of one man, “so that if one of them errs, the other can remind her.” These are not marginal details; they are explicit legal rules in the Qur’an. A system that gives women half the inheritance and, in key contexts, half the evidentiary weight of men cannot be said to promote full equality.

Third, **marriage law reflects male privilege rather than mutual autonomy**. Qur’an 4:3 permits men to marry up to four women, while women are not given the same right. Qur’an 2:228 says women have rights similar to their obligations, but also that “men have a degree over them.” In many traditional schools of Islamic law, men have easier access to unilateral divorce, while women’s divorce rights are more restricted or conditional. Again, this is not equal partnership; it is structured male advantage.

Fourth, some hadith reinforce ideas of female inferiority or obedience. In Sahih al-Bukhari, women are described as “deficient in intelligence and religion,” with the explanation tied to female testimony and menstruation. Another hadith says that if a wife refuses her husband’s bed, the angels curse her until morning. Whatever one’s theological interpretation, these texts have historically shaped norms in which women’s credibility, religious standing, and sexual autonomy are limited.

Supporters of the proposition may say Islam improved women’s status in 7th-century Arabia by limiting some abuses, granting inheritance, and recognizing women’s property rights. But historical improvement is not the same as promoting women’s rights in the modern sense. A law code may be better than what came before and still fall short of equality. The question is not whether Islam gave some rights compared with pre-Islamic customs; the question is whether Islam promotes women’s rights as equal rights. The evidence shows that traditional Islamic sources establish a gender hierarchy.

Therefore, I argue that Islam does not consistently promote women’s rights. It grants women certain protections, yes, but within a framework of male authority, unequal inheritance, unequal testimony, polygyny for men, and marital obedience. Protection is not the same as equality, and hierarchy is not the same as rights.

## Relevant citations

- **Qur’an 4:34** — Men are described as “in charge of women”; the verse addresses wives’ disobedience and includes the instruction often translated as “strike them.”  
- **Qur’an 4:11** — In inheritance, “the male shall have the equivalent of the share of two females.”  
- **Qur’an 2:282** — In financial contracts, two female witnesses may substitute for one male witness.  
- **Qur’an 4:3** — Men are permitted to marry up to four women under specified conditions.  
- **Qur’an 2:228** — States that women have rights similar to obligations, but “men have a degree over them.”  
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 304 / Sahih Muslim 79a** — Hadith describing women as “deficient in intelligence and religion.”  
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 3237; Sahih Muslim 1436** — Hadith stating that angels curse a wife who refuses her husband’s bed.  
- **Sunan Abi Dawud 2085; Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 1101** — Hadith often cited for the rule that marriage requires a guardian, though interpretations vary among legal schools.
steps.response_for:
Madam Chair, honorable judges:

The opposition’s argument rests on one major assumption: that “women’s rights” must mean identical rules in every legal context. But Islam’s claim is not that men and women are identical in every social obligation; it is that women possess dignity, moral agency, legal personality, property rights, marital consent, educational access, and protection from abuse. On that standard, Islam clearly promotes women’s rights.

Let me answer the opposition’s main points directly.

## 1. Qur’an 4:34 is not a license for male domination or abuse

The opposition cites Qur’an 4:34: “Men are qawwamun over women.” But *qawwamun* does not simply mean “superior.” It means maintainers, protectors, or those responsible for support. The verse itself gives the reason: because men are financially responsible for the family. In Islamic law, a husband must provide maintenance, while a wife’s wealth remains her own.

This must be read alongside the Qur’an’s broader marital ethic:

- “Live with them honorably” — Qur’an 4:19  
- “Do not retain them to harm them” — Qur’an 2:231  
- Marriage is based on “tranquility,” “affection,” and “mercy” — Qur’an 30:21  
- Spouses are “garments” for one another — Qur’an 2:187  

As for the controversial phrase often translated “strike them,” Islam’s own prophetic model severely restricts and morally undermines any abusive reading. The Prophet Muhammad, the practical interpreter of the Qur’an, **never struck a woman**.

Aisha reported:

> “The Messenger of God never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant.”  
> — Sahih Muslim 2328

He also said:

> “The best of you are those who are best to their wives.”  
> — Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3895

And he condemned men who beat their wives and then approach them intimately:

> “How does one of you beat his wife as he beats a slave and then sleep with her at the end of the day?”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 5204

So if Qur’an 4:34 is used to justify cruelty, control, or domestic violence, that contradicts the Prophet’s own example and the Qur’an’s command of honorable treatment. Islam promotes women’s rights by limiting male power under moral accountability, not by giving men unrestricted authority.

## 2. Inheritance rules do not mean women are “worth half”

The opposition cites Qur’an 4:11, where in one inheritance scenario a son receives the share of two daughters. But this is not a universal rule that women are always given half. Islamic inheritance law contains many cases where women inherit equally or even more than men.

For example:

- The mother and father each receive one-sixth when the deceased leaves children — Qur’an 4:11  
- Maternal siblings inherit equally, male and female — Qur’an 4:12  
- Women are explicitly guaranteed inheritance, which was revolutionary in a society where they could be deprived entirely — Qur’an 4:7  

The reason sons receive more in some cases is tied to financial obligation. In Islamic law, the man must pay the marriage gift, provide housing, food, and maintenance. The woman’s wealth remains her own. The Qur’an says:

> “For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned.”  
> — Qur’an 4:32

And:

> “Give women their bridal gifts graciously.”  
> — Qur’an 4:4

So inheritance is part of a broader economic structure in which women have property rights but are not burdened with the same financial duties. One may debate whether that model should be applied identically today, but it is inaccurate to claim that Islam denies women economic rights. On the contrary, it gave women legally protected ownership, inheritance, and marital wealth.

## 3. Qur’an 2:282 is not a blanket statement that women are less credible

The opposition also cites Qur’an 2:282, where two women may serve in place of one man in a specific type of financial contract. But the verse is about written deferred-debt transactions, not all testimony and not women’s general credibility.

The Qur’an does not establish a universal rule that “one man equals two women” in every legal or moral matter. In other contexts, testimony is not framed that way. For example, in cases of marital accusation, the Qur’an allows the husband and wife to give parallel oaths before God — Qur’an 24:6–9. In matters of faith, hadith, education, and law, women’s reports were accepted. Aisha, the Prophet’s wife, became one of the greatest authorities in Islamic knowledge and transmitted a large body of hadith consulted by male and female scholars alike.

There is even a hadith where the testimony of a woman concerning breastfeeding affected the validity of a marriage:

> Uqbah ibn al-Harith reported that a woman testified she had nursed him and his wife, and the Prophet instructed him to separate from her.  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 2640/2659

So the opposition overgeneralizes one commercial-contract rule into a sweeping claim that Islam considers women half-persons. That is not supported by the wider tradition.

## 4. Polygyny is restricted, not promoted as male privilege
