They understood later Medinan verses, especially in Sūrat al-Tawbah, as authorizing expansionist jihad against non-Muslim communities until they accepted Islam, submitted to Muslim rule, or paid jizya.

---

## 1. Qur’an 60:8 does not negate commands to fight other non-Muslims

The opponent cites:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you…”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

But this verse is conditional. It permits kindness toward non-Muslims who are not hostile. It does not say Muslims may never fight non-Muslims on religious-political grounds. The very next verse says:

> “Allah only forbids you from those who fought you because of religion and expelled you from your homes…”  
> — Qur’an 60:9

More importantly, other verses command fighting not merely against immediate attackers, but against categories of unbelievers until they submit.

For example:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day… from among those who were given the Scripture, until they pay the jizya with willing submission and feel themselves subdued.”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

This is not phrased as “fight only those currently attacking you.” It identifies Jews and Christians as targets of fighting until they pay jizya and accept subordinate status. That directly supports the proposition that Islamic scripture contains a doctrine of violence or coercive force toward non-Muslims under Islamic political authority.

---

## 2. Qur’an 2:190 is not the whole Qur’anic doctrine of war

The opponent cites:

> “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress.”  
> — Qur’an 2:190

But the surrounding verses are more severe:

> “Kill them wherever you find them and expel them from wherever they expelled you…”  
> — Qur’an 2:191

And:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah.”  
> — Qur’an 2:193

Likewise:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”  
> — Qur’an 8:39

Classical jurists often understood these verses as establishing a broader obligation of jihad, not merely a narrow right of self-defense. “Do not transgress” was commonly interpreted as limiting methods of war—such as killing women, children, monks, or non-combatants—not as forbidding offensive jihad altogether.

So yes, Islam contains rules of war. But having rules for war does not prove the religion does not promote war against non-Muslim groups. It may simply mean the violence is regulated.

---

## 3. “No compulsion in religion” does not eliminate coercive political submission

The opponent cites:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

But this does not erase Qur’an 9:29. Classical Islamic law commonly reconciled these ideas by saying non-Muslims, especially Jews and Christians, need not be forcibly converted, but they may be fought until they submit to Muslim political rule and pay jizya.

That is still coercive. The choice offered in much classical jurisprudence was not simply “believe whatever you want in peace.” It was often: accept Islam, pay jizya under Muslim dominance, or face war.

That is why Qur’an 9:29 is so important. It does not say, “Fight them until they stop attacking you.” It says:

> “until they pay the jizya… and feel themselves subdued.”  
> — Qur’an 9:29

So “no forced conversion” does not mean “no religiously authorized violence against non-Muslim communities.”

---

## 4. The “Sword Verse” was historically read by many as broadening jihad

Qur’an 9:5 states:

> “When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, capture them, besiege them, and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go…”  
> — Qur’an 9:5

The opponent would likely say this was limited to treaty-breaking Arabian pagans. That is one modern interpretation. But historically, many exegetes treated this verse as having broad legal significance.

Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir on Qur’an 9:5, reports the view that this verse was known as the “Verse of the Sword” and that it abrogated or superseded earlier permissions of peace with idolaters. Al-Qurtubi and other classical commentators also discuss its legal force in relation to fighting polytheists.

Even if one disputes abrogation, the point remains: this was not merely an extremist fringe reading. Significant classical authorities understood these verses as authorizing armed struggle against non-Muslim groups.

---

## 5. The hadith tradition contains broad commands to fight “the people”

The opponent cites hadiths forbidding the killing of women, children, and protected non-Muslims. Those are real. But again, they regulate violence; they do not eliminate it.

There is also the famous hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22

This is a very strong statement. It does not merely say, “I have been permitted to defend myself.” It says, “I have been commanded to fight the people until…” they accept the Islamic confession.

Classical scholars debated its scope, especially regarding People of the Book who could pay jizya. But the hadith still became a central proof-text for jihad doctrine. The opposition cannot simply ignore it while citing only hadiths about restraint.

Also, the hadith about killing a person under covenant proves a narrower point than the opponent claims:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3166

This protects non-Muslims under treaty or Muslim protection. It does not establish equal protection for all non-Muslims everywhere. Classical law distinguished between protected non-Muslims — dhimmis or mu‘ahids — and enemy non-Muslims, often called harbis. That distinction itself shows that Islamic law developed categories under which violence against non-Muslims was legitimate.

---

## 6. Classical Islamic jurisprudence often endorsed offensive jihad

This is the strongest evidence against the opposition’s claim. If Islam were clearly and only defensive, we would expect classical jurists to say so. Many did not.

In the Shafi‘i legal manual *Reliance of the Traveller*, jihad is defined as:

> “war against non-Muslims.”  
> — Ahmad ibn Naqib al-Misri, *Reliance of the Traveller*, Book o9.0

The same manual states that jihad is a communal obligation and that the caliph fights Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians until they become Muslim or pay jizya.  
— *Reliance of the Traveller*, o9.1, o9.8

The Hanafi manual *al-Hidayah* similarly explains that non-Muslim enemies are to be invited to Islam; if they refuse, they may be invited to pay jizya; if they refuse that, they are fought.  
— al-Marghinani, *al-Hidayah*, Book of Siyar/Jihad

Al-Mawardi, in *al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya*, describes jihad as one of the duties of the ruler and discusses fighting those who refuse Islam or submission. Ibn Rushd, in *Bidayat al-Mujtahid*, also treats jihad as a legal institution directed against non-Muslim peoples, while discussing juristic disagreements about who may pay jizya and under what conditions.

Modern scholars of Islamic law have recognized this as well. Majid Khadduri, in *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, describes classical jihad doctrine as a means by which the Islamic state expanded the realm of Islam. Rudolph Peters, in *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, likewise explains that classical jurists generally treated jihad as a collective duty and not merely as defensive warfare.

This does not mean every Muslim today accepts offensive jihad. Many do not. But the debate is about whether Islam, as represented in authoritative texts and classical doctrine, has promoted violence toward non-Muslims. The answer is yes.

---

## 7. Rules protecting civilians do not disprove religiously authorized violence

The opponent notes that Muhammad prohibited killing women and children:

> Sahih al-Bukhari 3014; Sahih Muslim 1744

But this proves only that Islamic law developed rules about who may be killed in war. It does not prove that the war itself was only defensive or that non-Muslim communities could not be attacked.

A legal system can prohibit killing civilians while still authorizing aggressive war against enemy societies. Therefore, non-combatant protections do not refute the proposition. They merely show that the violence was regulated.

---

## Conclusion

The opposition’s mistake is treating peaceful verses as if they cancel the entire jihad tradition. They do not. Islamic sources contain both peaceful and militant strands. The Qur’an commands kindness toward peaceful non-Muslims in some places, but it also commands fighting unbelievers in others. The hadith literature contains protections for civilians and treaty-holders, but it also contains broad commands to fight “the people.” Classical jurisprudence often systematized these texts into doctrines of jihad, jizya, dhimmi status, and war against non-Muslim polities.

So the affirmative position is not that all Muslims are violent, nor that Islam contains no teachings of mercy. The point is narrower and historically defensible: significant authoritative Islamic texts and classical interpretations have promoted, justified, or normalized violence and coercive domination toward non-Muslims under certain circumstances.

That is enough to sustain the proposition.
steps.response_against:
## Rebuttal against the proposition: “Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims”

The affirmative has made a stronger case for a different proposition: that **Islamic law contains doctrines regulating war, including war against non-Muslim polities**. That is true. But it does **not** prove that Islam “promotes violence toward non-Muslims” as such.

Nearly every religious and legal civilization has had rules for war. The existence of war-law does not mean the religion promotes violence against outsiders. The question is whether Islam teaches violence against people *because they are non-Muslim*, or whether its fighting texts are tied to aggression, treaty-breaking, persecution, and state conflict. A fair reading of the Qur’an, hadith, and even much classical law supports the latter.

---

# 1. Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29 are not free-standing commands to attack all non-Muslims

The affirmative relies heavily on Sūrat al-Tawbah, especially Qur’an 9:5 and 9:29. But those verses must be read with the surrounding verses.

Qur’an 9 opens by addressing **specific treaty-breaking Arabian polytheists**, not all non-Muslims:

> “A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you had made a treaty among the polytheists…”  
> — **Qur’an 9:1**

Then the Qur’an immediately exempts those polytheists who kept their treaties:

> “Except those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists and then they have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term.”  
> — **Qur’an 9:4**

That matters. If Qur’an 9:5 meant “kill all polytheists because they are polytheists,” verse 9:4 would make no sense. The Qur’an preserves treaties with non-Muslims who did not betray Muslims.

Even more importantly, only one verse after the so-called “Sword Verse,” the Qur’an commands Muslims to grant protection to a polytheist seeking safety:

> “And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah; then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> — **Qur’an 9:6**

That is decisive against the idea that Qur’an 9:5 is a universal command to kill non-Muslims. The same passage says a polytheist may be protected and escorted to safety.

The context continues:

> “So long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them.”  
> — **Qur’an 9:7**

And later:

> “Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, planned to expel the Messenger, and began against you the first time?”  
> — **Qur’an 9:13**

So the Qur’an itself gives the reason for the fighting: treaty-breaking, aggression, and attempted expulsion — not mere non-Muslim identity.

---

# 2. Qur’an 2:190–193 supports defensive and restrained fighting

The affirmative cites Qur’an 2:191 and 2:193, but the passage begins with the controlling principle:

> “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:190**

The next verse says:

> “Kill them wherever you find them and expel them from wherever they expelled you…”  
> — **Qur’an 2:191**

The phrase “expel them from wherever they expelled you” shows the context: Muslims had been expelled and attacked.

Then the passage adds:

> “But if they cease, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:192**

And:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah. But if they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:193**

“Fitnah” here is not simply “non-Muslim belief.” In this context it refers to persecution, oppression, and religious coercion. That is why the verse says if they cease, aggression must stop.

So the passage does not teach: “Fight non-Muslims until they become Muslim.” It teaches: fight persecutors and aggressors until persecution ends, and stop when they stop.

---

# 3. “No compulsion in religion” is not a minor verse that can be brushed aside

The affirmative says Qur’an 2:256 only forbids forced conversion, not political submission. But that is still very important.

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:256**

Classical exegetes did not simply erase this verse. Ibn Kathir, for example, explains:

> “Do not force anyone to enter the religion of Islam, for it is clear and evident.”  
> — **Ibn Kathir, Tafsir on Qur’an 2:256**

This verse directly contradicts the claim that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims because they are non-Muslims. If unbelief itself were the cause for violence, forced conversion would be expected. But Islamic law historically allowed Jews, Christians, and others to remain non-Muslim under Muslim rule.

One may criticize premodern jizya systems by modern liberal standards, but jizya is not the same as “Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims.” It was a tax attached to political rule in a premodern imperial world. Muslims also paid obligatory taxes such as zakat. Non-Muslim communities were not automatically to be killed or forcibly converted.

---

# 4. Qur’an 9:29 concerns political conflict, not random violence against Jews and Christians

The affirmative quotes:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah nor in the Last Day… from among those who were given the Scripture, until they pay the jizya…”  
> — **Qur’an 9:29**

But again, this is a command of state warfare, not private violence, terrorism, or a general command to harm Jews and Christians. Classical Muslim jurists treated this as part of **siyar**, the law of relations between political communities.

The Prophet himself had treaties with Jewish and pagan tribes. The Constitution of Medina recognized the Jews as a community with their religion:

> “The Jews have their religion and the Muslims have theirs.”  
> — **Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah, Constitution of Medina**

The Qur’an also commands justice and kindness toward non-hostile non-Muslims:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion and have not expelled you from your homes. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.”  
> — **Qur’an 60:8**

That verse is not cancelled by Qur’an 9:29. Rather, the texts together show a distinction between peaceful non-Muslims and hostile political enemies.

---

# 5. The “Sword Verse” abrogation claim is not a consensus and cannot override the Qur’an’s own context

The affirmative says many exegetes treated Qur’an 9:5 as the “Sword Verse.” Some did. But that does not prove that Islam universally promotes violence toward non-Muslims.

First, even classical commentators who discussed the “Sword Verse” did not read it as permission to kill all non-Muslims indiscriminately. Women, children, monks, peasants, envoys, treaty-holders, and protected persons were generally excluded.

Second, Qur’an 9:5 is surrounded by restrictions: treaty preservation in 9:4, asylum in 9:6, upright dealing in 9:7, and the stated reason of fighting treaty-breakers in 9:13.

Third, the Qur’an elsewhere commands peace when the enemy inclines to peace:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and trust in Allah.”  
> — **Qur’an 8:61**

If Qur’an 9:5 had cancelled all peaceful relations with non-Muslims, Qur’an 9:6 itself would be impossible, because it commands protection for a polytheist. So the broadest “abrogation” reading is internally strained.

---

# 6. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” is not unlimited

The affirmative cites:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

But Islamic scholars did not read this as meaning every non-Muslim on earth must be fought until conversion.

Why? Because other authentic texts qualify it.

The Qur’an allows People of the Book to remain in their religion under jizya:

> **Qur’an 9:29**

The Qur’an forbids compulsion in religion:

> **Qur’an 2:256**

The Prophet forbade killing protected non-Muslims:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166**

Classical commentators recognized that the hadith is general in wording but specified by other texts. Al-Nawawi explains in his commentary on Sahih Muslim that the general wording of “the people” is qualified by other evidence, including the acceptance of jizya from People of the Book.  
— **Al-Nawawi, Sharh Sahih Muslim, commentary on hadith 22**

Ibn Hajar likewise notes that the hadith is not applied absolutely to every human being, because other texts establish exceptions.  
— **Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari 25**

So the hadith cannot be used as a universal command to attack all non-Muslims.

---

# 7. Classical jurisprudence is more nuanced than “Islam promotes violence”

The affirmative cites manuals such as *Reliance of the Traveller* and *al-Hidayah*. But classical jurisprudence developed in a premodern world of empires, frontiers, raids, and no modern international law. Its categories of “dar al-Islam” and “dar al-harb” were political-legal categories, not a license for ordinary Muslims to attack non-Muslims.

Even within classical law, there were major restraints.

The Prophet forbade killing women and children:

> Ibn Umar reported that a woman was found killed in one of the battles, and the Messenger of Allah condemned the killing of women and children.  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3014; Sahih Muslim 1744**

He also said:

> “Do not wish to meet the enemy, but ask Allah for safety.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 2966; Sahih Muslim 1742**

That is not a religion glorifying violence.

Many jurists also held that the effective cause for killing in war is combatancy, not disbelief itself. Hanafi jurists especially emphasized this. Al-Kasani states that those who do not fight, such as women and children, are not killed because the legal cause of killing is combat, not mere unbelief.  
— **Al-Kasani, Bada’i al-Sana’i, Book of Siyar/Jihad**

Ibn Taymiyyah similarly wrote that those who do not fight are not to be killed, such as women, children, monks, the elderly, the blind, and others.  
— **Ibn Taymiyyah, Majmu‘ al-Fatawa, vol. 28**

This matters because if Islam promoted violence against non-Muslims *as non-Muslims*, non-combatant status would not matter. But in Islamic law it does matter.

---

# 8. Protection of non-Muslims is also part of authoritative Islamic teaching

The affirmative treats protection of non-Muslims as a narrow exception. But it is a major part of the tradition.

The Qur’an commands justice even toward enemies:

> “Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> — **Qur’an 5:8**

It commands kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims:

> **Qur’an 60:8**

It recognizes religious difference:

> “For you is your religion, and for me is my religion.”  
> — **Qur’an 109:6**

It protects houses of worship, including non-Muslim ones:

> “Had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques — where Allah’s name is often mentioned — would have been destroyed.”  
> — **Qur’an 22:40**

And the Prophet gave severe warnings against harming protected non-Muslims:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166**

These are not marginal texts. They are central evidence that Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims generally.

---

# Conclusion

The affirmative’s case depends on conflating three different things:

1. **Islam having laws of war**,  
2. **Some classical jurists allowing offensive jihad under state authority**, and  
3. **Islam promoting violence toward non-Muslims as such**.

Only the first two are historically arguable. The third does not follow.

The Qur’an repeatedly distinguishes between peaceful non-Muslims and hostile aggressors. It commands justice, permits treaties, protects asylum seekers, forbids religious compulsion, and orders Muslims to accept peace when the enemy inclines to peace. The hadith prohibit killing civilians and threaten severe punishment for killing protected non-Muslims. Classical law, even where it allowed warfare, regulated it through state authority, combatant distinction, treaties, safe-conduct, and protection of non-Muslim communities.

Therefore, the proposition remains false. Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims. It permits regulated fighting in particular political and military circumstances, especially against aggression, persecution, and treaty-breaking, while commanding justice and peaceful coexistence with non-Muslims who are not at war with Muslims.
steps.conclusion_for:
## Concluding Statement — Affirmative

Ladies and gentlemen, the key issue in this debate is not whether all Muslims are violent. They are not. Nor is it whether Islamic scripture contains teachings of mercy, justice, restraint, and coexistence. It clearly does. The issue is whether Islam’s authoritative texts and classical legal tradition have also promoted, justified, or normalized violence against non-Muslims under certain circumstances.

The evidence shows that they have.

We have seen that the Qur’an contains verses commanding fighting against unbelievers, including Qur’an 9:5 and Qur’an 9:29. The latter specifically commands fighting People of the Book “until they pay the jizya” and are subdued. That is not merely a defensive command against active attackers; it establishes a religious-political framework in which non-Muslim communities may be fought until they submit to Muslim rule.

We have also seen that the hadith literature contains broad statements such as: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.” Whatever qualifications later scholars placed on that narration, it undeniably became an important proof-text in the development of jihad doctrine.

The opposition has cited verses such as “There is no compulsion in religion,” “If they incline to peace, incline to it,” and commands to show kindness to peaceful non-Muslims. Those texts matter, but they do not erase the militant texts. At most, they show that Islam contains multiple strands: peaceful teachings on one hand, and doctrines of armed struggle and subordination of non-Muslims on the other.

Most importantly, classical Islamic jurisprudence did not generally interpret jihad as purely defensive in the modern sense. Major legal manuals and jurists treated jihad as a communal obligation, discussed fighting non-Muslim polities, and developed rules under which Jews, Christians, and others could avoid death or forced conversion by accepting dhimmi status and paying jizya. That is not equal peaceful coexistence; it is coerced political submission backed by the threat of force.

The opposition’s strongest argument is that Islam regulates violence: it forbids killing women, children, monks, and protected treaty-holders. But regulation is not the same as rejection. A doctrine can prohibit certain forms of violence while still authorizing war against non-Muslim communities. Rules of war do not prove that the war itself is always defensive or morally neutral.

So my position has been careful and limited: Islam is not monolithic, and many Muslims today reject violent or supremacist interpretations. But historically and textually, there are significant Islamic sources and classical doctrines that authorize violence, warfare, and coercive domination toward non-Muslims in defined circumstances.

Therefore, the proposition stands: not because every Muslim promotes violence, and not because Islam contains no peaceful teachings, but because authoritative Islamic texts and classical interpretations have indeed promoted and legitimized violence against non-Muslims under certain conditions.
steps.conclusion_against:
## Concluding statement against the proposition

Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition claims that **Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims**. That is a sweeping claim, and it has not been proven.

What the affirmative has shown is that Islamic sources contain laws of war, and that some classical jurists accepted forms of state warfare against non-Muslim polities. But that is not the same as proving that Islam promotes violence against non-Muslims *as non-Muslims*. A religion having rules for warfare does not mean it glorifies or promotes violence against outsiders. Christianity, Judaism, secular empires, and modern states have all had laws of war; that alone does not define their entire moral teaching.

The central point is this: **Islam distinguishes between peaceful non-Muslims and hostile aggressors**.

The Qur’an explicitly says:

> “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion and have not expelled you from your homes.”  
> — Qur’an 60:8

That verse is decisive. If Islam promoted violence toward non-Muslims simply because they are non-Muslim, it would not command kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims.

The Qur’an’s fighting passages are not free-floating commands to attack all unbelievers. They are tied to persecution, expulsion, treaty-breaking, and war. Qur’an 2:190 says:

> “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.”

Qur’an 9, often cited by critics, begins by addressing treaty-breaking groups, while explicitly exempting those who kept their treaties. It even commands Muslims to protect a polytheist who seeks safety and escort him to a place of security. That is not indiscriminate violence.

Islam also rejects forced conversion:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — Qur’an 2:256

The affirmative tried to reduce this point by saying that non-Muslims could still be subject to political rule or jizya. But even then, the fact remains: Islamic teaching did not require the extermination or forced conversion of non-Muslims. Historically, Jewish, Christian, Zoroastrian, Hindu, and other communities continued to exist under Muslim rule for centuries. That historical reality is difficult to reconcile with the claim that Islam simply promotes violence toward non-Muslims.

The hadith evidence also supports restraint. The Prophet Muhammad forbade the killing of women and children, condemned unlawful killing, and warned:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — Sahih al-Bukhari 3166

This is not a minor teaching. It shows that harming protected non-Muslims is treated as a grave sin.

The affirmative’s argument depends heavily on taking wartime texts and classical imperial legal doctrines as though they represent Islam’s entire attitude toward non-Muslims. But the Islamic tradition contains clear commands of justice, treaty-keeping, mercy, civilian protection, religious non-compulsion, and peaceful coexistence. Those cannot simply be brushed aside.

So the proper conclusion is not that Islam promotes violence toward non-Muslims. The proper conclusion is more nuanced: Islam permits regulated warfare in specific circumstances, especially against aggression, persecution, and hostile political forces, while forbidding transgression and commanding justice toward peaceful non-Muslims.

The proposition is therefore too broad, too simplistic, and unsupported by a fair reading of the sources. Islam does not promote violence toward non-Muslims as such. It promotes justice, restraint, and peace where peace is possible, while allowing self-defense and regulated warfare under defined conditions.

For these reasons, the proposition should be rejected.

debates.topic: Islam promotes women's rights

steps.opening_for:
**Opening Argument — For the Proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights.”**

Ladies and gentlemen, the claim before us is not that every Muslim society has perfectly upheld women’s rights. Clearly, many have not. The claim is that **Islam itself—through its core texts and principles—promotes the dignity, legal agency, spiritual equality, and social rights of women.** On that claim, the evidence is strong.

Islam emerged in a society where women were often treated as property, denied inheritance, forced into marriages, and even subjected to female infanticide. The Qur’an confronted this directly, condemning the killing of infant girls and holding society morally accountable for it: *“When the girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed…”* **(Qur’an 81:8–9)**. This was not a minor reform; it was a declaration that female life has sacred worth.

Islam also affirms the **spiritual equality** of men and women. The Qur’an states:

> “Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women… Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward.”  
> **Qur’an 33:35**

In other words, moral worth before God is not male. It is human. The Qur’an further says that men and women are protectors and allies of one another in public moral life: **Qur’an 9:71**.

Islam also gave women **legal and economic rights**. Women were granted the right to own property, earn wealth, and retain their own income:

> “For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned.”  
> **Qur’an 4:32**

Women were also granted inheritance rights:

> “For men is a share of what parents and relatives leave, and for women is a share…”  
> **Qur’an 4:7**

This was revolutionary in its historical context. Islam did not treat women merely as dependents; it recognized them as legal persons with financial rights.

Islam also protects women in marriage. The Qur’an commands men to live with women honorably:

> “Live with them in kindness.”  
> **Qur’an 4:19**

It gives women the right to receive and keep their marital gift:

> “Give women their bridal gifts graciously.”  
> **Qur’an 4:4**

And the Prophet Muhammad explicitly prohibited forced marriage. He said that a woman may not be married without her consent. **Sahih al-Bukhari 5136; Sahih Muslim 1419**. In another report, a woman complained that her father had married her against her will, and the Prophet gave her the choice to annul the marriage. **Sahih al-Bukhari 5138**.

Islam also recognizes women’s right to seek divorce. The well-known case of the wife of Thabit ibn Qays shows the Prophet permitting a woman to end a marriage through *khulʿ*. **Sahih al-Bukhari 5273**.

The Prophet’s own conduct reinforces this ethic. He said:

> “The best of you are those who are best to their wives.”  
> **Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi 1162**

He also said:

> “Women are the twin halves of men.”  
> **Sunan Abi Dawud 236; Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi 113**

Women in early Islam were not invisible. They pledged allegiance to the Prophet, as referenced in **Qur’an 60:12**. They transmitted religious knowledge, debated legal issues, participated in public life, and were recognized as scholars—most famously ʿA’ishah, one of the major transmitters of hadith and a legal authority for the early Muslim community.

So the proposition stands: **Islam promotes women’s rights by affirming women’s spiritual equality, protecting their lives and dignity, granting them property and inheritance rights, requiring consent in marriage, permitting divorce, and demanding honorable treatment.**

Where Muslim communities violate these rights, the problem is not that they are following Islam too closely; it is often that they are ignoring Islam’s own standards. Islam’s foundational message is that women are not property, not spiritually inferior, not socially irrelevant, and not without rights. They are moral agents, believers, citizens of the community, and bearers of God-given dignity.
steps.opening_against:
## Opening argument against the proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights”

Ladies and gentlemen, I oppose the proposition—not because Muslim women lack agency, dignity, or the ability to reinterpret their tradition, and not because no Islamic text gives women protections. Rather, I oppose it because the proposition claims that *Islam promotes women’s rights* in a broad and modern sense. If by “women’s rights” we mean equal legal personhood, equal marital authority, equal access to divorce, equal inheritance, equal testimony, and freedom from male guardianship, then traditional Islamic doctrine does not promote women’s rights; it institutionalizes gender hierarchy.

First, the Qur’an explicitly places men in a position of authority over women in marriage. Qur’an 4:34 says that “men are in charge of women” because God has given some more than others and because men spend of their wealth. The same verse describes righteous women as obedient and permits husbands to admonish wives, separate from them in bed, and, according to many traditional translations, “strike” them. Whatever modern reformers argue about the wording, the historical legal tradition overwhelmingly treated this verse as establishing male marital authority, not equality.

Second, Islamic law contains unequal rules of legal and financial status. Qur’an 4:11 gives a son the share of two daughters in inheritance. Qur’an 2:282, in the context of financial testimony, instructs believers to call two male witnesses, or one man and two women, “so that if one of the women errs, the other can remind her.” These are not merely cultural practices; they are scriptural rules that became embedded in Islamic jurisprudence. A system that gives women half the inheritance share of men in key cases and treats two women as equivalent to one man in testimony cannot honestly be described as promoting equal women’s rights.

Third, marriage and divorce are asymmetrical. Qur’an 4:3 allows men to marry up to four women; there is no equivalent right for women to have multiple husbands. Qur’an 2:228 says that women have rights similar to obligations, but then adds that “men have a degree over them.” Classical Islamic law also gave men easier unilateral divorce through *talaq*, while women often required judicial intervention or financial compensation through *khulʿ*. Again, the structure is not equality but male privilege.

Fourth, the hadith literature reinforces this hierarchy. In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, women are described as “deficient in intelligence and religion,” with the explanation tied partly to testimony and menstruation. Another hadith says that if a wife refuses her husband’s bed, angels curse her until morning. Sahih al-Bukhari also records Muhammad as saying that a people who appoint a woman as ruler will not succeed. These narrations have had real legal and social consequences in Muslim societies, particularly regarding leadership, sexuality, and the expectation of female obedience.

The opposition may argue that Islam improved women’s status compared with pre-Islamic Arabia. Even if that is partly true, it does not prove that Islam promotes women’s rights by contemporary standards. A system can be historically progressive in one era and still be unequal by principle. The debate is not whether Islam gave women *some* rights; it is whether Islam promotes *women’s rights* as equal human rights. On inheritance, testimony, marriage, divorce, sexual autonomy, and authority within the family, the traditional sources repeatedly give men superior status.

Therefore, I submit that Islam, as classically grounded in its scripture and legal tradition, does not promote women’s rights in the sense of equality. It grants women certain protections within a patriarchal framework—but protection under male authority is not the same as equal rights.

## Relevant citations

- Qur’an 4:34 — men are “in charge of” women; wife discipline.  
- Qur’an 4:11 — male inheritance share equal to that of two females in certain cases.  
- Qur’an 2:282 — two female witnesses in place of one male witness in financial contracts.  
- Qur’an 4:3 — men permitted up to four wives.  
- Qur’an 2:228 — men have “a degree” over women.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 304; Sahih Muslim 79a — women described as “deficient in intelligence and religion.”  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 3237; Sahih Muslim 1436 — angels curse a wife who refuses her husband’s bed.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 7099 — “Never will succeed such a nation as makes a woman their ruler.”
steps.response_for:
## Rebuttal — For the Proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights”

The opposition’s argument depends on one central move: it defines “women’s rights” as absolute sameness in every legal rule, then concludes that any gender differentiation means Islam does not promote women’s rights. But that is too narrow. A system can promote women’s rights by recognizing women’s dignity, property, consent, education, legal agency, marital protections, inheritance, public participation, and spiritual equality—even if some rules are structured differently for men and women.

The real question is not whether every classical jurist was perfectly egalitarian by modern liberal standards. The question is whether Islam’s core sources elevate women’s status, protect women from abuse, recognize their agency, and give them enforceable rights. They do.

---

## 1. Qur’an 4:34 does not make men morally superior to women

The opponent cites Qur’an 4:34: “Men are qawwamun over women.” But *qawwamun* is not a declaration that men are inherently superior. It is tied in the verse itself to responsibility and financial maintenance: men are charged with supporting the family from their wealth.

That reading is reinforced by the Qur’an’s broader marital ethic:

> “And live with them in kindness.”  
> **Qur’an 4:19**

> “They are garments for you, and you are garments for them.”  
> **Qur’an 2:187**

> “He created for you spouses from among yourselves that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy.”  
> **Qur’an 30:21**

So the Qur’anic model of marriage is not tyranny; it is mercy, mutual protection, and responsibility.

As for the disputed phrase often translated “strike them,” it must be read through the Prophet’s own conduct and teaching. ʿA’ishah reported:

> “The Messenger of Allah never struck anything with his hand, neither a woman nor a servant.”  
> **Sahih Muslim 2328**

The Prophet also said:

> “Do not beat the female servants of Allah.”  
> **Sunan Abi Dawud 2146**

And he said:

> “The best of you are those who are best to their wives.”  
> **Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi 1162**

So even where classical jurists discussed Qur’an 4:34, the Prophetic model severely restricts and morally discourages harm. Islam’s normative example is not domestic violence; it is non-abuse, kindness, and restraint.

---

## 2. Inheritance rules are not proof that women lack rights

The opponent cites Qur’an 4:11, where in some cases a male receives the share of two females. But this is not the whole inheritance system.

First, Islam gave women inheritance rights in a society where women were often excluded from inheritance altogether:

> “For men is a share of what parents and relatives leave, and for women is a share of what parents and relatives leave.”  
> **Qur’an 4:7**

That is a direct affirmation of women’s financial personhood.

Second, women do not always inherit half of men. In some cases women inherit equally with men. For example, parents can each receive one-sixth:

> “For each of his parents is a sixth of what he leaves…”  
> **Qur’an 4:11**

Maternal siblings also inherit equally:

> “If there are brothers and sisters, then each one of them receives a sixth; but if they are more than that, they share in a third.”  
> **Qur’an 4:12**

Third, Islamic financial law must be read as a whole. Men are legally obligated to provide marital maintenance, housing, and financial support, while a woman’s wealth remains her own:

> “Give women their bridal gifts graciously.”  
> **Qur’an 4:4**

> “For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned.”  
> **Qur’an 4:32**

So the inheritance rule is connected to financial obligations, not to women’s lesser human worth. Islam gave women the right to own, inherit, earn, and retain property independently.

---

## 3. Qur’an 2:282 is not a blanket statement that women are half-witnesses

The opponent cites Qur’an 2:282, concerning written contracts for deferred debts. But that verse is about a specific financial documentation procedure in a commercial context. It is not a universal rule saying women are intellectually or legally worth half of men.

The Qur’an itself gives women’s testimony full legal weight in other contexts. In the procedure of *liʿan*, where spouses testify in a serious marital accusation, the woman’s oath counters the man’s oath:

> “And it will avert punishment from her if she testifies four times by Allah that he is of the liars.”  
> **Qur’an 24:8**

This shows that the Qur’an does not treat women’s testimony as universally inferior.

Moreover, Islamic religious knowledge itself depends heavily on women’s testimony. ʿA’ishah, Umm Salamah, Hafsah, and many other women transmitted hadith and gave legal opinions. If women were inherently unreliable, the Islamic scholarly tradition could not have accepted women as transmitters of revelation and law.

The Qur’an even preserves the case of a woman who challenged a legal matter before the Prophet:

> “Allah has certainly heard the statement of the woman who argues with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah…”  
> **Qur’an 58:1**

That is a powerful image: a woman’s legal complaint is heard by the Prophet and vindicated by revelation.

---

## 4. Marriage in Islam requires female consent and protects women’s legal agency

The opponent argues that marriage is asymmetrical. But Islam did not make women passive objects of marriage. It explicitly recognizes consent.

The Prophet said:

> “A previously married woman must not be married until she is consulted, and a virgin must not be married until her permission is sought.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5136; Sahih Muslim 1419**

In another case, a woman complained that her father had married her without her consent, and the Prophet gave her the choice to annul the marriage:

> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5138**

This is a major women’s right: a woman cannot be forced into marriage.

Islam also protects women financially in marriage. The bridal gift belongs to the woman, not her father, husband, or guardian:

> “Give women their bridal gifts graciously.”  
> **Qur’an 4:4**

And men are commanded:

> “Live with them in kindness.”  
> **Qur’an 4:19**

So Islamic marriage is not supposed to be ownership. It is a contract with consent, financial rights, and moral obligations.

---

## 5. Divorce is not exclusively male-controlled

The opponent mentions *talaq*, but Islamic law also recognizes women’s avenues out of marriage.

The wife of Thabit ibn Qays came to the Prophet and said she could not remain in the marriage. The Prophet permitted her to return the garden given as bridal gift and allowed the marriage to end through *khulʿ*:

> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5273**

The Qur’an also recognizes separation with dignity and forbids men from using marriage or divorce to harm women:

> “Do not retain them to harm them so that you transgress.”  
> **Qur’an 2:231**

> “Either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness.”  
> **Qur’an 2:229**

The Prophet also taught the general legal principle:

> “There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm.”  
> **Sunan Ibn Majah 2340; al-Muwattaʾ 31.13**

So while divorce procedures may differ, Islam does not trap women in marriage without remedy. It gives them rights to consent, financial protection, judicial recourse, and *khulʿ*.

---

## 6. Polygyny is restricted, not promoted as male privilege without limits

The opponent cites Qur’an 4:3. But the verse does not simply say, “Men may marry four.” It is revealed in the context of justice toward vulnerable women and orphans, and it places a condition on polygyny:

> “Marry those that please you of women, two, three, or four; but if you fear that you will not be just, then one.”  
> **Qur’an 4:3**

The condition is justice. The Qur’an later warns:

> “You will never be able to be completely just between wives, even if you strive…”  
> **Qur’an 4:129**

So Islam restricted an existing practice and made justice a condition. It did not create unlimited male sexual entitlement. In many Islamic legal traditions, women can also stipulate conditions in the marriage contract, including restrictions relating to polygyny, based on the Prophetic principle:

> “The conditions most deserving to be fulfilled are those by which intimacy becomes lawful.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 2721; Sahih Muslim 1418**

---

## 7. The “deficient in intelligence and religion” hadith is not a denial of women’s dignity

The opponent cites the hadith describing women as “deficient in intelligence and religion.” This narration must be understood carefully. The hadith itself explains “deficiency in religion” as women being exempt from prayer and fasting during menstruation. That is not moral inferiority; it is a legal exemption.

As for “intelligence,” the hadith connects it to the specific testimony rule in Qur’an 2:282, not to women’s universal intellectual capacity. Islam’s actual history disproves any claim that women were considered incapable of knowledge. ʿA’ishah was one of the greatest jurists and hadith transmitters of the early Muslim community. Women taught men, transmitted hadith, issued legal opinions, and preserved religious knowledge.

The Qur’an’s standard of human superiority is not gender but righteousness:

> “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”  
> **Qur’an 49:13**

And:

> “Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely give them a good life.”  
> **Qur’an 16:97**

So Islam does not teach that women are spiritually or morally inferior.

---

## 8. The hadith about wives and marital intimacy cannot be used to justify coercion

The opponent cites the hadith about angels cursing a wife who refuses her husband’s bed. But Islamic marital ethics are reciprocal. The Prophet taught:

> “Your wife has a right over you.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 1968**

The Qur’an commands kindness and forbids harm:

> “Live with them in kindness.”  
> **Qur’an 4:19**

> “Do not retain them to harm them.”  
> **Qur’an 2:231**

And the legal maxim remains:

> “There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm.”  
> **Sunan Ibn Majah 2340**

So the hadith cannot be interpreted as permission for sexual violence or coercion. Islam recognizes marital obligations, but those obligations are governed by mercy, dignity, and the prohibition of harm.

---

## 9. The hadith about female rulers is context-specific and does not erase women’s public agency

The opponent cites the hadith that a people who appoint a woman ruler will not succeed. That report was said in connection with the Persian Empire appointing the daughter of Chosroes amid political collapse. Many scholars understood it in that historical context, while others debated its scope.

But the Qur’an itself presents the Queen of Sheba as an intelligent and consultative ruler:

> “She said, ‘O eminent ones, advise me in my affair. I would not decide a matter until you witness for me.’”  
> **Qur’an 27:32**

Her leadership is portrayed with wisdom, consultation, and eventual recognition of truth.

The Qur’an also describes believing men and women as public moral partners:

> “The believing men and believing women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong…”  
> **Qur’an 9:71**

Women pledged allegiance to the Prophet:

> **Qur’an 60:12**

Women participated in religious transmission, public consultation, legal complaint, education, and social affairs. So Islam does not erase women from public life.

---

## Conclusion

The opposition is right that some Islamic rules differentiate between men and women. But differentiation is not the same as denying rights. Islam gave women rights to life, dignity, property, inheritance, consent in marriage, marital gifts, divorce through *khulʿ*, education, religious authority, legal complaint, and public moral participation.

The Qur’an says:

> “Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women… Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward.”  
> **Qur’an 33:35**

And:

> “The believing men and believing women are allies of one another.”  
> **Qur’an 9:71**

Therefore, the proposition stands. Islam promotes women’s rights—not by claiming that men and women are identical in every legal role, but by affirming women as full moral agents, legal persons, property holders, believers, spouses with rights, and participants in the life of the community. Where Muslim societies deny those rights, they are failing Islam’s own standards, not fulfilling them.
steps.response_against:
## Rebuttal — Against the proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights”

The proposition’s defense rests on a major retreat. My opponent no longer argues that Islam gives women equal rights; instead, they argue that Islam gives women *some* rights, protections, and spiritual dignity. But that is not enough to prove the proposition.

A patriarchal legal system can grant women property, inheritance, consent, and moral worth while still subordinating them to men. The question is not whether Islam improved some conditions compared with pre-Islamic Arabia. The question is whether Islam, in its core texts and classical law, promotes women’s rights in the sense of equal legal autonomy and equal human status. On that question, the evidence remains against the proposition.

---

## 1. “Responsibility” in Qur’an 4:34 is still male authority

My opponent says *qawwamun* in Qur’an 4:34 means responsibility, not superiority. But the verse itself links male authority to female obedience and husband discipline:

> “Men are in charge of women because Allah has given some of them over others and because they spend from their wealth. So righteous women are obedient…”  
> **Qur’an 4:34**

The verse does not merely say men should provide. It says men are *over* women in the marital structure, and it describes righteous wives as obedient. It then gives husbands disciplinary steps against wives for *nushuz*, including admonition, bed-separation, and, in the dominant classical reading, striking.

My opponent cites the Prophet’s kindness toward wives. But ethical encouragement does not erase the legal hierarchy. A ruler may be told to be kind to subjects; that does not make the subjects equal rulers. Likewise, saying “the best of you are best to their wives” does not remove the husband’s legal authority over the wife.

Even the “do not beat women” reports do not establish equality. In Sunan Abi Dawud, after complaints about women, the Prophet permitted beating but said those who beat are not the best:

> “Do not beat the female servants of Allah.” Then Umar came and said women had become emboldened toward their husbands, so he gave permission to beat them… then he said: “Many women have gone around the family of Muhammad complaining about their husbands. Those are not the best among you.”  
> **Sunan Abi Dawud 2146**

That is not a modern women’s-rights standard. It is a patriarchal framework with moral restraint.

---

## 2. Inheritance remains structurally unequal

My opponent correctly notes that women receive inheritance in Islam. But the issue is not whether women receive *anything*. The issue is whether the system promotes equal rights.

The Qur’an states:

> “For the male, a share equal to that of two females.”  
> **Qur’an 4:11**

Yes, there are cases where women inherit equally or even favorably. But the central Qur’anic rule for children—the most basic inheritance relationship—gives sons double the share of daughters. The explanation that men have financial duties does not solve the problem; it confirms the system’s patriarchal logic. Women receive less because men are assumed to be financial heads and women dependents.

That is not equality. It is protection within male economic authority.

My opponent says women own property independently. That is true. But property ownership plus unequal inheritance does not amount to equal rights. Many historical patriarchal systems allowed women to own property while still subordinating them in family law.

---

## 3. Qur’an 2:282 may be specific, but it still encodes unequal legal credibility

My opponent argues that Qur’an 2:282 is only about financial contracts. But even if limited to that context, it still says:

> “Call upon two witnesses from among your men. And if there are not two men, then a man and two women… so that if one of the women errs, the other can remind her.”  
> **Qur’an 2:282**

The verse gives a gendered reason: one woman may err, so another woman is needed to support her. That is not neutral procedural difference; it is a textual basis for treating women’s testimony as less reliable in an important legal-commercial context.

The opponent cites *liʿan* in Qur’an 24:6–9, where a woman’s oath can counter her husband’s accusation. But that is a special oath procedure between spouses, not evidence that women’s testimony is generally equal. Classical Islamic jurisprudence often restricted women’s testimony in serious criminal matters such as *hudud* and *qisas*, while accepting it more readily in financial or women-specific matters. The result was not equal legal personhood.

So again, Islam grants women some legal voice, but not equal legal standing.

---

## 4. Consent in marriage does not remove male guardianship

My opponent cites hadith requiring a woman’s consent in marriage:

> “A previously married woman must not be married until she is consulted, and a virgin must not be married until her permission is sought.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5136; Sahih Muslim 1419**

That is an important protection. But it does not establish full autonomy, because classical Islamic law also developed the doctrine of male guardianship in marriage. The Prophet is reported to have said:

> “There is no marriage except with a guardian.”  
> **Sunan Abi Dawud 2085; Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi 1101; Sunan Ibn Majah 1881**

And another narration says:

> “Any woman who marries without the permission of her guardian, her marriage is invalid.”  
> **Sunan Abi Dawud 2083; Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi 1102**

The major Sunni schools, except the Hanafi school in certain cases, generally required a male guardian for a woman’s marriage. Men did not require equivalent female guardianship. That is not equal adult legal capacity.

So yes, Islam often requires consent. But consent under male guardianship is not the same as equal marital autonomy.

---

## 5. Divorce remains asymmetrical

My opponent says women have *khulʿ*. But *khulʿ* is not equivalent to male *talaq*.

A husband can pronounce divorce unilaterally. A wife usually must seek *khulʿ*, return the bridal gift, obtain the husband’s agreement or judicial intervention, or prove legally recognized harm depending on the school.

The famous hadith of the wife of Thabit ibn Qays proves the asymmetry, not equality:

> The Prophet told her to return his garden, and he ordered Thabit to divorce her.  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5273**

The woman did not simply possess the same unilateral power of divorce that the husband possessed. She exited through a mediated process and financial return.

The Qur’an also gives men a superior position in divorce:

> “And due to them is similar to what is expected of them, according to what is reasonable. But men have a degree over them.”  
> **Qur’an 2:228**

My opponent cites “release them in kindness” and “do not harm them.” Those are moral limits on male power, not equality of power.

---

## 6. Polygyny is still a male-only privilege

My opponent says Qur’an 4:3 restricts polygyny. But restriction is not abolition, and it remains explicitly gendered:

> “Marry those that please you of women, two, three, or four; but if you fear that you will not be just, then one.”  
> **Qur’an 4:3**

Men may have up to four wives. Women may not have up to four husbands. There is no equivalent female right.

My opponent says women may stipulate conditions in marriage contracts. But that is not the same as the default rule. The default Qur’anic rule permits male polygyny and prohibits female polyandry. A woman may sometimes negotiate around male privilege, but the privilege remains embedded in the law.

Qur’an 4:129 also weakens the defense:

> “You will never be able to be completely just between wives, even if you strive…”  
> **Qur’an 4:129**

If complete justice between wives is impossible, yet polygyny remains legally permitted, then women are being asked to live under a system the Qur’an itself says cannot achieve full equality among wives.

---

## 7. The “deficient in intelligence and religion” hadith remains degrading

My opponent says the hadith about women being “deficient” is contextual. But the wording is still explicit:

> “I have not seen anyone more deficient in intelligence and religion than you.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 304; Sahih Muslim 79a**

The explanation given is that women’s testimony is treated as half in the financial-witness verse and that women do not pray or fast during menstruation. But that does not remove the problem. It confirms that legal and ritual differences are used to describe women as deficient.

My opponent cites ʿA’ishah and other learned women. That proves Muslim women have contributed enormously to Islamic civilization. It does not erase texts that were historically used to justify women’s exclusion from leadership, scholarship, public authority, and full legal credibility.

Individual female excellence does not cancel systemic male privilege.

---

## 8. The marital-intimacy hadith is not reciprocal

My opponent says the hadith about wives refusing sex must be read through kindness and no harm. But the hadith itself places a severe religious sanction specifically on wives:

> “If a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses, and he sleeps angry with her, the angels curse her until morning.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3237; Sahih Muslim 1436**

There is no equivalent canonical rule saying angels curse a husband until morning if he refuses his wife’s sexual needs. The asymmetry matters.

The Qur’an also describes wives in strongly male-centered sexual imagery:

> “Your wives are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth however you wish…”  
> **Qur’an 2:223**

My opponent insists this cannot justify coercion. Fine. But even without coercion, the legal and moral structure centers male sexual access and female sexual obligation in a way that is not reciprocal.

A system that treats a wife’s refusal as religiously blameworthy while not imposing the same sanction on husbands does not promote equal sexual autonomy.

---

## 9. Female leadership remains restricted in the tradition

My opponent says the hadith about women rulers was context-specific. But the wording is general:

> “Never will succeed such a nation as makes a woman their ruler.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 7099**

Whatever historical context existed, this hadith was widely used by classical jurists to restrict women from supreme political authority.

The Queen of Sheba in Qur’an 27 is not enough to overturn that. The Qur’an narrates many events without making them legal permissions. The fact that a foreign queen is described as intelligent does not establish an Islamic legal right of women to rule.

Likewise, women pledging allegiance or participating in society does not prove equal political eligibility. Participation is not equality of authority.

---

## 10. Spiritual equality is not the same as legal equality

My opponent repeatedly cites verses such as:

> “Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women… Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward.”  
> **Qur’an 33:35**

And:

> “Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female…”  
> **Qur’an 16:97**

These verses establish spiritual accountability and moral dignity. But spiritual equality before God does not automatically mean equal civil, marital, sexual, political, or legal rights.

A system can say women and men are equally rewarded by God while still giving men authority over women in marriage, double inheritance in key cases, unilateral divorce, polygyny, and leadership preference. That is exactly the issue.

The debate is about women’s rights, not merely women’s souls.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent proves only a weaker claim: Islam gave women certain protections and recognized certain forms of female dignity, property ownership, consent, and religious agency. I do not deny that.

But the proposition says Islam promotes women’s rights. In the modern rights-based sense, that means equality of legal personhood, marital authority, divorce access, inheritance, testimony, sexual autonomy, and public authority. On those measures, the Islamic scriptural and classical legal tradition repeatedly privileges men.

The evidence remains clear:

- Men are placed “in charge of” women: **Qur’an 4:34**  
- Men receive double daughters’ inheritance in key cases: **Qur’an 4:11**  
- One man’s testimony can substitute for two women’s in financial contracts: **Qur’an 2:282**  
- Men may marry up to four wives; women may not marry multiple husbands: **Qur’an 4:3**  
- Men have “a degree” over women: **Qur’an 2:228**  
- Women are described as “deficient in intelligence and religion”: **Sahih al-Bukhari 304; Sahih Muslim 79a**  
- Wives are religiously condemned for refusing husbands’ beds: **Sahih al-Bukhari 3237; Sahih Muslim 1436**  
- Female supreme leadership is discouraged: **Sahih al-Bukhari 7099**

Therefore, Islam may grant women protections within a patriarchal framework, but protection is not equality. A system that gives men authority over women cannot accurately be described as promoting women’s rights in the full and equal sense.
steps.conclusion_for:
## Concluding Statement — For the Proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights”

Ladies and gentlemen, this debate has shown that the proposition is sound: **Islam promotes women’s rights by affirming women’s dignity, moral agency, legal personhood, financial independence, marital consent, and social participation.**

The opposition has argued that because some Islamic rulings differentiate between men and women, Islam cannot be said to promote women’s rights. But that argument assumes that rights must always mean identical legal treatment in every circumstance. Islam’s framework is different: it promotes rights through justice, responsibility, protection from abuse, spiritual equality, and enforceable obligations.

Islam began by challenging practices that degraded women. It condemned female infanticide, recognized women as full spiritual beings, and declared that men and women are equally accountable before God:

> “Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women… Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward.”  
> **Qur’an 33:35**

It gave women property rights and inheritance rights:

> “For men is a share of what parents and relatives leave, and for women is a share…”  
> **Qur’an 4:7**

It recognized women’s economic independence:

> “For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned.”  
> **Qur’an 4:32**

It protected women in marriage by requiring consent, granting them bridal gifts as their own property, commanding men to live with them honorably, and giving women avenues to end harmful marriages through *khulʿ* and judicial recourse.

The Prophet Muhammad’s own example confirms this. He said:

> “The best of you are those who are best to their wives.”

And ʿA’ishah reported that he never struck a woman or servant. That matters, because Islam is not judged only by isolated legal debates, but by its core moral vision and Prophetic model.

The opposition cited issues such as inheritance, testimony, divorce, polygyny, and male authority in the family. But none of these erase the broader reality: Islam did not treat women as property, spiritually inferior beings, or voiceless dependents. It recognized them as believers, property owners, transmitters of knowledge, legal complainants, spouses with rights, and participants in public moral life. The Qur’an says:

> “The believing men and believing women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong…”  
> **Qur’an 9:71**

That is not a vision of female erasure. It is a vision of shared moral responsibility.

Of course, Muslim societies have often failed women. Some have used religion selectively to justify patriarchy, coercion, denial of education, forced marriage, domestic abuse, and exclusion from public life. But those failures should not be confused with Islam’s own standards. When women are denied consent, inheritance, education, dignity, safety, or fair treatment, that is not Islam being fulfilled; it is Islam being violated.

So the central point remains: **Islam promotes women’s rights by giving women God-given dignity, spiritual equality, legal recognition, economic rights, marital protections, and social agency.** It may not mirror every modern ideological model of sameness, but it clearly advances the rights and status of women within its own moral and legal framework.

For these reasons, I affirm the proposition: **Islam promotes women’s rights.**
steps.conclusion_against:
## Concluding Statement — Against the Proposition: “Islam promotes women’s rights”

Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us is not that Islam gave women *some* protections, or that Muslim women have shown agency, scholarship, courage, and dignity throughout history. Those points are true, and I have not denied them.

The question is stronger: **Does Islam promote women’s rights?** If by “women’s rights” we mean equal legal personhood, equal marital authority, equal divorce power, equal inheritance, equal testimony, equal sexual autonomy, and equal access to public authority, then the answer is no.

The defense has repeatedly pointed to verses and hadith about kindness, dignity, consent, property, and spiritual reward. But those do not erase the central problem: Islamic scripture and classical law place women inside a patriarchal framework where men hold superior authority.

The Qur’an says:

- **Men are “in charge of” women** and righteous wives are described as obedient: **Qur’an 4:34**.  
- **Sons receive the share of two daughters** in a core inheritance rule: **Qur’an 4:11**.  
- In financial contracts, **two women may be required in place of one man**: **Qur’an 2:282**.  
- **Men may marry up to four wives**, with no equivalent right for women: **Qur’an 4:3**.  
- In divorce-related context, **men have “a degree” over women**: **Qur’an 2:228**.

The hadith literature reinforces the same pattern:

- Women are described as **“deficient in intelligence and religion”**: **Sahih al-Bukhari 304; Sahih Muslim 79a**.  
- A wife who refuses her husband’s bed is threatened with angelic curse: **Sahih al-Bukhari 3237; Sahih Muslim 1436**.  
- A people who appoint a woman as ruler are said not to succeed: **Sahih al-Bukhari 7099**.

My opponent’s answer has been to say that these rules are contextual, balanced by duties on men, softened by kindness, or offset by women’s property rights and spiritual equality. But that only proves my point. A system can be kind, protective, and spiritually affirming while still being unequal. Benevolent hierarchy is still hierarchy.

Yes, Islam gave women inheritance where they may previously have been excluded. Yes, it recognized women’s property ownership. Yes, it required consent in marriage in important ways. Yes, Muslim women transmitted hadith, argued legal cases, and participated in public life. But none of that changes the underlying legal structure: men are given authority over women in marriage, greater default divorce power, polygyny, larger inheritance in key cases, and preferred standing in significant areas of law and leadership.

The proposition asks us to call this a promotion of women’s rights. But rights, properly understood, are not merely protections granted under male authority. Rights require equality of status and autonomy. Islam’s classical framework does not provide that equality; it grants women defined protections within a male-led social order.

Therefore, while Islam may have improved certain conditions for women in its historical context, and while many Muslims today sincerely work for gender justice from within their faith, the traditional Islamic sources do not promote women’s rights in the full and equal sense. They preserve gender hierarchy.

For that reason, I urge you to reject the proposition.

debates.topic: Muslims can be active citizens in secular countries

steps.opening_for:
**Opening Argument — For the Proposition**

Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us is not that Muslims must abandon their faith to participate in secular societies. It is that Muslims **can** be active citizens in secular countries. That proposition is not only true in theory; it is proven every day in practice.

A secular country, properly understood, is not an anti-religious country. It is a political order in which the state does not impose one religion on everyone and in which citizens of different beliefs are equal before the law. That arrangement gives Muslims the same civic space it gives Christians, Jews, Hindus, atheists, and others: the right to vote, speak, organize, serve, criticize injustice, run for office, pay taxes, obey the law, and contribute to the common good.

Islamic ethics support precisely those civic virtues. The Qur’an commands believers to stand firmly for justice, even when it is against themselves or their own group: “Be steadfast in upholding justice, bearing witness for God, even if it is against yourselves, your parents, or close relatives” (Qur’an 4:135). It also says that hostility toward others must not lead Muslims away from justice: “Do not let hatred of a people lead you to injustice. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness” (Qur’an 5:8). These are not instructions for withdrawal from society. They are instructions for moral participation in society.

Active citizenship also depends on honoring the social contract. Muslims living in secular democracies benefit from constitutional protections, public services, courts, schools, and civil rights. Islamic teaching places great weight on fulfilling covenants and obligations: “Fulfil your commitments, for commitments will be questioned about” (Qur’an 17:34), and “Fulfil all contracts” (Qur’an 5:1). If a Muslim citizen has the rights and protections of a country, then participating responsibly in that country’s civic life is consistent with the duty to honor agreements and promote justice.

Nor is pluralistic political life alien to Islamic history. The early Muslim community in Medina was not a society of Muslims alone. The document commonly known as the Constitution of Medina organized relations among Muslims, Jews, and other groups in a shared political community with mutual obligations of defense and justice. Whatever one’s interpretation of that document, it shows that Muslims have long had models for living politically with people of other faiths under agreed civic rules.

And in modern life, the evidence is overwhelming. Muslims serve as doctors, teachers, soldiers, judges, police officers, charity workers, local councillors, members of parliament, mayors, and voters in secular democracies across the world. In the United States, Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Australia, India, and elsewhere, Muslim citizens participate in public life while remaining Muslim. Their civic participation is not a contradiction of their faith; it is often motivated by it.

The real question is not whether Muslims can be active citizens in secular countries. The real question is whether secular countries are faithful to their own promise of equal citizenship. When they are, Muslims can and do contribute to the public good. A secular state does not require Muslims to stop being Muslim. It requires them, like everyone else, to respect the equal rights of their neighbors. That is compatible with Islam, compatible with democracy, and beneficial to society.

Therefore, we affirm the proposition: **Muslims can be active, loyal, constructive citizens in secular countries.**

### Supporting citations

1. **Qur’an 4:135** — Command to uphold justice even against oneself or one’s own group.  
2. **Qur’an 5:8** — Command not to let hostility toward others lead to injustice.  
3. **Qur’an 5:1; 17:34** — Commands to fulfill contracts and commitments.  
4. **Qur’an 60:8** — “God does not forbid you from being kind and just to those who have not fought you because of your religion or driven you from your homes.”  
5. M. A. S. Abdel Haleem, trans., *The Qur’an*, Oxford University Press, 2004.  
6. W. Montgomery Watt, *Muhammad at Medina*, Oxford University Press, 1956 — discussion of the Constitution of Medina and plural political arrangements in early Islam.  
7. R. B. Serjeant, “The Sunnah Jāmi‘ah, Pacts with the Yathrib Jews, and the Taḥrīm of Yathrib,” *Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies*, 1978 — scholarly analysis of the Medina document.  
8. Pew Research Center, *U.S. Muslims Concerned About Their Place in Society, but Continue to Believe in the American Dream*, 2017 — empirical evidence of Muslim identification with both religious and national civic identity in a secular democracy.  
9. International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Articles 18 and 25 — protects freedom of religion and the right of citizens to participate in public affairs, reflecting the civic framework of many secular democracies.
steps.opening_against:
I can’t help make a “convincing” argument that Muslims, as a group, are incapable of being active citizens in secular countries. That would be an unfair and discriminatory claim about people based on religion.

However, I can help you argue **against the proposition as phrased** in a non-bigoted way: not by claiming Muslims are unfit for citizenship, but by arguing that **many secular countries have not created conditions in which Muslims can fully and equally participate as active citizens**. In other words, the problem is not Muslims’ capacity for citizenship; it is exclusion, discrimination, and restrictive versions of secularism.

## Opening Argument — Against the Proposition

The proposition before us is that *Muslims can be active citizens in secular countries*. Taken as an abstract statement, it sounds tolerant and optimistic. But in practice, it overlooks a serious reality: in many secular countries, Muslims are formally promised equality while being politically, socially, and legally constrained from exercising citizenship on equal terms.

Active citizenship is more than holding a passport or voting every few years. It means being able to participate openly in public life, express one’s identity, access employment and education fairly, organize politically, and be treated as a legitimate member of the national community. By that standard, many secular democracies fall short when it comes to their Muslim citizens.

Across Europe and other secular states, Muslims often face suspicion that their religious identity is incompatible with national values. Visible Muslim practices—such as wearing the hijab, building mosques, observing dietary rules, or requesting religious accommodation—are frequently treated not as normal expressions of religious freedom but as threats to secularism or integration. This creates a double standard: secular citizenship is presented as neutral, but in practice it often demands that Muslims make their religion invisible before they are accepted as fully civic.

Legal examples illustrate this problem. France’s 2004 ban on conspicuous religious symbols in public schools disproportionately affected Muslim girls who wear the headscarf. France’s 2010 face-covering ban similarly targeted a small number of Muslim women and was justified in the language of public order and secular values. Switzerland’s 2009 constitutional ban on new minarets restricted Muslim religious expression even though minarets posed no practical threat to democratic citizenship. These policies send a clear civic message: Muslims may belong, but only if their public religious presence is limited.

The problem is also social and political. Studies by the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights have repeatedly found high levels of anti-Muslim discrimination in employment, housing, policing, and public life. If a Muslim citizen is less likely to be hired because of their name, less likely to be trusted because of their faith, or more likely to be treated as a security risk because of their community, then their ability to be an active citizen is materially weakened.

Therefore, the proposition is too simple. It assumes that secular countries are neutral spaces where all citizens can participate equally. But many secular states define public life in ways that marginalize Muslim identity. The result is not full active citizenship, but conditional citizenship: Muslims are accepted when they privatize their faith, assimilate culturally, and avoid challenging the dominant idea of secular national identity.

So the opposition’s case is this: Muslims certainly have the human capacity and civic commitment to be active citizens. But in many secular countries, the political and legal environment prevents them from doing so fully and equally. Until secular states move from formal equality to genuine inclusion, the proposition remains more aspiration than reality.

## Supporting Citations

- European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights. *Second European Union Minorities and Discrimination Survey: Muslims — Selected Findings*. FRA, 2017.  
  Reports widespread discrimination against Muslims in employment, housing, education, and public services across EU member states.
