steps.opening_for:
Honourable judges, the proposition is straightforward: **Islam permits Muslims to eat ordinary beef sold in Christian countries**, unless a Muslim has specific, reliable knowledge that a particular item is prohibited—such as carrion, pork contamination, or meat dedicated to an idol. The default is not suspicion; the default is the permission Allah Himself gave.

The decisive text is the Qur’an:

> “Today all good things have been made lawful for you. **The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you**, and your food is lawful for them.”  
> — **Qur’an 5:5**

Classical Muslim exegetes understood “the food of those given the Scripture” to include their slaughtered animals. Ibn Kathīr, commenting on this verse, reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, and others that “their food” means **their slaughtered animals**. So the Qur’anic rule is not limited to vegetables, bread, or fish; it directly covers meat slaughtered by Jews and Christians.

This permission is especially powerful because the Qur’an already knew Christian theology and criticized aspects of it elsewhere. Yet despite that, Allah still says their food is lawful. In other words, the permissibility of Christian meat does not depend on Christians having identical theology, identical ritual practice, or Muslim-style slaughter procedures. The verse creates a broad legal allowance.

The Sunnah confirms this practical approach. ʿĀ’ishah reported that some people asked the Prophet ﷺ about meat brought to them, saying:

> “We do not know whether they mentioned the name of Allah over it or not.”  
> The Prophet ﷺ replied: **“Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat.”**  
> — **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 5507**

This hadith is crucial. The Prophet ﷺ did not command Muslims to investigate the slaughterhouse, interrogate the butcher, or assume prohibition because of uncertainty. He gave a simple rule: say “Bismillah” and eat. If that is true even when Muslims were unsure about meat brought to them, it is even more reasonable when the Qur’an has already declared the food of the People of the Book lawful.

We also know that the Prophet ﷺ accepted meat from Jews. At Khaybar, a Jewish woman served him roasted sheep, and he ate from it before discovering it had been poisoned.  
— **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 2617; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, no. 2190**

The legal implication is clear: the Prophet ﷺ did not treat meat from the People of the Book as inherently forbidden or requiring prior religious inspection.

The prohibited categories are named in the Qur’an: carrion, flowing blood, pork, and what is dedicated to other than Allah.  
— **Qur’an 2:173; 5:3; 6:145**

Beef is not pork. It is from an animal normally lawful in Islam. When sold as beef for human consumption in a Christian country, it falls under the Qur’anic permission of the food of the People of the Book, unless one has definite knowledge that this particular meat falls into a prohibited category.

Major jurists recognized this broad permission. Ibn Rushd states that the scholars agreed in principle that the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book are lawful, based on Qur’an 5:5.  
— **Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Book of Foods/Slaughter**

Ibn Qudāmah likewise records the general permissibility of the slaughtered animals of Jews and Christians.  
— **Ibn Qudāmah, al-Mughnī, Book of Hunting and Slaughter**

So the stronger Islamic position is not fear-based restriction but Qur’an-based permission. Islam did not make Muslims forensic auditors of every meal. It gave them clear prohibitions, and it gave them a clear permission: **the food of the People of the Book is lawful**.

Therefore, ordinary beef sold in Christian countries is permissible for Muslims to eat, unless there is specific proof that a particular item is forbidden. Suspicion does not override the Qur’an. Certainty is not removed by doubt. And Allah has explicitly made the food of the People of the Book lawful for us.
steps.opening_against:
Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us is not: “Can Muslims ever eat beef in Christian countries?” The proposition is much broader: **“Islam permits Muslims to eat any beef sold in Christian countries.”** That word **“any”** makes the claim untenable.

Islam does allow the food of the People of the Book in principle. The Qur’an says:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you…”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

But that verse is not a blank cheque for every package of beef in a supermarket merely because the country has a Christian history or a Christian majority. The same Qur’an also says:

> “Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which has been invoked the name of other than Allah; and animals killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a fall, by goring, and those partly eaten by a wild animal—except what you are able to slaughter…”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

So the Islamic rule is not “beef in a Christian country is halal.” The rule is: meat must come from a lawful animal, slaughtered in a lawful manner, by a lawful slaughterer, and not dedicated to other than Allah. The allowance for the People of the Book does not override the prohibition of carrion, animals killed by improper means, or meat dedicated to other deities.

This is crucial in the modern context. A “Christian country” today is often a secular, multi-religious society. The animal may have been slaughtered by a Christian, a Jew, a Muslim, an atheist, a Hindu, a Buddhist, or by an automated industrial process. The animal may have died before the cut because of stunning or mechanical killing. The beef may pass through a supply chain where no one knows who slaughtered it or how. Calling the country “Christian” does not answer the Islamic legal questions.

The Qur’an also warns:

> “Do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned…”  
> **Qur’an 6:121**

Scholars differ on details—especially regarding the slaughter of Jews and Christians and whether explicit mention of Allah’s name is required in every case—but no serious Islamic position says that *all* beef sold in a Christian-majority country is automatically permissible regardless of slaughterer, method, dedication, or whether the animal was already dead.

The Prophet ﷺ also taught caution where the cause of death is uncertain. Regarding hunted game, he said that if a person sends his trained dog with Allah’s name, but then finds another dog involved, he should not eat, because he does not know which dog killed the animal.  
**Sahih al-Bukhari 5486; Sahih Muslim 1929**

That principle matters here: if the permissibility depends on how the animal was killed, then we cannot declare *any* beef permissible simply based on the country of sale.

Some may cite the hadith in which people asked the Prophet ﷺ about meat brought by people who were new Muslims, not knowing whether Allah’s name had been mentioned over it. He replied:

> “Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5507**

But that report does not prove the proposition. The meat was being brought by Muslims; the doubt was whether they had remembered to say Allah’s name, not whether the animal was carrion, killed by a prohibited method, slaughtered by an unqualified person, or dedicated to another deity. It cannot be stretched into a rule that every piece of beef in every Christian country is halal.

Therefore, my position is simple: Islam may permit some beef sold in Christian countries—especially where it is properly slaughtered by Muslims, Jews, or Christians and no prohibited factor is present. But Islam does **not** permit Muslims to eat **any** beef sold there without qualification. The proposition is too sweeping, ignores explicit Qur’anic restrictions, and confuses a country’s religious label with the actual Islamic requirements for lawful meat.

**Conclusion:** The Qur’an permits the food of the People of the Book, but it also forbids carrion, improperly killed animals, and meat dedicated to other than Allah. Therefore, “any beef sold in Christian countries” cannot be declared permissible in Islam.

> “The scholars are agreed upon the permissibility of the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book.”  
> — **Ibn Qudāmah, al-Mughnī, Kitāb al-Ṣayd wa-l-Dhabāʾiḥ**

Ibn Rushd likewise records the agreement that the slaughter of Jews and Christians is lawful in principle, based on Qur’an 5:5.  
— **Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Book of Foods/Slaughter**

So the opponent’s claim that the verse is not a “blank cheque” is true only in the trivial sense that no Islamic permission includes known exceptions. But Qur’an 5:5 is still a broad operative permission. It means Muslims are allowed to eat the meat of the People of the Book without treating every meal as legally suspect.

---

## 2. Qur’an 5:3 does not cancel Qur’an 5:5

The opponent cites:

> “Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, pork, and that over which has been invoked the name of other than Allah…”  
> — **Qur’an 5:3**

Of course. Nobody disputes that carrion, pork, blood, and meat dedicated to other than Allah are forbidden.

But notice: **Qur’an 5:3 and Qur’an 5:5 are in the same sūrah, only two verses apart.** Allah lists prohibited categories, then explicitly says the food of the People of the Book is lawful. Therefore the correct reconciliation is:

- If one **knows** the meat is carrion, pork-contaminated, killed unlawfully, or dedicated to other than Allah, it is forbidden.
- If one does **not know** that, and the meat is ordinary food of Jews/Christians, Qur’an 5:5 applies.

The opponent’s argument effectively makes Qur’an 5:5 almost useless, because every Christian or Jewish piece of meat would still require investigation into the slaughterhouse. That is not how the Prophet ﷺ or the jurists treated the verse.

---

## 3. The Sunnah teaches non-investigation, not suspicion

ʿĀ’ishah reported:

> Some people said: “O Messenger of Allah, people bring us meat and we do not know whether they mentioned Allah’s name over it or not.”  
> He replied: **“Mention Allah’s name over it yourselves and eat.”**  
> — **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 5507**

The opponent says this involved new Muslims, not Christians. But that misses the legal point. The point is that the Prophet ﷺ did **not** command investigation when the meat was outwardly from a lawful source. He did not say: “Find out exactly what happened.” He said: **say Bismillah and eat.**

When this principle is combined with Qur’an 5:5, it applies even more clearly to the People of the Book, because Allah has already declared their food lawful.

The Prophet ﷺ also accepted and ate from meat served by a Jewish woman at Khaybar:

> A Jewish woman brought poisoned roasted sheep to the Prophet ﷺ, and he ate from it.  
> — **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 2617; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, no. 2190**

The legal relevance is obvious: the Prophet ﷺ did not first demand to know the slaughterer, the exact slaughter method, or whether the Jewish preparer pronounced the name of Allah in a Muslim formula. He treated the meat of the People of the Book as outwardly lawful.

---

## 4. Qur’an 6:121 must be read with Qur’an 5:5

The opponent cites:

> “Do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned…”  
> — **Qur’an 6:121**

But Qur’an cannot be read against Qur’an. The same Allah who revealed 6:121 also revealed 5:5. Therefore, the verse cannot mean: “Never eat any meat unless you personally verify the tasmiyah.” If that were so, Qur’an 5:5 would be practically meaningless.

Classical jurists reconciled the texts by saying that the prohibition applies to meat known to be unlawful: carrion, sacrifice to other than Allah, or cases where a legally required condition is known to be absent. It does not impose a duty to investigate every unknown detail of People-of-the-Book meat.

Ibn Kathīr, while affirming the permissibility of the People of the Book’s slaughter, states that their meat is lawful because Allah specifically permitted it in 5:5.  
— **Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, commentary on 5:5**

So uncertainty is not the same as proof of prohibition. Islam distinguishes between **known haram** and **unverified suspicion**.

---

## 5. The “two dogs” hunting hadith is not analogous

The opponent cites the hadith where a hunter finds another dog with his game and is told not to eat because he does not know which dog killed it.  
— **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, no. 5486; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, no. 1929**

But that case involves **positive evidence of an unlawful cause**: another dog is physically present at the kill. The Prophet ﷺ did not say, “Whenever you eat meat, imagine that another dog may have been involved.” He ruled on a specific suspicious carcass.

Ordinary beef in a Christian market is the opposite situation. It is presented as lawful human food from a people whose slaughter Allah has permitted. There is no specific “second dog.” The opponent wants speculation to function as evidence. Islamic law does not work that way.

---

## 6. Modern slaughter concerns do not overturn the default rule

The opponent says modern Christian countries are secular and industrial, and the slaughterer may be Christian, atheist, Hindu, Buddhist, or automated. But again, this is speculation unless tied to a specific item.

Contemporary scholars who allow meat from People-of-the-Book countries make exactly this distinction.

Shaykh Ibn Bāz states that meat from Jews and Christians is lawful unless it is known that it was slaughtered in a prohibited way, because Allah permitted their food in Qur’an 5:5.  
— **Ibn Bāz, Majmūʿ Fatāwā wa-Maqālāt Mutanawwiʿah, rulings on imported meats and slaughter**

Shaykh Ibn ʿUthaymīn similarly said that what comes from Jews and Christians is eaten and one is not required to ask how it was slaughtered or whether Allah’s name was mentioned, unless one knows it was killed by an unlawful method. He cites the Prophet’s acceptance of Jewish meat as evidence.  
— **Ibn ʿUthaymīn, Fatāwā Nūr ʿalā al-Darb; Liqāʾ al-Bāb al-Maftūḥ, rulings on meat of the People of the Book**

This is precisely the proposition’s position: **ordinary beef in Christian countries is permissible; definite contrary knowledge creates an exception.**

---

## 7. “Christian country” means the legal market of the People of the Book

The opponent says a Christian country may contain atheists, Hindus, Buddhists, and others. True. But Islamic law normally judges by outward attribution, not hidden possibilities.

If meat is sold in the ordinary food market of a People-of-the-Book society, it is treated as their food unless one has specific evidence otherwise. Otherwise Muslims would have to investigate every loaf of bread, every cheese ingredient, every restaurant, every supply chain, and every butcher’s private belief. That is exactly the hardship the Sharīʿah does not impose.

Allah says:

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> — **Qur’an 22:78**

And the legal maxim applies:

> **Certainty is not removed by doubt**  
> — A foundational fiqh maxim, derived from numerous legal texts

Here the certainty is the Qur’anic permission of the food of the People of the Book. Doubt about what may have happened in an unseen slaughterhouse does not cancel that permission.

---

## Conclusion

The opponent is right that Muslims may not eat known carrion, pork, blood, or meat dedicated to other than Allah. But that does not defeat the proposition. It only states exceptions that the proposition already recognizes.

The decisive rule remains:

- Beef is a lawful animal.
- The food/slaughter of the People of the Book is lawful by Qur’an 5:5.
- The Prophet ﷺ did not require investigation into meat from lawful sources.
- Suspicion about modern supply chains does not equal proof of prohibition.
- Therefore, ordinary beef sold in Christian countries is permissible for Muslims unless there is specific reliable knowledge that a particular item is haram.

So the proposition stands: **Islam permits Muslims to eat beef sold in Christian countries, and Muslims are not required to treat such beef as forbidden merely because of uncertainty or speculation.**
steps.response_against:
Honourable judges, my opponent has not defended the proposition as stated. He has defended a much narrower proposition:

> “Some ordinary beef in People-of-the-Book markets may be eaten unless one has reliable evidence of prohibition.”

That is not the same as:

> **“Islam permits Muslims to eat any beef sold in Christian countries.”**

My position remains: Islam permits **some** beef in Christian countries, but not **any** beef merely because it is sold there.

---

## 1. Qur’an 5:5 permits the food of the People of the Book, not all meat in their countries

The verse says:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you…”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

Classical tafsīr often explains “their food” as their slaughtered animals. I accept that. But the key phrase is **“of those who were given the Scripture”** — not “whatever is sold in a country historically associated with Christianity.”

A modern “Christian country” may have meat slaughtered by:

- atheists,
- Hindus,
- Buddhists,
- secular companies with no religious identity,
- machines,
- or workers whose religion is completely unknown.

Qur’an 5:5 does not say the slaughter of atheists, idolaters, or non-Kitābīs is lawful.

Imām al-Nawawī states:

> “The slaughtered animal of one who is not a Muslim nor from the People of the Book is not lawful.”  
> **al-Nawawī, al-Majmūʿ Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab, Kitāb al-Ḍaḥāyā / al-Dhabāʾiḥ**

Ibn Qudāmah similarly says that the slaughter of a Muslim or Kitābī is lawful, but not the slaughter of those outside these categories.  
**Ibn Qudāmah, al-Mughnī, Kitāb al-Ṣayd wa-l-Dhabāʾiḥ**

So the question is not simply: “Is the country Christian?” The legal question is: **Was this actually slaughtered by a Muslim, Jew, or Christian in a valid manner?**

---

## 2. Qur’an 5:3 remains a real restriction

Allah says:

> “Prohibited to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which has been invoked the name of other than Allah; and animals killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a fall, by goring…”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

This verse applies whether the animal is in Makkah, London, Paris, Texas, or Rome. If cattle are killed by a prohibited method before valid slaughter, they are not halal simply because the shop is located in a Christian-majority country.

Ibn Qudāmah explains that if an animal is killed by a blow or similar cause and is not properly slaughtered while still alive, it falls under the forbidden category of **al-mawqūdhah** — the animal killed by a violent blow.  
**Ibn Qudāmah, al-Mughnī, Kitāb al-Ṣayd wa-l-Dhabāʾiḥ**

This is directly relevant to modern slaughter. Many contemporary slaughter systems involve stunning, electrocution, gassing, captive-bolt stunning, or mechanical processes. Scholars differ on which forms are acceptable, but they do not say: “Any beef from a Christian country is automatically halal regardless of whether the animal died before slaughter.”

The Islamic Fiqh Academy of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation ruled that stunning may only be tolerated under conditions, including that the animal must remain alive until proper slaughter; if it dies from the stunning, it is not lawful.  
**International Islamic Fiqh Academy, Resolution No. 95 (3/10), concerning slaughter and stunning**

So again: the permissibility is conditional, not automatic.

---

## 3. “Food of the People of the Book” does not include meat dedicated to other than Allah

The Qur’an also forbids:

> “that over which has been invoked the name of other than Allah”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

And:

> “Do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has not been mentioned…”  
> **Qur’an 6:121**

My opponent says Qur’an 6:121 must be read with Qur’an 5:5. Correct — but Qur’an 5:5 must also be read with Qur’an 5:3. The permission of Kitābī meat does not include meat knowingly dedicated to Christ, a saint, an idol, or any being besides Allah.

Ibn Kathīr, while affirming that the food of the People of the Book includes their slaughtered animals, also discusses the issue of meat over which other than Allah is mentioned, and notes the prohibition held by major jurists when the name of other than Allah is invoked.  
**Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, commentary on Qur’an 5:5 and 5:3**

Ibn Rushd also records juristic disagreement over animals slaughtered by Christians for their churches and festivals, precisely because Qur’an 5:3 remains relevant.  
**Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Kitāb al-Aṭʿimah / al-Dhabāʾiḥ**

That proves my point: classical jurists did not understand Qur’an 5:5 as an unconditional licence for every piece of meat associated with Christians.

---

## 4. The ʿĀ’ishah hadith does not prove “any beef in Christian countries”

My opponent relies heavily on the hadith:

> People said: “O Messenger of Allah, some people bring us meat and we do not know whether they mentioned Allah’s name over it or not.”  
> He said: “Mention Allah’s name over it yourselves and eat.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5507**

But the same narration states:

> “They had recently left disbelief” — meaning they were new Muslims.  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5507**

So the doubt was not: “Was this slaughtered by an atheist, idolater, machine, or by a prohibited method?” The doubt was whether new Muslims remembered to say the name of Allah. The Prophet ﷺ did not turn unknown slaughter by any person into halal. He dealt with meat coming from an outwardly Muslim source.

That hadith cannot be stretched to say: “Any supermarket beef in any Christian country is permissible.”

---

## 5. The Jewish woman at Khaybar proves Kitābī meat can be lawful — not that all modern market beef is lawful

The Prophet ﷺ ate from a sheep prepared by a Jewish woman at Khaybar.  
**Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2617; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2190**

I accept the legal point: Jewish slaughter is lawful in principle. But that only proves that actual People-of-the-Book meat may be eaten. It does not prove that beef slaughtered by secular industrial processes, unknown workers, or non-Kitābīs is automatically lawful.

The narration concerns a known Jewish source. The proposition concerns **any beef sold in Christian countries**. Those are not equivalent.

---

## 6. The “two dogs” hadith is relevant because uncertainty about the cause of death matters

The Prophet ﷺ told the hunter not to eat the game if another dog was found with it, because he did not know which dog killed it.  
**Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5486; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1929**

My opponent says this involved “positive evidence.” Exactly — and in many modern cases we also have positive evidence: labels, slaughterhouse rules, industry practice, regulatory information, or knowledge that the meat is not ritually slaughtered and may have been killed by stunning before the cut.

Islamic law does not require impossible paranoia, but neither does it require wilful blindness. If there is reliable reason to believe the Islamic conditions were not met, one cannot hide behind “Christian country.”

The Prophet ﷺ also said:

> “The halal is clear and the haram is clear, and between them are doubtful matters…”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 52; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1599**

And:

> “Leave that which makes you doubt for that which does not make you doubt.”  
> **Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 2518; Sunan al-Nasāʾī 5711**

So caution in doubtful meat is not an innovation; it is a Prophetic principle.

---

## 7. The legal maxim is being misused

My opponent cites:

> “Certainty is not removed by doubt.”

But what is the certainty here?

It is not certain that supermarket beef in a secular country was slaughtered by a Christian or Jew in a valid manner. That is precisely what is unknown.

Many jurists state the opposite principle regarding meat: the default with slaughtered animals is caution until a valid cause of permissibility is established. This is expressed in the legal maxim:

> “The default concerning meat is prohibition until lawful slaughter is established.”  
> Mentioned by jurists in discussions of hunting and slaughter; see also al-Suyūṭī, **al-Ashbāh wa-l-Naẓāʾir**, under legal maxims concerning default rulings.

Now, if the meat is genuinely from Muslims or People of the Book and there is no sign of invalid slaughter, many scholars allow eating without investigation. But that is a presumption based on a lawful source. It is not a universal rule for every beef product in every Christian country.

---

## 8. “No hardship” does not cancel dietary law

My opponent cites:

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

True. But the same religion also says:

> “Prohibited to you are carrion…”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

The principle of removing hardship does not make carrion halal, nor does it erase the conditions of slaughter. If hardship alone made all doubtful meat permissible, then the detailed Qur’anic rules of food would become meaningless.

Islam allows alternatives: halal meat, kosher meat according to many scholars, fish, vegetarian food, or meat from verified lawful sources. Avoiding doubtful beef is not an unbearable hardship.

---

## 9. Even the scholars cited by my opponent do not support “any beef”

My opponent cites Shaykh Ibn Bāz and Shaykh Ibn ʿUthaymīn. But even their permissive view is conditional. They allow meat from Jews and Christians **unless it is known** to have been slaughtered in an impermissible way. They do not say meat slaughtered by atheists, idolaters, or killed before slaughter is halal.

Shaykh Ibn ʿUthaymīn, for example, repeatedly conditions permissibility on the meat being from Muslims or People of the Book and not known to have been killed unlawfully.  
**Ibn ʿUthaymīn, Fatāwā Nūr ʿalā al-Darb; Liqāʾ al-Bāb al-Maftūḥ, rulings on imported meats**

That supports my case: the permissibility is not because the country is Christian; it is because the slaughter is attributed to a lawful slaughterer and no invalidating factor is known.

---

## Conclusion

The proposition says:

> **“Islam permits Muslims to eat any beef sold in Christian countries.”**

That is too broad.

Islam permits the slaughter of the People of the Book in principle:

> **Qur’an 5:5**

But Islam also forbids carrion, animals killed by improper means, and meat dedicated to other than Allah:

> **Qur’an 5:3; Qur’an 6:121**

Therefore, the correct Islamic position is:

- Beef from a lawful animal may be halal.
- Meat slaughtered by Muslims, Jews, or Christians may be halal.
- Muslims are not necessarily required to investigate every meal.
- But beef is not automatically halal merely because it is sold in a Christian country.
- If the slaughterer is not Muslim/Jew/Christian, or the animal died before proper slaughter, or it was dedicated to other than Allah, it is not permissible.

So the opponent has proven only a limited rule: **some beef in Christian countries may be permissible.** He has not proven the proposition that **any** beef sold there is permissible.
steps.conclusion_for:
Honourable judges, the proposition rests on a clear Islamic principle: **ordinary beef sold as food in Christian/People-of-the-Book lands is permissible for Muslims unless there is specific, reliable evidence that a particular item is haram.**

The Qur’an gives the central rule:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you…”  
> — Qur’an 5:5

Classical tafsīr and fiqh understood this to include the slaughtered animals of Jews and Christians. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd b. Jubayr and others explained “their food” as their slaughtered meat, and jurists such as Ibn Qudāmah and Ibn Rushd recorded the general permissibility of the slaughter of the People of the Book.

Yes, Islam forbids carrion, blood, pork, animals improperly killed, and meat dedicated to other than Allah. But those prohibitions apply when such a forbidden factor is known or established. They do not erase Qur’an 5:5, nor do they require Muslims to investigate every slaughterhouse, butcher, supermarket, and supply chain before eating.

The Sunnah confirms this practical approach. When people asked the Prophet ﷺ about meat whose tasmiyah they were unsure of, he did not order an inquiry. He said:

> “Mention the name of Allah over it yourselves and eat.”  
> — Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5507

And the Prophet ﷺ accepted meat from Jews, including the roasted sheep served at Khaybar. This shows that meat from the People of the Book was treated as outwardly lawful, not presumptively forbidden.

The opponent’s case depends on turning uncertainty into prohibition. But Islamic law does not operate on imagined possibilities. The presence of theoretical concerns—perhaps the slaughterer was not Christian, perhaps the method was invalid, perhaps something improper occurred—does not create a ruling of haram without evidence. Suspicion does not override a Qur’anic permission.

The correct balance is simple:

- If beef is known to be carrion, pork-contaminated, dedicated to another deity, or killed in a clearly prohibited way, it is forbidden.
- But if it is ordinary beef sold as food in a Christian/People-of-the-Book country, Islam permits it under Qur’an 5:5.
- Muslims are not required to conduct forensic investigations into unseen details before eating.

Therefore, the proposition stands. **Islam permits Muslims to eat beef sold in Christian countries, unless there is definite evidence that the particular meat is prohibited.** This is the Qur’anic allowance, the Prophetic practice, and the sound legal default.
steps.conclusion_against:
Honourable judges,

The proposition before us is not merely that Muslims may eat some beef in Christian countries, nor that the slaughter of Jews and Christians is lawful in principle. I have never denied that. The proposition is much broader:

> **“Islam permits Muslims to eat any beef sold in Christian countries.”**

That claim is too sweeping, and it cannot be sustained by the Qur’an, Sunnah, or fiqh.

The Qur’an does say:

> “The food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you.”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

But the same Qur’an also says:

> “Prohibited to you are carrion, blood… that over which has been invoked the name of other than Allah; and animals killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a fall, by goring…”  
> **Qur’an 5:3**

So Qur’an 5:5 is a real permission, but it is not an unconditional licence. It permits the food and slaughter of the People of the Book within the limits of Islamic law. It does not make carrion lawful. It does not make meat killed before slaughter lawful. It does not make the slaughter of atheists, idolaters, Hindus, Buddhists, or unknown non-Kitābī slaughterers lawful. And it does not make meat dedicated to other than Allah lawful.

My opponent repeatedly shifted the proposition into a narrower and more defensible claim: that ordinary meat in People-of-the-Book markets may be eaten unless one has reliable evidence of prohibition. But that is not the same as saying **any beef sold in Christian countries** is permissible.

A modern “Christian country” is not the same thing as a market where every animal is slaughtered by a Christian or Jew in a valid manner. Modern meat may come through secular industrial systems, unknown slaughterers, automated processes, stunning methods, or supply chains involving people who are not from the People of the Book. The religious label of the country does not answer the Islamic legal questions.

The Sunnah also does not prove the proposition. The hadith of ʿĀ’ishah, where the Prophet ﷺ said, “Mention Allah’s name over it yourselves and eat,” concerned meat brought by people who had recently become Muslims. It addressed doubt about whether they remembered the tasmiyah; it did not legalize meat from any slaughterer by any method. Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ eating from meat prepared by a Jewish woman proves that Jewish meat can be lawful — not that every modern beef product sold in a Christian country is automatically halal.

Nor does the principle of avoiding hardship erase the dietary laws. Islam is not a religion of paranoia, but neither is it a religion of wilful blindness. If there is reliable reason to know that meat was killed unlawfully, slaughtered by an unqualified person, or dedicated to other than Allah, then it is not permissible merely because it was sold in a Christian-majority country.

So the correct position is balanced:

- The slaughter of Muslims, Jews, and Christians is lawful in principle.
- Muslims are not always required to investigate every unknown detail.
- Some beef sold in Christian countries may be halal.
- But not **any** beef sold there is halal.
- If a prohibited factor is known or established, the meat is forbidden.

Therefore, the proposition fails because it overstates the Islamic ruling. Islam permits lawful beef, including valid People-of-the-Book slaughter, but it does not permit Muslims to eat **any beef whatsoever** merely because it is sold in a Christian country.

For that reason, I stand firmly against the proposition.

debates.topic: Islam permits Muslims to take mortgages with interest

steps.opening_for:
**Opening argument — for the proposition**

Islam’s default moral teaching is clear: Muslims should avoid *riba*, and the Qur’an condemns exploitative usury and unjust enrichment. But the question before us is not “Is interest generally encouraged?” It is: **Does Islam permit Muslims to take mortgages with interest?** My answer is yes — **in genuine cases of need, especially for purchasing a primary family home where no realistic Sharia-compliant alternative exists.**

Islamic law is not a rigid system that ignores human realities. It is a law built on mercy, necessity, public welfare, and the removal of hardship. The Qur’an says, **“Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship”** and **“He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”** Likewise, the Qur’an repeatedly allows otherwise prohibited matters in cases of necessity. These are not loopholes; they are foundational principles of Islamic jurisprudence.

Housing is not a luxury. A stable home protects family life, dignity, privacy, children’s upbringing, wealth, and community belonging — all of which are among the objectives of Sharia. In many countries, especially for Muslims living as minorities, long-term renting can be financially ruinous, insecure, and sometimes more harmful than ownership. In some places, so-called “Islamic mortgages” are unavailable, legally impractical, or significantly more expensive while economically mirroring conventional financing. To say that Islam categorically forbids a Muslim family from buying a modest primary residence in such circumstances would impose a hardship the Sharia itself rejects.

This is why respected contemporary scholars and fatwa bodies have permitted conventional mortgages under strict conditions. The **European Council for Fatwa and Research**, for example, issued a well-known resolution allowing Muslims in non-Muslim countries to purchase a needed primary residence through a conventional mortgage when no viable Islamic alternative is available, provided the house is for personal need and not investment or luxury. Scholars such as **Yusuf al-Qaradawi** defended this view under the principles of *hajah* — pressing need — and the jurisprudence of Muslim minorities.

The argument is not that all interest is halal, nor that Muslims should casually enter interest-based debt. The argument is more careful and more faithful to Islamic law: **where a Muslim faces a genuine need for secure housing, and lawful alternatives are unavailable or materially impractical, Islam permits taking a mortgage to the extent needed.** That is consistent with the Qur’an’s insistence on justice, mercy, and the removal of hardship.

In short, Islam prohibits exploitation — but it does not prohibit families from securing shelter when the only practical path is a regulated mortgage. The Sharia is not designed to trap believers in hardship; it is designed to guide them toward responsible, dignified, and morally conscious living.

---

### Supporting citations

1. **Qur’an 2:275–279** — prohibition of *riba* as the default rule.  
   > “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba…”  

2. **Qur’an 2:185** — principle of ease.  
   > “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”

3. **Qur’an 22:78** — removal of hardship.  
   > “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”

4. **Qur’an 2:173; 5:3; 6:119; 16:115** — necessity can permit what is otherwise forbidden.  
   > “Whoever is compelled by necessity… there is no sin upon him…”

5. **Hadith: “No harm and no reciprocating harm.”**  
   Reported in **Ibn Mājah, Sunan Ibn Mājah, no. 2340**, and widely used as a legal maxim in Islamic jurisprudence.

6. **Legal maxim:**  
   > *Al-darūrāt tubīḥ al-maḥẓūrāt* — “Necessities permit prohibited matters.”  
   See: **al-Suyūṭī, al-Ashbāh wa’l-Naẓāʾir**; also reflected in **Majallat al-Aḥkām al-ʿAdliyyah**, article 21.

7. **Legal maxim:**  
   > *Al-ḥājah tanzilu manzilat al-darūrah, ʿāmmah kānat aw khāṣṣah* — “Need may be treated like necessity, whether public or private.”  
   See: **Majallat al-Aḥkām al-ʿAdliyyah**, article 32.

8. **European Council for Fatwa and Research**, Resolution on purchasing houses with conventional mortgages for Muslims in the West, **Fourth Ordinary Session, Dublin, 1999**.  
   The Council permitted such mortgages for a primary residence where no suitable Islamic alternative exists, relying on necessity/need and the circumstances of Muslim minorities.

9. **Yusuf al-Qaradawi**, *Fiqh of Muslim Minorities: Contentious Issues and Recommended Solutions*.  
   Qaradawi supports the permissibility of conventional mortgages for Muslims in Western countries under conditions of genuine need and lack of viable alternatives.
steps.opening_against:
## Opening Argument Against the Proposition

Honourable judges, respected opponent, and audience:

The proposition before us is: **“Islam permits Muslims to take mortgages with interest.”** I stand firmly against it. The issue is not whether Muslims may own homes, nor whether Islam recognises financial hardship. The issue is whether a Muslim may voluntarily enter a loan contract in which repayment of money is increased by a stipulated interest charge. The mainstream Islamic answer, grounded in the Qur’an, Sunnah, and juristic consensus, is **no**.

A conventional mortgage is, in legal and financial substance, an **interest-bearing loan**: the bank lends money to the buyer, and the buyer repays the principal plus a predetermined additional amount called interest. In Islamic law, this is precisely the category of **riba al-duyun** or **riba al-nasi’ah**—an increase required in return for deferment of a debt. Changing the name from “riba” to “interest,” or securing the loan against a house, does not change its legal reality.

The Qur’an speaks about riba in some of the strongest language used for any financial sin. Allah says:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

This verse is decisive. Islam does not prohibit profit, commerce, or home ownership. It permits trade. What it forbids is a guaranteed increase on a loan simply because time has passed. That is the essence of interest.

Allah further says:

> “O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of riba, if you are believers. And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger.”  
> **Qur’an 2:278–279**

This is not a minor discouragement; it is a grave prohibition. No ordinary consumer preference—such as wanting to buy rather than rent—can be treated as permission to enter a contract against which the Qur’an gives such a severe warning.

The Sunnah is equally clear. The Prophet ﷺ did not only condemn the one who receives riba. He also condemned the one who pays it. Jabir ibn Abdullah reported:

> “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it, and he said: ‘They are all the same.’”  
> **Sahih Muslim, 1598**

This hadith directly addresses the claim that only the lender is sinful. It says the payer of interest is also included. A conventional mortgage requires the Muslim borrower to pay interest for many years. That falls squarely within the warning of this hadith.

The position is not merely a narrow reading by a few scholars. Classical Muslim jurists agreed that a stipulated increase over a loan is prohibited riba. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Qudamah, al-Nawawi, and others transmitted consensus that any loan which brings a stipulated benefit to the lender is impermissible. Modern fiqh bodies have applied the same principle to bank interest. The International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC resolved that interest on loans, whether for consumption or production, is prohibited riba.

Some may argue that Muslims in modern societies “need” mortgages. But Islamic law distinguishes between **need**, **convenience**, and **necessity**. Necessity may allow the prohibited only in exceptional cases—such as preserving life or avoiding unavoidable ruin—and even then only to the extent required. But wanting to own a home, build equity, avoid renting, or access a larger property is not automatically a darurah. Renting remains available in many cases. Smaller housing may be available. Delaying purchase may be possible. Cooperative and Sharia-compliant financing structures may exist. Therefore, ordinary homeownership cannot be used to declare a Qur’anic prohibition broadly permissible.

If we accept the proposition, we effectively say that one of the clearest prohibitions in Islamic commercial ethics disappears whenever the prohibited contract is common, socially normal, or economically attractive. That would undermine the entire moral discipline of Islamic finance. Islam’s prohibition of riba exists precisely because money should not generate guaranteed profit without risk, trade, labour, or asset ownership. A conventional mortgage does exactly that: the lender earns guaranteed interest on a debt, while the borrower bears the burden.

So my position is simple: **Islam permits Muslims to buy homes through lawful means, but it does not permit Muslims to take conventional interest-based mortgages except, at most, in rare and genuine necessity assessed with serious scholarly guidance.** The general proposition that Islam permits such mortgages is therefore false.

## Key Citations

1. **Qur’an 2:275**  
   > “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”

2. **Qur’an 2:278–279**  
   > “O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of riba, if you are believers. And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger…”

3. **Qur’an 3:130**  
   > “O you who believe, do not consume riba, doubled and multiplied, but fear Allah that you may be successful.”

4. **Qur’an 4:161**  
   Condemns those who took riba though they had been forbidden from it.

5. **Sahih Muslim, 1598**  
   The Prophet ﷺ cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and its witnesses.

6. **Sahih Muslim, 1584 / related narrations on riba**  
   The Prophet ﷺ prohibited forms of exchange involving unlawful increase, establishing the seriousness of riba in transactions.

7. **Ibn Qudamah, *al-Mughni***  
   Reports the juristic principle that every loan stipulating a benefit or increase for the lender is prohibited.

8. **Al-Nawawi, *Sharh Sahih Muslim***  
   Discusses the prohibition of riba and the inclusion of those who participate in riba-based contracts.

9. **International Islamic Fiqh Academy, OIC, Resolution on Bank Interest**  
   Declares that stipulated interest on loans is prohibited riba, whether the loan is for consumption or investment.

10. **AAOIFI Sharia Standards on loans and riba**  
   Modern Islamic finance standards treat interest-bearing loans as impermissible and distinguish them from permissible sale, lease, and partnership-based financing.
steps.response_for:
## Rebuttal — for the proposition

My opponent’s argument proves something important, but not what he needs to prove. He proves that **riba is prohibited as a default rule**. I agree. He proves that a conventional mortgage contains stipulated interest. I also accept that, for the sake of argument. But the actual debate is whether Islam **ever permits** Muslims to take such mortgages. On that question, his own argument is too absolute.

Islamic law contains both **ʿazīmah** — the original strict rule — and **rukhsah** — legal concession in cases of necessity, hardship, or pressing need. The prohibition of riba is real, but so are the Qur’anic principles of necessity, removal of hardship, and preservation of essential human welfare.

The correct position is therefore not: “interest is halal.” It is:

> **Interest-based mortgages remain normally prohibited, but they may be permitted for a genuine primary housing need where no viable lawful alternative exists and the transaction is limited to what is necessary.**

That is enough to affirm the proposition.

---

## 1. The opponent proves the default rule, not the absence of exceptions

The opponent cites:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

And:

> “Give up what remains of riba…”  
> **Qur’an 2:278**

These verses establish the baseline prohibition. But Islamic law has many baseline prohibitions that become temporarily permitted under necessity or serious need.

The Qur’an forbids carrion, blood, and pork, yet says:

> “But whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him.”  
> **Qur’an 2:173**

Similar necessity clauses appear in:

- **Qur’an 5:3**
- **Qur’an 6:119**
- **Qur’an 16:115**

So the question is not whether riba is normally forbidden. It is whether a Muslim family’s need for secure shelter can, in some circumstances, fall under recognised principles of necessity or pressing need. Many contemporary scholars and fatwa bodies have answered yes.

---

## 2. Islamic law recognises serious need, not only life-or-death necessity

My opponent narrows necessity almost to starvation or imminent death. But that is not the full structure of Islamic jurisprudence.

Classical legal maxims state:

> **Al-mashaqqah tajlib al-taysīr** — “Hardship brings facilitation.”

And:

> **Al-ḍarūrāt tubīḥ al-maḥẓūrāt** — “Necessities permit prohibited matters.”

And importantly:

> **Al-ḥājah tanzilu manzilat al-ḍarūrah, ʿāmmah kānat aw khāṣṣah** — “Need may be treated like necessity, whether general or specific.”

These maxims are found in works such as:

- **al-Suyūṭī, *al-Ashbāh wa’l-Naẓāʾir***
- **Ibn Nujaym, *al-Ashbāh wa’l-Naẓāʾir***
- **Majallat al-Aḥkām al-ʿAdliyyah**, articles 17, 21, 22, and 32

The Sharia does not require a Muslim to wait until collapse, homelessness, or destitution before relief is considered. Serious hardship affecting family stability, safety, children, dignity, and long-term financial harm can be legally relevant.

Al-Shāṭibī explains in *al-Muwāfaqāt* that the Sharia’s objectives include not only absolute necessities but also **ḥājiyyāt** — needs whose absence causes hardship and distress, even if life itself is not immediately destroyed.

Housing is exactly such a need.

---

## 3. A primary family home is not a luxury

The opponent repeatedly frames the issue as “wanting to buy instead of rent.” That is too simplistic.

A home can be tied to:

- family stability,
- protection of children,
- privacy and dignity,
- safety,
- access to schools and community,
- protection of wealth,
- avoiding exploitative or insecure rental conditions,
- the ability to accommodate religious and family needs.

The Qur’an says:

> “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 2:185**

And:

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

And:

> “Allah does not intend to make difficulty for you.”  
> **Qur’an 5:6**

Therefore, where renting is genuinely stable, affordable, and suitable, a mortgage may not be justified. But where renting is insecure, excessively expensive, unsuitable for family needs, or financially destructive over time, the matter changes.

The proposition is not that every Muslim may buy any house with interest. The proposition is that Islam can permit such a mortgage **under need-based conditions**.

---

## 4. The hadith cursing the payer of riba is not denied — it is qualified by necessity

The opponent cites the hadith:

> “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it…”  
> **Sahih Muslim, 1598**

This is a serious text. But again, it states the default ruling. It does not erase the Qur’anic doctrine of compulsion and necessity.

Islamic jurists make similar distinctions in other areas. For example, bribery is condemned, but many jurists allowed a person to pay money to recover a right or repel oppression, while the sin remains on the unjust taker. The reason is that the payer is not seeking corruption; he is escaping harm.

Likewise, in the mortgage case, the Muslim borrower is not seeking to profit from riba. He is seeking shelter and family stability in a system where housing is often only realistically accessible through regulated mortgage finance.

So the hadith remains fully valid: paying riba voluntarily, casually, or for enrichment is prohibited. But where serious need exists and no viable alternative exists, the concession may apply.

---

## 5. Scholarly consensus on riba does not eliminate concessions

My opponent invokes consensus that a stipulated increase on a loan is riba. But that does not settle the debate.

There is also consensus that pork is prohibited. Yet pork may be eaten under necessity. The exception does not deny the prohibition; it confirms that Islamic law is humane and contextual.

So even if we accept that a conventional mortgage contains riba, the question remains: can a Muslim enter it under exceptional need? Contemporary scholars have said yes.

The **European Council for Fatwa and Research** issued a resolution in its **Fourth Ordinary Session, Dublin, 1999**, permitting Muslims living in non-Muslim countries to purchase a necessary primary residence through a conventional mortgage where no suitable Islamic alternative exists. The Council relied on the principles of necessity, need, public welfare, and the particular circumstances of Muslim minorities.

Shaykh **Yusuf al-Qaradawi**, in works on the fiqh of Muslim minorities, similarly argued that a Muslim family in the West may take a conventional mortgage for a needed primary home where Islamic alternatives are unavailable or materially impractical.

This is not a fringe “anything goes” position. It is a structured fatwa position based on recognised usūlī principles.

---

## 6. “Renting exists” is not a complete answer

The opponent says renting is available. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it is not meaningfully suitable.

Islamic law does not ask only: “Is there technically another option?” It asks whether the alternative removes the hardship in a real way.

For example, renting may involve:

- repeated displacement,
- inability to house a large family,
- unsafe neighbourhoods,
- excessive rent increases,
- inability to modify the property for disability or family needs,
- lack of long-term security,
- financial loss greater than a modest mortgage,
- exclusion from stable schooling and community life.

If rent is affordable, safe, stable, and suitable, then yes, the concession may not apply. But if renting creates serious hardship, then saying “just rent forever” may itself contradict the Sharia principle of removing hardship.

---

## 7. The permission is conditional, not general

To avoid misunderstanding, the permissive position has strict limits:

1. The property must be a **primary residence**, not an investment or luxury purchase.  
2. There must be a **genuine need**, not mere preference or status-seeking.  
3. No viable Sharia-compliant alternative should be available on reasonable terms.  
4. The buyer should borrow only what is needed.  
5. The buyer should choose the least harmful available option.  
6. The mortgage should not expose the family to reckless debt or likely default.  
7. The matter should be assessed honestly and, where possible, with qualified scholarly guidance.

This is not legalising riba as a normal financial tool. It is recognising a concession for real human need.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent’s evidence establishes that riba is normally forbidden. I accept that. But Islamic law is not built only on prohibitions; it is also built on mercy, necessity, need, and the removal of hardship.

The Qur’an itself says:

> “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 2:185**

And:

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

Therefore, where a Muslim family genuinely needs a primary home, cannot access a viable Islamic alternative, and would face serious hardship without conventional financing, Islam can permit taking a mortgage with interest to the extent required.

So the proposition stands: **Islam does permit Muslims to take mortgages with interest in genuine cases of need under strict conditions.**
steps.response_against:
## Rebuttal Against the Proposition

My opponent’s case rests on one move: he admits that a conventional mortgage is normally **riba**, but argues that **necessity or need** can make it permissible. That sounds nuanced, but it does not prove the proposition. It proves only that in a rare emergency, a prohibited act may be temporarily excused. That is not the same as saying: **“Islam permits Muslims to take mortgages with interest.”**

If a starving person may eat pork, we do not therefore say, “Islam permits pork.” Likewise, if an extreme and genuine necessity might excuse a Muslim from sin in a particular case, we do not therefore say Islam permits interest-based mortgages as a valid housing solution.

The default ruling remains decisive: a conventional mortgage is an interest-bearing loan, and stipulated increase on a loan is riba.

Allah says:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

And:

> “O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of riba, if you are believers. And if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger.”  
> **Qur’an 2:278–279**

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “The Messenger of Allah cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it, and he said: ‘They are all the same.’”  
> **Sahih Muslim, 1598**

A mortgage borrower is not merely near riba; he is contractually agreeing to pay it.

---

## 1. Emergency concession is not general permission

The opponent relies on necessity verses such as:

> “Whoever is compelled by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him.”  
> **Qur’an 2:173**

But this verse proves the opposite of what the opponent needs. It shows that exceptions are limited to genuine compulsion and must be restricted by two conditions:

1. **Not desiring the prohibited thing**, and  
2. **Not exceeding the limit of necessity**.

Classical legal maxims say:

> **Al-ḍarūrāt tubīḥ al-maḥẓūrāt** — necessities permit prohibited matters.

But they also say:

> **Al-ḍarūrah tuqaddar bi-qadarihā** — necessity is measured according to its extent.  
> **Majallat al-Aḥkām al-ʿAdliyyah**, article 22.

And:

> **Mā jāza li-ʿudhr baṭala bi-zawālihi** — what is allowed due to an excuse ceases when the excuse disappears.  
> **Majallah**, article 23.

So even if one grants an extreme case, it would be individual, temporary, and tightly limited. It cannot become a broad rule that Muslims may take conventional mortgages whenever home ownership is difficult.

---

## 2. The need is for shelter, not ownership

The opponent repeatedly equates “housing need” with “home ownership.” That is the central mistake.

Islam recognises the need for shelter, safety, and dignity. But that does not automatically mean a person must own property through an interest-bearing loan. In many cases, the lawful alternative is renting, living in a smaller home, relocating, delaying purchase, sharing accommodation, or using Sharia-compliant financing.

The fact that renting may be less financially attractive does not create a darūrah. If “building equity,” “avoiding rent,” or “long-term financial benefit” made riba permissible, then almost every interest-based loan could be justified. Business loans, student loans, investment loans, and personal loans are also often taken to improve one’s financial future. But that is exactly why the prohibition of riba must remain firm.

Allah says:

> “If you repent, you may have your principal — neither wronging nor being wronged.”  
> **Qur’an 2:279**

The Qur’anic remedy is not: “Pay riba if it helps your financial stability.” The remedy is: abandon the increase and return to principal only.

---

## 3. “Hardship brings ease” cannot erase explicit riba texts

The opponent cites:

> “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 2:185**

And:

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

These verses are true, but they cannot be used to cancel explicit prohibitions. If general hardship were enough, then many major prohibitions would collapse. Avoiding haram often involves hardship. A Muslim may face hardship avoiding alcohol in business, avoiding zina in society, avoiding gambling-based income, or refusing riba-based finance. The existence of hardship alone does not make the prohibited lawful.

The maxim:

> **Al-ḥājah tanzilu manzilat al-ḍarūrah** — need may be treated like necessity

is not an unrestricted licence. Classical jurists applied such maxims with conditions. They do not mean that any serious inconvenience or financial disadvantage permits a major sin established by Qur’an, Sunnah, and consensus.

If a person is truly facing homelessness, danger, or unavoidable severe harm, that is a different discussion. But the opponent’s examples — school access, rent increases, wealth preservation, community preference, and financial loss — may be real concerns, yet they do not automatically reach the level required to override the prohibition of riba.

---

## 4. The bribery analogy fails

The opponent compares paying interest to paying a bribe to recover one’s right. But the analogy is weak.

In the bribery example, a person may be forced to pay an unjust official to obtain something already owed to him or to repel oppression. The payer is under coercion.

A conventional mortgage is different. The borrower voluntarily enters a new contract to purchase an asset he does not yet own. The bank is not withholding his existing right. He is choosing an interest-bearing loan as a means to acquire property.

And the hadith specifically mentions not only the receiver of riba, but also:

> “the one who pays it.”  
> **Sahih Muslim, 1598**

So we cannot dismiss the payer’s responsibility by saying he is not profiting from riba. The Prophet ﷺ explicitly included the payer.

---

## 5. Scholarly consensus on riba is stronger than a disputed modern fatwa

The opponent cites the European Council for Fatwa and Research and Shaykh Yusuf al-Qaradawi. But this is a disputed contemporary minority concession, particularly framed around Muslim minorities in non-Muslim countries. It is not a consensus, and it cannot overturn the overwhelming legal principle that interest-bearing loans are riba.

Classical jurists transmitted consensus that a stipulated increase over a loan is prohibited.

Ibn al-Mundhir stated that scholars agreed that if a lender stipulates an increase over the loan, that increase is riba.

Ibn Qudāmah wrote:

> “Every loan in which it is stipulated that more be repaid is haram, without disagreement.”  
> **Ibn Qudāmah, al-Mughnī**

Al-Nawawī likewise affirmed the consensus on the prohibition of riba in loans and explained the seriousness of participation in riba-based transactions.  
**Al-Nawawī, Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**

Modern fiqh bodies have also reaffirmed this.

The **International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC** resolved that interest on loans is prohibited riba, whether the loan is for consumption or production.  
**OIC Islamic Fiqh Academy, Resolution on Bank Interest**

AAOIFI states that a loan may not bring a stipulated benefit to the lender, because that is riba.  
**AAOIFI Sharia Standards, Standard on Qard / Loans**

So the opponent’s cited fatwa is not the Islamic ruling as such. It is a contested emergency-based opinion, and even that opinion does not permit luxury homes, investment properties, avoidable borrowing, or ordinary preference for ownership over renting.

---

## 6. If the opponent’s argument is accepted, the riba prohibition becomes practically hollow

The danger in my opponent’s reasoning is that “need” becomes elastic. Once we say that:

- rent is expensive,
- ownership is more stable,
- buying is better financially,
- children need better schools,
- the family wants community security,

therefore riba is allowed, then the prohibition is no longer meaningful in modern life. Most people who take interest loans can describe a serious benefit or hardship. But Islamic law did not prohibit riba only when it is unnecessary. It prohibited riba precisely because people are tempted to use it for real economic needs.

The Qur’an’s command was not revealed in a world without financial hardship. It was revealed to regulate real economic life.

---

## Conclusion

My opponent has not proven that Islam permits interest-based mortgages as a valid general option. He has only argued that in exceptional circumstances, necessity may excuse what is otherwise prohibited. But that does not establish the proposition.

The correct ruling remains:

1. A conventional mortgage is an interest-bearing loan.  
2. Interest on a loan is riba.  
3. Riba is prohibited by the Qur’an, Sunnah, and consensus.  
4. The payer of riba is explicitly condemned in **Sahih Muslim 1598**.  
5. Home ownership is not automatically a necessity when lawful shelter alternatives exist.  
6. At most, an extreme, case-specific necessity may be assessed by qualified scholars.

Therefore, Islam permits Muslims to own homes through lawful means, but it does **not** generally permit Muslims to take mortgages with interest. The proposition should be rejected.
steps.conclusion_for:
## Concluding Statement — For the Proposition

This debate is not about whether *riba* is generally prohibited in Islam. It is. The Qur’an condemns *riba*, and the Sunnah warns strongly against participating in it. I have never argued that interest is normally halal, nor that Muslims should casually enter interest-based debt.

The real question is narrower and more practical:

> **Can Islam permit a Muslim to take an interest-based mortgage in genuine circumstances of need, especially for a primary home where no viable Sharia-compliant alternative exists?**

My answer remains: **yes, under strict conditions.**

Islamic law is not only a system of prohibitions; it is also a system of mercy, necessity, hardship removal, and public welfare. The Qur’an says:

> “Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 2:185**

And:

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

The Sharia recognises that exceptional circumstances can qualify the normal rule. That is why Islamic jurisprudence contains maxims such as:

> **Necessities permit prohibited matters.**

And:

> **Need may be treated like necessity, whether public or private.**

These principles do not abolish the prohibition of *riba*. They explain how Islamic law responds when strict application of a rule would create serious hardship.

A primary family home is not automatically a luxury. It can be tied to safety, dignity, privacy, children’s upbringing, family stability, community life, and long-term financial security. In many modern societies, especially for Muslim minorities, renting may be insecure, unaffordable, unsuitable, or financially destructive. Meanwhile, Islamic financing may be unavailable, legally impractical, or significantly more expensive while achieving the same economic result. In such cases, insisting that a family must rent indefinitely can impose hardship that the Sharia itself seeks to remove.

This is why respected contemporary scholars and bodies, including the **European Council for Fatwa and Research** and scholars such as **Yusuf al-Qaradawi**, have permitted conventional mortgages for a needed primary residence in non-Muslim countries where no viable Islamic alternative exists. Their position is not that *riba* is harmless. Their position is that a concession may apply because of genuine need.

So the permissive position is not open-ended. It is conditional:

1. The home must be a **primary residence**, not an investment or luxury property.  
2. There must be a **real need**, not mere convenience or status-seeking.  
3. No viable Sharia-compliant alternative must be reasonably available.  
4. The borrowing must be limited to what is necessary.  
5. The buyer must avoid reckless debt and choose the least harmful option.  
6. The decision should be made sincerely and, where possible, with scholarly guidance.

My opponent has shown that interest-bearing loans are normally prohibited. I agree. But he has not shown that Islamic law contains no exception for genuine housing need. The Qur’an itself teaches that hardship and necessity matter. Classical legal maxims confirm this. Contemporary fatwa bodies have applied these principles to the reality of Muslim life in modern housing markets.

Therefore, the most balanced conclusion is this:

> **Islam does not generally permit interest-based mortgages as a normal financial choice, but it can permit them in genuine cases of need for a primary home when lawful alternatives are unavailable or impractical.**

That is the proposition I have defended, and on that basis, the proposition stands.
steps.conclusion_against:
## Concluding Statement Against the Proposition

Honourable judges and audience:

This debate has not been about whether Muslims may own homes, seek stability, or protect their families. Islam recognises all of those needs. The real question is narrower and clearer: **does Islam permit Muslims to take conventional mortgages with interest?**

My answer remains: **No, not as a general Islamic ruling.**

A conventional mortgage is an interest-bearing loan. The bank lends money and requires repayment of the principal plus a stipulated increase. In Islamic law, that is riba. The Qur’an is explicit:

> “Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba.”  
> **Qur’an 2:275**

And Allah warns:

> “Give up what remains of riba… and if you do not, then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger.”  
> **Qur’an 2:278–279**

The Sunnah is equally direct. The Prophet ﷺ cursed not only the one who receives riba, but also:

> “the one who pays it, the one who records it, and the two witnesses to it.”  
> **Sahih Muslim, 1598**

That directly includes the borrower who knowingly agrees to pay interest.

My opponent has not denied that conventional mortgages involve riba. Instead, he has argued that necessity or serious need may create an exception. But that does not prove the proposition. If a starving person may eat pork, we do not say, “Islam permits pork.” We say pork remains prohibited, but an exceptional necessity may excuse a person to the extent required. The same principle applies here.

Islamic law does recognise necessity, but necessity is not the same as convenience, financial advantage, or preference for ownership over renting. The need is for **shelter**, not necessarily for **ownership through an interest-based loan**. In many cases, lawful alternatives exist: renting, delaying purchase, buying smaller, relocating, sharing accommodation, or using Sharia-compliant financing. Where such alternatives are reasonably available, the prohibition of riba cannot be set aside.

The juristic consensus is also clear: a loan with a stipulated increase is prohibited. Classical scholars such as Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Qudāmah, and al-Nawawī affirmed this principle, and modern fiqh bodies such as the OIC Islamic Fiqh Academy and AAOIFI have applied it to bank interest.

The permissive view cited by my opponent is a disputed modern concession, limited to exceptional circumstances, usually for Muslim minorities, where there is genuine need and no viable lawful alternative. Even that view does not make interest-based mortgages generally halal. It does not permit luxury purchases, investment properties, avoidable borrowing, or ordinary preference for home ownership.

So the key distinction is this: **Islam may excuse a prohibited act in a rare case of genuine necessity, but that does not transform the prohibited act into a permitted norm.**

Therefore, the correct conclusion is:

1. Conventional mortgages contain interest.  
2. Interest on loans is riba.  
3. Riba is prohibited by the Qur’an, Sunnah, and consensus.  
4. The payer of riba is explicitly condemned in authentic hadith.  
5. Home ownership is not automatically a necessity when lawful shelter alternatives exist.  
6. Any claimed exception must be rare, case-specific, and assessed carefully by qualified scholars.

Islam permits Muslims to buy homes through lawful means. But it does **not** generally permit Muslims to take mortgages with interest.

For these reasons, the proposition — **“Islam permits Muslims to take mortgages with interest”** — should be rejected.

debates.topic: Islam permits homosexuality

steps.opening_for:
Opening argument for the proposition:

Islam permits homosexuality when it is understood as an innate same-sex orientation and as loving, consensual, ethical same-sex intimacy—not exploitation, rape, coercion, or promiscuity. The case rests on the Qur’an’s moral principles, the actual content of the story of Prophet Lot, and the absence of any clear Qur’anic prohibition of same-sex love or partnership.

First, the Qur’an does not explicitly condemn “homosexuality” as an orientation. The modern concept of sexual orientation—an enduring, involuntary pattern of attraction—is not addressed in the Qur’an. Islamic law has long recognized that people are not morally blameworthy for involuntary states. A well-known hadith states that God forgives what occurs within a person so long as it is not acted upon or spoken of in a wrongful way: “Allah has forgiven my community for what occurs in their minds, so long as they do not speak of it or act upon it.” —Sahih al-Bukhari 5269; Sahih Muslim 127. If same-sex attraction is not chosen, then it cannot be sinful in itself.

Second, the Qur’an repeatedly teaches that human diversity is part of divine creation. “Among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the diversity of your languages and your colors.” —Qur’an 30:22. “We created you into nations and tribes so that you may know one another.” —Qur’an 49:13. These verses do not specifically mention sexuality, but they establish a broad theological principle: difference is not automatically deviance. Islam does not require every person to fit one social pattern in order to possess dignity before God.

Third, the story most often cited against homosexuality—the story of Lot—is not about loving same-sex relationships. The Qur’anic descriptions of Lot’s people emphasize public indecency, aggression, coercion, and violation of guests. In Qur’an 29:28–29, Lot condemns his people not merely for approaching men, but for “committing highway robbery” and practicing evil in their assemblies. In Qur’an 11:77–83, the men of the city surround Lot’s house and seek access to his guests—an attempted gang rape and an act of violent humiliation. This is not a description of two consenting adults in a faithful relationship. It is a story about sexual violence, abuse of strangers, and social corruption.

The Qur’an’s language also supports this reading. Lot’s people are accused of approaching men “with desire instead of women” —Qur’an 7:80–81; 27:54–55. But the text addresses a people already characterized by excess, aggression, and wrongdoing. It does not discuss people who are constitutionally same-sex attracted, nor does it discuss mutual commitment, marriage-like companionship, or lifelong love. To take a condemnation of rape and violent domination and apply it to all gay people is a moral and interpretive leap.

Fourth, Islamic law is not built only on inherited precedent; it is built on justice, mercy, and the prevention of harm. The Qur’an says, “God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.” —Qur’an 2:286. It also says, “We have honored the children of Adam.” —Qur’an 17:70. If gay Muslims are told that their only religiously acceptable life is permanent loneliness, celibacy, secrecy, or self-hatred, then that interpretation imposes an extraordinary burden not clearly required by the Qur’an. A more faithful Islamic ethic would ask whether a relationship embodies the values Islam actually demands: consent, fidelity, responsibility, modesty, honesty, and protection from harm.

Fifth, there is no Qur’anic punishment for homosexuality. This matters because the Qur’an is explicit about certain sexual offenses, such as zina. See Qur’an 24:2. Yet it gives no comparable legal punishment for consensual same-sex intimacy. Classical jurists disagreed widely over how to treat liwat, precisely because the Qur’an does not provide a clear hadd punishment for it. That disagreement shows that the matter was interpretive, not settled by an explicit Qur’anic command.

Finally, contemporary Muslim scholars have made serious arguments that affirming same-sex relationships is compatible with Islam. Scott Siraj al-Haqq Kugle argues that the Qur’an condemns the coercive and violent acts of Lot’s people, not loving same-sex relationships, in *Homosexuality in Islam: Critical Reflection on Gay, Lesbian, and Transgender Muslims* (Oneworld, 2010). Junaid Jahangir and Hussein Abdullatif make a detailed Islamic legal and ethical case for recognizing Muslim same-sex unions in *Islamic Law and Muslim Same-Sex Unions* (Lexington Books, 2016). Kecia Ali also emphasizes that Muslim sexual ethics must be read historically and critically rather than reduced to inherited patriarchal assumptions in *Sexual Ethics and Islam* (Oneworld, 2006; revised ed. 2016).

So the proposition is not that every classical jurist approved of homosexuality; many did not. The proposition is that Islam, when grounded in the Qur’an’s core principles of justice, mercy, human dignity, and moral accountability, does not clearly prohibit same-sex orientation or ethical same-sex love. What Islam condemns is lust without responsibility, sex without consent, exploitation, rape, humiliation, and social corruption. A loving, faithful same-sex relationship is not the sin of Lot’s people. It can be understood as permissible within an Islamic moral framework.
steps.opening_against:
Ladies and gentlemen, the proposition before us is: **“Islam permits homosexuality.”** I oppose that proposition—not out of hostility toward any person, but because the claim does not accurately reflect the Qur’an, the Sunnah, or the overwhelming consensus of Islamic legal tradition.

First, we must define terms carefully. If by “homosexuality” one means **involuntary same-sex attraction**, Islamic law generally does not treat unchosen feelings as sins in themselves. Moral accountability concerns what a person chooses to do. But if the proposition means that Islam permits **same-sex sexual acts, same-sex marriage, or homosexual relationships as a lawful sexual outlet**, then the mainstream Islamic answer is clearly no.

The Qur’an repeatedly presents sexual relations between males as part of the wrongdoing of the people of Prophet Lūṭ. It says:

> “Do you commit such immorality as no one has preceded you with from among the worlds? Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a transgressing people.”  
> **Qur’an 7:80–81**

Similarly:

> “Do you approach males among the worlds and leave what your Lord has created for you as spouses? Rather, you are a transgressing people.”  
> **Qur’an 26:165–166**

And again:

> “Do you indeed approach men with desire instead of women? Rather, you are a people behaving ignorantly.”  
> **Qur’an 27:54–55**

These verses are not merely condemning violence, rape, or inhospitality—though Islam condemns those too. The text specifically identifies “approaching men with desire instead of women” as the moral violation.

Second, the Qur’an defines the lawful sexual framework as marriage and chastity. It praises believers:

> “Those who guard their private parts except from their spouses… but whoever seeks beyond that, then those are the transgressors.”  
> **Qur’an 23:5–7; see also 70:29–31**

Islamic marriage, as understood by the Qur’an and classical fiqh, is a male-female institution. The Qur’an describes spouses in the context of male and female complementarity:

> “And among His signs is that He created for you from yourselves spouses that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy.”  
> **Qur’an 30:21**

Third, the Sunnah reinforces this understanding. The Prophet ﷺ warned against the act associated with the people of Lūṭ:

> “What I fear most for my community is the deed of the people of Lūṭ.”  
> **Sunan al-Tirmidhī 1457; also reported in Ibn Mājah**

Classical Muslim jurists across the major schools agreed that same-sex sexual acts are prohibited, even though they differed over legal penalties and evidentiary standards. For example, Ibn Qudāmah states in *al-Mughnī* that the scholars agreed on the prohibition of the act of Lūṭ’s people. Ibn Rushd in *Bidāyat al-Mujtahid* likewise discusses disagreement over punishment while assuming the underlying prohibition.

So the central point is this: **Islam does not permit every desire to be acted upon.** Islamic ethics channels sexuality into a specific lawful framework: marriage between man and woman. Desires outside that framework—whether heterosexual or homosexual—do not become permissible simply because they are sincerely felt.

At the same time, this position must be stated with justice and compassion. Islam forbids cruelty, humiliation, vigilantism, and oppression. Every human being has dignity and must be treated with fairness. But compassion does not require rewriting Islamic law. The evidence from the Qur’an, Sunnah, and juristic consensus shows that Islam does **not** permit same-sex sexual conduct or homosexual relationships as lawful. Therefore, the proposition that “Islam permits homosexuality” is not supported by the primary sources of Islam.
steps.response_for:
The opponent’s case depends on treating the classical majority view as if it were identical with the Qur’an itself. But the proposition is not that most premodern jurists affirmed same-sex unions; the proposition is that Islam, read from its primary moral sources, does not clearly prohibit homosexuality as an innate orientation or ethical same-sex love. The opponent has not overcome that point.

## 1. The Qur’an condemns the people of Lūṭ for violent sexual corruption, not loving same-sex unions
