The opponent quotes Qur’an 7:80–81, 26:165–166, and 27:54–55:

> “You approach men with desire instead of women…”

But those verses cannot be isolated from the rest of the Lūṭ narrative. The Qur’an itself describes the people of Lūṭ as guilty of a broader pattern of violent public corruption:

> “Do you approach men, commit highway robbery, and commit evil in your assemblies?”  
> **Qur’an 29:29**

And in the narrative with Lūṭ’s guests, the men of the city rush toward his house seeking to violate the guests:

> “The people of the city came rejoicing… He said: These are my guests, so do not disgrace me.”  
> **Qur’an 15:67–69**

Likewise:

> “They had demanded his guests from him…”  
> **Qur’an 54:37**

This is not the picture of two consenting adults in a faithful relationship. It is an attempted mob assault, humiliation of strangers, public indecency, and social predation. The Qur’an links their sexual behavior with robbery, coercion, and communal evil. Therefore, to say “Lūṭ condemns all homosexual love” is an interpretive expansion beyond the text.

Qur’an 26:165–166 is especially important:

> “Do you approach males among the worlds and leave what your Lord created for you as spouses?”

This sounds like men who already had women/wives available and were abandoning them for predatory lust. It does not describe people whose enduring orientation is same-sex attraction, nor does it address committed same-sex partnership.

## 2. “Approaching men with desire” does not automatically mean all same-sex intimacy

The opponent argues that because the Qur’an says “approach men with desire,” the issue must be homosexuality itself. But desire, in the Qur’an, is morally evaluated by context. Desire can be lawful or unlawful depending on whether it is exploitative, unjust, adulterous, coercive, or irresponsible.

The people of Lūṭ are described as:

> “a transgressing people” — **Qur’an 7:81**  
> “a people behaving ignorantly” — **Qur’an 27:55**  
> committing “evil in your assemblies” — **Qur’an 29:29**

The Qur’an is not giving an abstract anthropology of sexual orientation. It is condemning a corrupt society’s abusive sexual practices. The opponent assumes that the condemned “deed of Lūṭ” equals every possible same-sex relationship. But that is precisely what must be proven.

## 3. The marriage verses do not explicitly exclude same-sex spouses

The opponent cites:

> “Those who guard their private parts except from their spouses…”  
> **Qur’an 23:5–7; 70:29–31**

But this proves that Islam channels sexuality into committed lawful relationship. It does not, by itself, prove that a spouse must always be opposite-sex in every possible case. The Qur’an says believers may have sexual intimacy with “azwāj” — spouses. The question is whether same-sex couples can be recognized through a covenantal, responsible, modest union.

The Qur’an describes marriage as a place of tranquility, affection, and mercy:

> “Among His signs is that He created for you from yourselves spouses, that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy.”  
> **Qur’an 30:21**

That verse is not merely about reproduction. Infertile couples, elderly couples, and couples who never have children are still valid spouses in Islamic law. The verse emphasizes *sukūn*, *mawadda*, and *raḥma* — tranquility, love, and mercy. A faithful same-sex relationship can embody those same ethical goods.

The Qur’an also says:

> “Marry the unmarried among you…”  
> **Qur’an 24:32**

The ethical aim is to protect people from isolation, exploitation, and illicit sexual conduct. If a gay Muslim cannot realistically form an opposite-sex marriage without deception or harm, then a responsible same-sex union better fulfills the Qur’anic purposes of honesty, chastity, mercy, and protection from harm.

## 4. The Sunnah reports do not settle the matter as clearly as claimed

The opponent cites reports about “the deed of the people of Lūṭ.” But even those reports require interpretation. What is “the deed of the people of Lūṭ”? The Qur’an defines that deed in context: coercion, assault against guests, public corruption, and predatory lust.

Moreover, there is no Qur’anic ḥadd punishment for consensual same-sex intimacy. The Qur’an is explicit when it wants to legislate a sexual punishment, as in:

> “The woman and the man guilty of zinā, flog each of them one hundred lashes…”  
> **Qur’an 24:2**

No comparable Qur’anic punishment is given for same-sex conduct. Classical jurists therefore disagreed over punishment: some analogized it to zinā, some prescribed discretionary punishment, some relied on contested reports. Ibn Rushd discusses this disagreement in *Bidāyat al-Mujtahid*, noting that jurists differed over the legal penalty. That disagreement itself shows that the issue was not as textually straightforward as the opponent suggests.

Also, no sound, widely accepted report shows the Prophet ﷺ actually prosecuting and punishing a consensual same-sex couple. If the matter were a central, clearly defined ḥadd offense, we would expect more explicit Qur’anic or Prophetic legal treatment.

## 5. Classical consensus was about “liwāṭ” as they understood it, not modern sexual orientation or equal same-sex partnership

The opponent invokes ijmāʿ. But classical jurists were not discussing “homosexuality” in the modern sense: an enduring, unchosen same-sex orientation expressed through mutual adult partnership. They were usually discussing *liwāṭ*, often framed as anal intercourse, pederasty, domination, or illicit lust outside marriage.

Even if many jurists prohibited what they called *liwāṭ*, that does not automatically answer whether Islam permits a faithful same-sex union between consenting adults who seek chastity, loyalty, and mutual care. The conceptual category is different.

Islamic law has always distinguished between the revealed text and human juristic interpretation. Jurists can be respected without treating every inherited social assumption as eternally binding.

## 6. Islamic moral principles support mercy, dignity, and the removal of hardship

The Qur’an repeatedly grounds law in justice and mercy:

> “God commands justice and excellence…”  
> **Qur’an 16:90**

> “Do not let hatred of a people cause you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to God-consciousness.”  
> **Qur’an 5:8**

> “God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”  
> **Qur’an 2:286**

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

> “We have honored the children of Adam.”  
> **Qur’an 17:70**

If same-sex attraction is unchosen — a point even the opponent concedes — then telling gay Muslims that their only permissible life is permanent celibacy, loneliness, concealment, or entering a heterosexual marriage under false pretenses imposes severe harm. Islamic ethics should not create unnecessary harm where the Qur’an has not clearly imposed it.

The Prophet ﷺ also taught:

> “There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm.”  
> **Sunan Ibn Mājah 2340; al-Muwaṭṭaʾ of Mālik**

A same-sex union based on consent, fidelity, honesty, and responsibility may reduce harm far more than forcing people into secrecy, shame, or fraudulent marriages.

## 7. Declaring something forbidden requires clear evidence

The Qur’an warns against inventing prohibitions in God’s name:

> “Do not say, concerning what your tongues falsely describe, ‘This is lawful and this is forbidden,’ so as to invent lies against God.”  
> **Qur’an 16:116**

> “Say: Have you considered what provision God has sent down for you, and you have made some of it unlawful and lawful? Say: Has God permitted you, or do you invent against God?”  
> **Qur’an 10:59**

The opponent has shown that the classical majority prohibited same-sex acts. But he has not shown that the Qur’an clearly prohibits loving, consensual same-sex unions as such. The primary Qur’anic evidence concerns the violent and corrupt people of Lūṭ, not gay Muslims seeking ethical companionship.

## Conclusion

Islam certainly forbids rape, coercion, adultery, promiscuity, humiliation, and exploitation. But those are not the same as homosexuality understood as innate orientation or faithful same-sex love.

The Qur’an does not explicitly condemn sexual orientation. It does not describe or prohibit committed same-sex unions. The Lūṭ narrative condemns predatory sexual violence and social corruption. The marriage verses require chastity and responsibility, but they do not necessarily exclude same-sex covenantal relationships. And Islamic principles of mercy, justice, dignity, and removal of hardship support an affirming interpretation.

Therefore, the proposition stands: Islam can permit homosexuality when understood as unchosen same-sex orientation and ethical, consensual, faithful same-sex intimacy.
steps.response_against:
Thank you. The opponent’s argument rests on a crucial move: it narrows the Qur’anic condemnation of the people of Lūṭ to rape, coercion, and inhospitality, then argues that faithful same-sex relationships are not addressed. But that reading does not fit the Qur’anic language, the Qur’anic legal framework for sex and marriage, the Sunnah, or the consensus of Islamic jurisprudence.

I will respond point by point.

---

## 1. The Lūṭ passages condemn male-male sexual desire itself, not only rape or violence

The Qur’an certainly condemns the people of Lūṭ for multiple evils: public indecency, attempted assault, highway robbery, and social corruption. But the Qur’an does not reduce their sin to coercion or rape. It repeatedly identifies the sexual object of their desire as part of the wrongdoing:

> “Do you commit such immorality as no one has preceded you with from among the worlds? Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a transgressing people.”  
> **Qur’an 7:80–81**

> “Do you approach males among the worlds and leave what your Lord created for you as spouses? Rather, you are a transgressing people.”  
> **Qur’an 26:165–166**

> “Do you indeed approach men with desire instead of women? Rather, you are a people behaving ignorantly.”  
> **Qur’an 27:54–55**

The wording is significant. The Qur’an does not merely say, “You rape,” “you assault guests,” or “you act violently.” It says: **“You approach men with desire instead of women.”** The contrast is explicitly between men and women as sexual objects.

If the only sin were rape, the gender of the victim would not be the defining issue, because rape of women is equally forbidden. If the only sin were inhospitality, the Qur’an would not repeatedly describe the evil as approaching males with desire. And if the only sin were violence, the Qur’an’s repeated contrast — “men instead of women” — would be unnecessary.

The opponent cites:

> “Do you approach men, commit highway robbery, and commit evil in your assemblies?”  
> **Qur’an 29:29**

But this verse lists multiple corruptions. It does not say that “approaching men” is only wrong when combined with highway robbery. Rather, it names “approaching men” as one distinct act among other evils.

Also, the phrase:

> “such immorality as no one has preceded you with from among the worlds”  
> **Qur’an 7:80**

is difficult to explain if the issue were merely rape, robbery, or public indecency, since those sins existed before. Classical exegetes understood the novelty to be the practice of men sexually approaching men.

---

## 2. Consent does not make a sexual act lawful in Islam

The opponent repeatedly says that the Qur’an condemns coercive or predatory acts, not “consensual” relationships. But in Islamic sexual ethics, consent alone is not the criterion of permissibility.

Consensual fornication is still forbidden:

> “Do not approach zinā. Indeed, it is an immorality and an evil way.”  
> **Qur’an 17:32**

The Qur’an prescribes punishment for consensual unlawful sex:

> “The woman and the man guilty of zinā, flog each of them one hundred lashes…”  
> **Qur’an 24:2**

So even if two adults are consenting, affectionate, and sincere, that does not by itself make the sexual relationship lawful. Islam permits sexual intimacy within the lawful institution of marriage as revealed and defined by Islamic law. It does not permit every emotionally meaningful or consensual sexual relationship.

---

## 3. The Qur’anic framework of marriage is male-female

The opponent argues that the word **azwāj** — “spouses” — does not explicitly exclude same-sex spouses. But the Qur’an’s treatment of marriage is consistently and structurally male-female.

For example:

> “Marry women of your choice, two, three, or four…”  
> **Qur’an 4:3**

> “Do not marry women whom your fathers married…”  
> **Qur’an 4:22**

> “Lawful to you are chaste women from among the believers and chaste women from those who were given the Scripture…”  
> **Qur’an 5:5**

> “Your wives are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth as you will…”  
> **Qur’an 2:223**

> “Allah has made for you from yourselves spouses and has made for you from your spouses children and grandchildren…”  
> **Qur’an 16:72**

The Qur’an’s marriage law concerns husbands and wives, men and women, mahr, waiting periods, pregnancy, divorce, lineage, inheritance, and family formation. Same-sex marriage is nowhere legislated, recognized, or implied.

The opponent cites:

> “Among His signs is that He created for you from yourselves spouses, that you may find tranquility in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy.”  
> **Qur’an 30:21**

But this verse does not exist in isolation. The Qur’anic concept of spouses is part of the broader male-female order of creation and marriage. Affection and mercy are essential goods in marriage, but they do not by themselves define what counts as a valid marriage. A relationship can contain affection and still be religiously unlawful if it falls outside the lawful marital framework.

For example, an adulterous relationship may involve affection, loyalty, and emotional support. That does not make it halal. Likewise, the presence of love and commitment does not create a new category of nikāḥ unknown to the Qur’an, Sunnah, and juristic tradition.

---

## 4. “Leave what your Lord created for you as spouses” supports the traditional reading

The opponent argues that Qur’an 26:165–166 may refer only to men abandoning their wives for predatory lust:

> “Do you approach males among the worlds and leave what your Lord created for you as spouses?”  
> **Qur’an 26:165–166**

But the verse’s logic is broader: Allah created lawful sexual companionship in women as spouses, and the people of Lūṭ turned instead to males. The contrast is between the lawful sexual avenue and the unlawful one.

Similarly, Prophet Lūṭ says:

> “O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests.”  
> **Qur’an 11:78**

Classical exegetes commonly understood “my daughters” either as his actual daughters or the women of his community, meaning lawful marriage with women. In either case, the contrast is clear: women in lawful relation are “purer” than approaching men.

---

## 5. The absence of a specific Qur’anic ḥadd does not mean permission

The opponent argues that because the Qur’an does not prescribe a specific ḥadd punishment for same-sex conduct, the matter is not clearly forbidden. That argument fails.

Many sins are clearly forbidden without having a specific Qur’anic ḥadd punishment. For example, the Qur’an forbids consuming riba, backbiting, bribery, and many forms of wrongdoing without assigning each a fixed worldly punishment in the Qur’an.

The distinction between **moral prohibition** and **legal punishment** is crucial. Jurists differed over the punishment for liwāṭ, but they did not differ over its prohibition. Ibn Rushd, in *Bidāyat al-Mujtahid*, discusses disagreement over the penalty, not over whether the act is lawful. Ibn Qudāmah likewise states in *al-Mughnī* that the scholars agreed on the prohibition of the act of the people of Lūṭ, while differing over punishment.

So disagreement over legal penalty does not imply permissibility. It only shows that jurists debated how the state should treat the offense procedurally and penally.

---

## 6. The Sunnah supports prohibition

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “What I fear most for my community is the deed of the people of Lūṭ.”  
> **Sunan al-Tirmidhī 1457; Sunan Ibn Mājah 2563**

There are also reports stating:

> “Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lūṭ, then punish the one who does it and the one to whom it is done.”  
> **Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4462; Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 1456; Sunan Ibn Mājah 2561**

Scholars have discussed the chains and legal implications of some of these reports, but they are part of the broader hadith and fiqh discourse that reinforces the prohibition. More importantly, the prohibition does not depend only on one hadith report; it rests on the Qur’anic passages, the Prophetic warnings, and the legal consensus of the schools.

---

## 7. Classical jurists were not only discussing rape or pederasty

The opponent says classical jurists discussed **liwāṭ** in contexts such as pederasty, domination, or illicit lust, not “modern sexual orientation.” But Islamic law regulates actions, not modern identity categories.

Whether a person experiences same-sex attraction as enduring or unchosen does not alter the ruling on the sexual act. Islam does not say every deep or persistent desire may be acted upon. A man may have a lifelong attraction to someone else’s wife; that does not make adultery permissible. A person may be unable to marry the person they desire; that does not create a new lawful sexual category.

The Qur’an says:

> “Let those who do not find the means to marry remain chaste until Allah enriches them from His bounty.”  
> **Qur’an 24:33**

And the Prophet ﷺ said:

> “O young men, whoever among you is able to marry, let him marry, for it is more effective in lowering the gaze and guarding chastity. Whoever is not able, then let him fast, for it will be a shield for him.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5066; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1400**

This shows that when a lawful sexual outlet is unavailable, the Islamic answer is chastity, not the creation of an alternative sexual institution.

---

## 8. Mercy and removal of hardship do not override explicit prohibitions

The opponent invokes important principles:

> “Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”  
> **Qur’an 2:286**

> “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”  
> **Qur’an 22:78**

> “There should be neither harm nor reciprocating harm.”  
> **Sunan Ibn Mājah 2340; al-Muwaṭṭaʾ**

These principles are real and important. But in Islamic legal theory, general principles of mercy and hardship do not cancel specific revealed prohibitions. They guide application, pastoral care, and removal of unnecessary burdens, but they do not make forbidden sexual acts lawful.

Prayer, fasting, zakāh, hijab, chastity, and avoidance of prohibited desires can all involve hardship. Yet hardship does not automatically negate obligation. The principle “no harm” cannot be used to legalize what the Qur’an and Sunnah prohibit.

Islamic compassion should mean: no humiliation, no vigilantism, no family cruelty, no dehumanization, no driving people to despair. But compassion does not require declaring same-sex sexual conduct or same-sex marriage halal.

---

## 9. The claim “do not invent prohibitions” cuts both ways

The opponent cites:

> “Do not say, concerning what your tongues falsely describe, ‘This is lawful and this is forbidden,’ so as to invent lies against Allah.”  
> **Qur’an 16:116**

That warning is serious. But it applies equally to declaring something lawful without evidence.

The Qur’an repeatedly condemns “approaching men with desire instead of women.” The Sunnah warns against the deed of the people of Lūṭ. The juristic tradition across the major schools treated same-sex sexual acts as prohibited. In that context, it is not “inventing a prohibition” to uphold the inherited ruling. Rather, it would be a major innovation to claim that Islam permits same-sex sexual relationships despite the consistent scriptural and legal record to the contrary.

---

## Conclusion

The opponent is correct about one thing: unchosen same-sex attraction, as an inner feeling, is not the same as sinful action. Islam does not punish people for involuntary inclinations.

But the proposition is not merely “Islam does not condemn involuntary feelings.” The proposition is: **“Islam permits homosexuality,”** and the opponent expands that to include “ethical, consensual, faithful same-sex intimacy.”

That claim is not supported by the Qur’an, the Sunnah, or the Islamic legal tradition.

The Qur’an condemns approaching men with desire instead of women. The Qur’anic model of marriage is male-female. The Sunnah warns against the deed of the people of Lūṭ. The jurists differed over punishment but overwhelmingly agreed on prohibition. And Islamic principles of mercy and dignity cannot be used to overturn explicit sexual boundaries.

Therefore, while Muslims must treat every person with justice, dignity, and compassion, Islam does not permit same-sex sexual conduct or same-sex marriage as lawful. The proposition remains false.
steps.conclusion_for:
In conclusion, the proposition I have defended is not that every classical jurist endorsed same-sex relationships, nor that Islam permits lust, exploitation, promiscuity, or sexual irresponsibility. The proposition is more precise: Islam can permit homosexuality when homosexuality means an unchosen same-sex orientation and a loving, consensual, faithful, ethical same-sex relationship.

The opposing side has relied mainly on two claims: first, that the story of Prophet Lūṭ condemns homosexuality as such; and second, that classical juristic consensus settles the matter. But neither claim is decisive.

The Qur’an’s account of Lūṭ’s people is not a neutral discussion of two consenting adults in a committed relationship. It is a story of social corruption, attempted sexual violence, humiliation of guests, public indecency, coercion, and predatory behavior. Qur’an 29:29 explicitly links their conduct with highway robbery and evil in assemblies. Other passages describe a mob attempting to violate Lūṭ’s guests. That is not the same moral category as a faithful same-sex partnership based on consent, love, and responsibility.

The Qur’an condemns the people of Lūṭ for transgression, aggression, and corruption. It does not describe modern sexual orientation. It does not address gay Muslims seeking companionship, fidelity, and moral stability. To take a condemnation of violent sexual abuse and apply it automatically to all same-sex love is an interpretation—not an unavoidable reading of the text.

Second, the Qur’an does not explicitly prohibit same-sex orientation. Even the opposing side concedes that involuntary attraction is not sinful in itself. Islamic moral accountability concerns chosen wrongdoing, not unchosen human constitution. If same-sex attraction is not chosen, then it cannot be condemned simply as a desire.

Third, the Qur’an provides a sexual ethic rooted in responsibility, modesty, fidelity, and protection from harm. Verses about guarding one’s private parts emphasize that sexuality should not be reckless or exploitative. They do not, by themselves, answer whether a same-sex couple can form a committed covenantal relationship embodying tranquility, affection, and mercy. Qur’an 30:21 describes marriage in terms of *sukūn*, *mawadda*, and *raḥma*—tranquility, love, and compassion. Those values are not limited to procreation, as Islamic law already recognizes valid marriages among infertile and elderly couples.

Fourth, there is no Qur’anic ḥadd punishment for consensual same-sex intimacy. This is significant. When the Qur’an legislates punishments for sexual offenses, such as zinā, it does so explicitly. The absence of such a punishment, and the later juristic disagreement over penalties, shows that the matter was not as clear-cut in the primary text as opponents often claim.

Fifth, Islamic law is not merely a repetition of inherited assumptions. It is meant to serve justice, mercy, dignity, and the removal of hardship. The Qur’an says God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity, that He has not placed unbearable hardship in religion, and that the children of Adam have been honored. If gay Muslims are told that their only religious options are lifelong loneliness, concealment, self-hatred, or dishonest heterosexual marriage, then that interpretation creates serious harm without a clear Qur’anic command requiring it.

Islam forbids rape, coercion, adultery, betrayal, abuse, humiliation, and sexual irresponsibility. But those are not the same as homosexuality understood as an innate orientation or as a faithful same-sex relationship. The Qur’an’s moral concern is not love, loyalty, and mutual care; it is injustice, exploitation, and corruption.

Therefore, my position stands: the Qur’an does not clearly prohibit homosexuality as orientation, nor does it clearly condemn committed, consensual same-sex love. A principled Islamic reading—grounded in mercy, justice, human dignity, and moral accountability—can recognize such relationships as permissible. Islam’s ethical demand is not compulsory loneliness; it is responsible, honest, compassionate, and God-conscious living.
steps.conclusion_against:
Ladies and gentlemen, the question before us is not whether Muslims with same-sex attraction deserve dignity, compassion, protection from cruelty, and fair treatment. They absolutely do. Nor is the question whether involuntary feelings are sinful in themselves. Islamic moral responsibility concerns chosen conduct, not unchosen inclinations.

The real question is whether Islam permits same-sex sexual relationships or same-sex marriage as a lawful expression of sexuality. On that question, the evidence is clear: it does not.

The Qur’an repeatedly condemns the conduct of the people of Lūṭ, and it does so in language that specifically identifies the act of “approaching men with desire instead of women.” While the people of Lūṭ were also guilty of violence, public corruption, and attempted assault, the Qur’an does not limit its condemnation to those crimes. It names male-male sexual desire and conduct as part of the transgression.

The Qur’anic framework for lawful sexuality is also clear. Sexual relations are permitted within marriage, and the Qur’an consistently presents marriage as a male-female institution: husbands and wives, men and women, lineage, waiting periods, mahr, pregnancy, inheritance, and family formation. The Qur’an speaks of spouses with affection, mercy, and tranquility, but those virtues do not redefine marriage outside the revealed framework.

The Sunnah reinforces this understanding through warnings against the “deed of the people of Lūṭ.” And across the major schools of Islamic law, jurists differed over penalties and legal procedures, but they overwhelmingly agreed that same-sex sexual acts are prohibited. Disagreement over punishment is not disagreement over permissibility.

The opposing side has argued that modern same-sex relationships based on consent, fidelity, and love are different from the abuses of Lūṭ’s people. But in Islam, consent and affection alone do not make a sexual relationship lawful. Consensual zinā remains forbidden. An emotionally meaningful relationship can still fall outside the limits set by Allah. Islamic law does not permit every sincere desire to be acted upon.

Nor can general principles of mercy, hardship, and dignity be used to overturn specific prohibitions. Those principles matter deeply: they forbid abuse, humiliation, vigilantism, family cruelty, and dehumanization. They require pastoral care and justice. But they do not authorize us to declare lawful what the Qur’an, Sunnah, and juristic tradition have treated as unlawful.

So my conclusion is simple and consistent: Islam distinguishes between a person and an act, between involuntary inclination and chosen conduct. A Muslim who experiences same-sex attraction is not to be hated, mocked, or oppressed. But Islam does not permit same-sex sexual conduct, same-sex marriage, or homosexual relationships as a lawful sexual outlet.

Therefore, the proposition “Islam permits homosexuality,” if it means permitting same-sex sexual relationships, is not supported by the primary sources of Islam or by the mainstream Islamic legal tradition. The proposition is false.

debates.topic: Islam permits music

steps.opening_for:
Honorable judges and respected opponents: I stand for the proposition that **Islam permits music**—not every lyric, not every setting, and not music used for sin—but music as a human art form is not categorically forbidden in Islam.

The first principle is this: in Islamic law, worldly things are presumed permissible unless there is clear evidence prohibiting them. The Qur’an repeatedly warns against declaring lawful things unlawful without authority. Allah says:

> “Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?”  
> **Qur’an 7:32**

And:

> “O you who believe, do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you…”  
> **Qur’an 5:87**

So the burden of proof is on anyone claiming that all music is haram. Yet the Qur’an contains no explicit verse saying, “music is forbidden.” Some cite verses about “idle talk” or Satan’s “voice,” but those verses condemn misguidance, mockery of revelation, and sinful distraction—not melody itself. Speech can be sinful or righteous; poetry can be sinful or righteous; likewise music depends on content, purpose, and context.

The Sunnah also shows that sound, rhythm, singing, and even instruments were permitted in appropriate settings. In the famous hadith of ʿA’ishah, two young girls were singing in the Prophet’s house on Eid. Abu Bakr objected, calling it “the instruments of Satan,” but the Prophet ﷺ corrected him and said:

> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 949; Sahih Muslim 892**

This is significant. If singing and rhythm were inherently forbidden, the Prophet ﷺ would not have allowed them in his own home, on a day of worship and celebration.

In another report, Abyssinians performed with spears in the mosque, and the Prophet ﷺ allowed ʿA’ishah to watch. This demonstrates that Islam does not demand a joyless culture stripped of art, rhythm, and public celebration.  
**Sahih al-Bukhari 454, 950; Sahih Muslim 892**

There are also narrations encouraging the announcement of marriage with the duff, a percussion instrument. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “Publicize this marriage…”  

And reports mention doing so with the duff.  
**Jamiʿ al-Tirmidhi 1089; Sunan Ibn Majah 1895**  
While scholars differed on grading and scope, these reports reflect a recognized practice: musical sound was not treated as inherently unlawful.

Now, our opponents will likely cite the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari mentioning people who “deem lawful fornication, silk, wine, and maʿazif.”  
**Sahih al-Bukhari 5590**

But this hadith does not settle the issue as a blanket ban on all music. First, scholars have debated its chain and interpretation, especially because Bukhari transmits it in a suspended form in his Sahih, though other chains exist. Second, even if accepted, the hadith lists music alongside wine and fornication in a scene of moral corruption. It can reasonably be understood as condemning music connected to vice, intoxication, sexual immorality, and heedlessness—not every melody, drumbeat, or song. Islamic law often distinguishes between a thing in itself and a sinful use of it.

This is why major scholars did not all agree on a total prohibition. **Ibn Hazm** held that the reports used to prohibit singing and instruments were not sound enough to establish a ban and argued for permissibility in principle. **Imam al-Ghazali**, in *Ihya’ ʿUlum al-Din*, discussed listening to singing and beautiful sounds and treated them as permissible unless they involve prohibited content or lead to prohibited conduct. **Al-Shawkani** also challenged claims of consensus on absolute prohibition in his writings on samaʿ. These are not marginal voices; they are serious jurists and hadith scholars within the Islamic tradition.

Therefore, the balanced Islamic position is not “all music is halal no matter what,” but rather:

- Music with obscene, blasphemous, or immoral content is forbidden.
- Music that leads to neglect of prayer, intoxication, lust, or sinful gatherings is forbidden.
- But music that is clean in content, moderate in use, and does not lead to sin remains permissible.

Islam prohibits corruption; it does not prohibit beauty. It condemns heedlessness; it does not condemn joy. It regulates culture; it does not erase it.

So I submit that the strongest reading of the Qur’an, Sunnah, and juristic tradition is that **Islam permits music in principle, while forbidding sinful uses of music**. That is the more textually grounded, legally balanced, and spiritually humane position.

**Key citations:**

- Qur’an 7:32 — prohibition against forbidding Allah’s adornments without proof.  
- Qur’an 5:87 — “Do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful.”  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 949; Sahih Muslim 892 — girls singing in the Prophet’s house on Eid.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 454, 950; Sahih Muslim 892 — Abyssinian performance witnessed by ʿA’ishah with the Prophet’s approval.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 5590 — hadith mentioning maʿazif, interpreted by many as tied to sinful contexts rather than a universal ban.  
- Al-Ghazali, *Ihya’ ʿUlum al-Din*, Book on Samaʿ and Wajd — permissibility with conditions.  
- Ibn Hazm, *al-Muhalla* — argues against a categorical prohibition of singing/music.  
- Al-Shawkani, *Nayl al-Awtar* and writings on samaʿ — rejects claims of consensus on absolute prohibition.
steps.opening_against:
**Opening argument against the proposition “Islam permits music”**

Respected judges and audience, the proposition before us is not whether Islam permits a pleasant voice, poetry, chanting, or the daff on special occasions. It is whether Islam generally permits *music*—especially musical instruments and entertainment music. The stronger position from the Qur’an, Sunnah, and the mainstream classical juristic tradition is that it does not.

The Qur’an condemns entertainment that diverts people from Allah. Allah says:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases *idle talk* to mislead others from the path of Allah…”  
> **Qur’an 31:6**

Major early authorities explained “idle talk” (*lahw al-hadith*) as singing and musical amusement. Ibn Mas‘ud—one of the greatest Qur’anic scholars among the Companions—said about this verse: “By Allah, it is singing.” Similar interpretations are reported from Ibn ‘Abbas, Jabir, Mujahid, and others. This is cited in classical tafsir works such as **al-Tabari, *Jami‘ al-Bayan* on Qur’an 31:6**, and **Ibn Kathir, *Tafsir al-Qur’an al-‘Azim* on Qur’an 31:6**.

The Sunnah is even more explicit. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “There will be people among my ummah who will consider lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5590**

The wording is powerful: musical instruments are listed alongside things already known to be unlawful—zina, wine, and silk for men—and the Prophet ﷺ criticizes people who will “consider them lawful.” This only makes sense if musical instruments are not generally lawful to begin with. Ibn Hajar, in **Fath al-Bari** under this hadith, explains that *ma‘azif* refers to musical instruments and that the hadith is evidence for their prohibition.

Those who argue for permissibility often cite the narration of two young girls singing in ‘A’ishah’s house on Eid. But that narration proves the opposite of a blanket permission. Abu Bakr objected, calling it “the instruments of Satan,” and the Prophet ﷺ allowed it specifically because it was Eid:

> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every people has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 952; Sahih Muslim, no. 892**

So the Prophet ﷺ did not establish unrestricted music; he allowed a limited exception: girls singing with the daff on a day of celebration. Islamic law often has exceptions—such as the daff at weddings or Eid—but exceptions do not erase the rule.

This is why the dominant position of the classical scholars across the four madhhabs was that musical instruments are prohibited, with narrow exceptions such as the daff in specific circumstances. Ibn Qudamah states in **al-Mughni** that instruments of amusement such as the lute and flute are prohibited. Al-Qurtubi likewise discusses the prohibition of musical instruments in his tafsir under Qur’an 31:6.

Therefore, the Islamic position is not “music is simply permitted.” Islam permits beneficial speech, poetry, nasheed without prohibited elements, and limited celebratory forms like the daff in recognized contexts. But instrumental music as entertainment—especially when tied to heedlessness, desire, and distraction from Allah—is not generally permitted. The Qur’an warns against it, the Sunnah explicitly censures it, and the mainstream juristic tradition upheld that prohibition.

For these reasons, the proposition “Islam permits music” should be rejected.
steps.response_for:
Respected judges, my opponent’s case rests on turning evidence against *sinful amusement* into a categorical ban on music itself. But that leap is not justified by the Qur’an, Sunnah, or the juristic record.

## 1. Qur’an 31:6 condemns misguidance, not melody itself

My opponent cites:

> “Among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead from the path of Allah…”  
> **Qur’an 31:6**

But the verse itself gives the reason for blame: **“to mislead from the path of Allah”** and to take revelation in ridicule. That is not a neutral description of all singing, rhythm, or instruments. It condemns entertainment used as a tool of disbelief, mockery, or diversion from guidance.

Yes, some Companions and early mufassirun interpreted *lahw al-hadith* as singing. But that shows that **singing can be a form of blameworthy idle amusement** when it misleads or distracts from Allah. It does not prove that every song, every rhythm, and every instrument is haram in every context.

The Qur’an also says:

> “Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has produced for His servants, and the good things of provision?”  
> **Qur’an 7:32**

And:

> “Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you.”  
> **Qur’an 5:87**

So if music is to be declared categorically forbidden, the evidence must be clear and comprehensive. Qur’an 31:6 is not that; it condemns corrupt use, not sound itself.

## 2. The hadith of *maʿazif* is not proof of an absolute ban

My opponent relies heavily on the hadith:

> “There will be people from my ummah who will consider lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments…”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5590**

Even if one accepts the hadith as authentic—and many scholars do—its interpretation is still debated. The hadith describes a group associated with moral corruption: zina, wine, luxury, heedlessness, and revelry. It is entirely reasonable to understand the condemnation as applying to **music used in sinful gatherings**, not every permissible form of musical sound.

Also, the list itself contains something context-specific: **silk** is forbidden for men but not women. So the mere fact that *maʿazif* appears in the list does not automatically prove an unconditional prohibition in all circumstances. Islamic law often distinguishes between the thing itself and the circumstances around it.

And if *maʿazif* meant every instrument without exception, that would conflict with other authentic reports where the Prophet ﷺ allowed musical expression.

## 3. The Prophet ﷺ permitted singing and the duff in his presence

The hadith of ʿA’ishah is crucial. Two girls were singing in the Prophet’s house on Eid. Abu Bakr objected, saying, “Instruments of Satan?” But the Prophet ﷺ said:

> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 949; Sahih Muslim 892**

My opponent says this is merely an “exception.” But an exception still proves an important principle: **music is not inherently impure or absolutely forbidden**. If singing and rhythmic celebration were intrinsically haram, the Prophet ﷺ would not have allowed them in his own home on Eid.

Even more direct is the wedding narration of al-Rubayyiʿ bint Muʿawwidh. She said the Prophet ﷺ entered upon her after her marriage while young girls were beating the duff and singing. When one girl said, “Among us is a Prophet who knows what will happen tomorrow,” the Prophet ﷺ corrected only that lyric and said:

> “Do not say that; say what you were saying before.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5147**

This is powerful. The Prophet ﷺ did not forbid the singing. He did not forbid the duff. He corrected the problematic content. That supports our position exactly: music is judged by content, context, and effect.

Likewise, when ʿA’ishah prepared a bride for an Ansari man, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> “O ʿA’ishah, was there no amusement? For the Ansar like amusement.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5162**

This shows that lawful celebration and artistic expression were recognized within Islam.

## 4. “Exceptions” undermine the claim of total prohibition

My opponent says: “Islam permits the duff at Eid and weddings, but that does not mean music is generally permitted.”

But the debate proposition is not “Islam permits every song in every nightclub.” Our proposition is: **Islam permits music in principle, while forbidding sinful forms and settings.**

If the Prophet ﷺ allowed singing and the duff at Eid and weddings, then the absolute claim “music is haram” is already false. The real legal question becomes: what types, contexts, and contents are permissible? That is exactly the conditional position I am defending.

## 5. There was no true consensus on absolute prohibition

My opponent appeals to the “mainstream classical position.” But even if many jurists restricted instruments, there was never an uncontested consensus that all music is forbidden.

Major scholars challenged a categorical prohibition:

- **Ibn Hazm**, in *al-Muhalla*, argued that the reports used to prohibit singing and instruments were not sufficient to establish a blanket ban.  
- **Imam al-Ghazali**, in *Ihya’ ʿUlum al-Din*, discussed *samaʿ* and held that beautiful sounds and singing are permissible unless accompanied by prohibited content or consequences.  
- **Al-Shawkani**, in *Nayl al-Awtar* and his writings on *samaʿ*, rejected claims of consensus on absolute prohibition.  
- **Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi** also noted weakness in many narrations cited for the total prohibition of singing.

So the opponent cannot simply say, “the classical tradition forbids music,” as though the matter is closed. The tradition contains serious disagreement.

## 6. The balanced Islamic ruling is conditional permissibility

Islam does not permit music that contains obscenity, shirk, blasphemy, sexual immorality, intoxication, or heedlessness from prayer. That is prohibited.

But clean music, lawful celebration, rhythmic expression, wedding songs, Eid songs, cultural art, and morally sound lyrics are not categorically forbidden by any decisive Qur’anic text.

The Prophet ﷺ corrected immoral content; he did not abolish song. He allowed celebration; he did not demand joyless silence. He condemned corruption; he did not condemn beauty.

Therefore, the strongest and most balanced conclusion is:

**Islam permits music in principle, while prohibiting music that contains or leads to sin.**

### Key citations

- **Qur’an 7:32** — warning against forbidding Allah’s adornments without proof.  
- **Qur’an 5:87** — “Do not forbid the good things Allah has made lawful.”  
- **Qur’an 31:6** — condemns idle talk used “to mislead” from Allah’s path, not all music categorically.  
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 949; Sahih Muslim 892** — girls singing in the Prophet’s house on Eid.  
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 5147** — girls beating duff and singing at a wedding; Prophet ﷺ corrected only the problematic lyric.  
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 5162** — Prophet ﷺ encouraged lawful amusement at marriage.  
- **Sahih al-Bukhari 5590** — *maʿazif* hadith, best read as condemning sinful musical revelry, not every lawful musical expression.  
- **Ibn Hazm, al-Muhalla** — rejects blanket prohibition.  
- **Al-Ghazali, Ihya’ ʿUlum al-Din**, Book of *Samaʿ* — permits beautiful sound with conditions.  
- **Al-Shawkani, Nayl al-Awtar** — rejects claims of consensus on absolute prohibition.
steps.response_against:
Respected judges, my opponent’s argument depends on redefining the proposition. We are not debating whether Islam permits *any* pleasant sound, poetry, chanting, or the daff in limited celebrations. I already affirmed those exceptions. The real question is whether Islam permits “music” as a general category—especially musical instruments and entertainment music. On that, the stronger evidence remains prohibition, with narrow exceptions.

## 1. Qur’an 31:6 is not a vague verse when read with the early tafsir

My opponent says Qur’an 31:6 only condemns “misguidance,” not singing or music itself:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead from the path of Allah…”  
> **Qur’an 31:6**

But the earliest authorities did not treat *lahw al-hadith* as a neutral category. Ibn Mas‘ud, one of the greatest Qur’anic scholars among the Companions, said regarding this verse:

> “By Allah, it is singing.”  
> Reported in **al-Tabari, Jami‘ al-Bayan**, tafsir of 31:6; also cited by **Ibn Kathir**, tafsir of 31:6.

Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Mas‘ud repeated this oath three times. Similar explanations are reported from Ibn ‘Abbas, Jabir, Mujahid, ‘Ikrimah, and others. See **al-Tabari**, **Ibn Kathir**, and **al-Qurtubi** under Qur’an 31:6.

My opponent says, “But the verse says ‘to mislead.’” Yes—but singing and entertainment are condemned here precisely because they become a means of diversion from revelation. The next verse says:

> “And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly…”  
> **Qur’an 31:7**

So the context is entertainment replacing receptivity to Allah’s guidance. That is exactly why the early mufassirun connected the verse to singing and musical amusement.

The verses my opponent cited—Qur’an 7:32 and 5:87—warn against forbidding what Allah has permitted. But they do not help if there is specific evidence that a thing is prohibited. Wine, gambling, and silk for men are also pleasurable or “adornments” in some sense, yet they are restricted by specific texts. General verses about lawful good things cannot override specific evidence about *lahw* and *ma‘azif*.

## 2. The hadith of *ma‘azif* is explicit and cannot be reduced to “sinful context only”

The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “There will be people among my ummah who will consider lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5590**

The key word is **“yastahillun”** — “they will deem lawful.” That means the things mentioned are being unlawfully treated as permissible.

My opponent argues that the hadith only condemns music when associated with zina, wine, and corrupt gatherings. But the wording lists separate objects of unlawful legalization: zina, silk, wine, and *ma‘azif*. If one says *ma‘azif* are only condemned because of the surrounding sins, the same could be said of silk or even zina, which is obviously false. The hadith is not merely saying, “Some people will drink wine while music happens to be present.” It says they will **consider lawful** these prohibited matters.

As for silk, my opponent says it is context-specific because it is prohibited for men but allowed for women. Correct—but that exception is known from separate evidence. Likewise, the daff is allowed in limited contexts by separate evidence. That does not make all instruments permissible.

Ibn Hajar explains in **Fath al-Bari**, under this hadith, that *ma‘azif* refers to musical instruments. He also defends the authenticity of the report. The hadith is in **Sahih al-Bukhari**, and its meaning is supported by other narrations, including reports in **Sunan Abi Dawud** and **Sunan Ibn Majah** mentioning wine being renamed and musical instruments being played.

So the hadith remains strong evidence that musical instruments are not generally permissible.

## 3. The Eid and wedding narrations prove limited exceptions, not general permissibility

My opponent’s strongest evidence is the hadith of the two girls singing in the house of ‘A’ishah on Eid. Abu Bakr objected, saying:

> “The instruments of Satan in the house of the Messenger of Allah?”  
> The Prophet ﷺ replied:  
> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every people has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 952; Sahih Muslim, no. 892**

But notice the Prophet’s reasoning: **“This is our festival.”** He did not say, “Music is generally lawful.” He allowed it because it was Eid. That is exactly an exception.

Also, in some wordings ‘A’ishah clarifies that they were **not professional singing girls**. This was not a general musical performance. It was young girls singing old verses about the battle of Bu‘ath on a day of celebration.

The wedding narration also supports the exception:

> Young girls were beating the daff and singing at a wedding. When one girl said, “Among us is a Prophet who knows what will happen tomorrow,” the Prophet ﷺ corrected her and said:  
> “Do not say that; say what you were saying before.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5147**

Again, this proves the permissibility of the **daff at weddings**, not the permissibility of musical instruments generally.

Likewise, when the Prophet ﷺ said:

> “O ‘A’ishah, was there no amusement? For the Ansar like amusement.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari, no. 5162**

This refers to lawful wedding celebration. It does not cancel the hadith of *ma‘azif*. Islamic law often has exceptions: the daff at weddings and Eid is one of them.

If all music and instruments were generally permissible, there would be no need for the Prophet ﷺ to justify the incident by saying, “This is our festival.” The very wording shows special allowance.

## 4. “Not inherently impure” does not mean “generally permissible”

My opponent says: if the Prophet ﷺ allowed singing and daff on Eid, then music cannot be inherently haram.

But this confuses two issues. Something can be prohibited generally while allowed in specific circumstances. For example:

- Silk is forbidden for men but allowed for women.
- Normally prohibited things can become allowed in necessity.
- The daff is allowed in weddings and Eid but that does not legalize all instruments.

So yes, the daff in specific contexts is allowed. But that does not establish a general rule that music is permissible. It establishes the opposite: a restricted allowance within a broader prohibition.

## 5. The dissenting scholars do not overturn the mainstream juristic position

My opponent cites Ibn Hazm, al-Ghazali, al-Shawkani, and others. But even if some scholars disputed the scope of prohibition, that does not prove music is permitted. At most, it proves there was disagreement. The question is: which view is stronger?

The dominant position of the four madhhabs was that musical instruments are prohibited, except for limited cases such as the daff.

Examples:

- **Ibn Qudamah**, Hanbali jurist, states in **al-Mughni** that instruments of amusement such as the lute and flute are prohibited.
- **Al-Nawawi**, Shafi‘i jurist, discusses the prohibition of instruments such as flutes and stringed instruments in works such as **Rawdat al-Talibin**.
- **Al-Qurtubi**, Maliki mufassir, under Qur’an 31:6, cites the verse as evidence used by scholars against singing and musical amusement.
- **Ibn Taymiyyah** states in **Majmu‘ al-Fatawa** that the well-known position of the four imams is the prohibition of musical instruments.
- **Ibn Hajar**, in **Fath al-Bari**, explains the *ma‘azif* hadith as evidence against musical instruments.

As for Ibn Hazm, his argument largely depends on challenging the authenticity or force of the hadith evidence. But the hadith is in **Sahih al-Bukhari**, and major hadith authorities such as Ibn Hajar defended it.

As for al-Ghazali, he cannot be used to justify modern instrumental music broadly. Even scholars who discussed *sama‘* often distinguished between poetry, voice, spiritual audition, and instruments associated with amusement and vice. Their discussions do not erase the explicit hadith of *ma‘azif* or the mainstream fiqhi restrictions.

As for al-Shawkani, even if he rejects a claimed consensus, rejecting consensus is not the same as proving permissibility. The evidence still has to be weighed, and the strongest hadith evidence remains against general instrumental music.

## 6. The opponent’s “conditional permissibility” is not the classical rule

My opponent concludes: “Islam permits music in principle, while forbidding sinful forms.”

But the classical rule is closer to the opposite:

> Islam prohibits musical instruments in principle, while allowing limited exceptions such as the daff at Eid and weddings, and allowing permissible poetry, chanting, and non-obscene singing in restricted forms.

That distinction matters.

If “music” means every pleasant sound, then the debate becomes meaningless, because no one denies beautiful recitation, poetry, or permissible chanting. But if “music” means musical instruments and entertainment music, then the Qur’anic warnings, the hadith of *ma‘azif*, and the mainstream madhhab tradition all point to prohibition.

Therefore, the proposition “Islam permits music” is misleading and should be rejected. Islam permits limited forms of celebratory sound, but it does not generally permit instrumental music as entertainment.
steps.conclusion_for:
Honorable judges, respected opponent, and audience:

This debate is not about defending immoral lyrics, sinful gatherings, intoxication, lust, or heedlessness from prayer. Islam clearly forbids those things. The real question is whether **music itself**—melody, rhythm, singing, and lawful artistic expression—is categorically prohibited in Islam. I have argued that it is not.

The foundation of Islamic law is that worldly matters are presumed permissible unless there is clear evidence of prohibition. The Qur’an warns us not to declare Allah’s adornments and good things forbidden without proof:

> “Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has produced for His servants?”  
> **Qur’an 7:32**

And:

> “Do not forbid the good things which Allah has made lawful for you.”  
> **Qur’an 5:87**

My opponent cited Qur’an 31:6 about “idle talk,” but the verse condemns entertainment used **to mislead from the path of Allah** and mock revelation. That proves that corrupt entertainment is forbidden; it does not prove that every song, rhythm, or instrument is forbidden in all contexts.

My opponent also relied on the hadith of *maʿazif* in Sahih al-Bukhari. But even accepting its authenticity, the hadith describes music in a setting of moral corruption: fornication, wine, indulgence, and heedlessness. It is therefore reasonable to understand it as condemning musical instruments associated with sinful revelry—not every form of lawful sound or celebration. Islamic law consistently distinguishes between a thing itself and its sinful use.

Most importantly, the Sunnah contains clear examples of permitted musical expression. In the house of the Prophet ﷺ, two girls sang on Eid, and when Abu Bakr objected, the Prophet ﷺ said:

> “Leave them, O Abu Bakr, for every nation has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari; Sahih Muslim**

At a wedding, young girls beat the duff and sang in the Prophet’s presence. When one lyric became theologically problematic, the Prophet ﷺ corrected the lyric—he did not prohibit the singing or the duff. This supports precisely the balanced view I have defended: music is judged by **content, context, and consequence**.

And the juristic tradition itself is not unanimous on a total ban. Scholars such as **Ibn Hazm**, **al-Ghazali**, and **al-Shawkani** challenged claims of absolute prohibition and argued for conditional permissibility. So it is not accurate to present the matter as if Islam has only one undisputed position: that all music is haram.

Therefore, my conclusion is simple and balanced:

- Music that contains obscenity, shirk, blasphemy, sexual immorality, or incitement to sin is forbidden.  
- Music that leads one to neglect prayer, indulge desires, or join sinful gatherings is forbidden.  
- But music that is clean in content, moderate in use, and free from sinful consequences remains permissible.

Islam forbids corruption, not beauty. It forbids heedlessness, not joy. It regulates human culture; it does not erase it.

For these reasons, the proposition stands: **Islam permits music in principle, while prohibiting its sinful forms and uses.**
steps.conclusion_against:
Respected judges and audience,

The question before us was not whether Islam permits a beautiful voice, poetry, permissible chanting, or the daff on Eid and at weddings. I have acknowledged from the beginning that these limited forms exist in the Sunnah. The real question is whether Islam permits music as a general category—especially instrumental entertainment music. On that question, the stronger evidence is prohibition, with narrow exceptions.

First, the Qur’an warns against *lahw al-hadith*—idle amusement that diverts people from the path of Allah:

> “And among mankind is he who purchases idle talk to mislead from the path of Allah…”  
> **Qur’an 31:6**

This was not treated by the early scholars as a vague or irrelevant verse. Ibn Mas‘ud, Ibn ‘Abbas, Jabir, Mujahid, and others connected it to singing and musical amusement, as recorded by major tafsir authorities such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and al-Qurtubi. The point is not that every pleasant sound is sinful, but that entertainment which distracts from Allah and replaces seriousness toward revelation is condemned.

Second, the Sunnah contains explicit evidence. The Prophet ﷺ said:

> “There will be people among my ummah who will consider lawful fornication, silk, wine, and musical instruments.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 5590**

The wording “they will consider lawful” is decisive. Musical instruments are mentioned alongside matters known to be prohibited, and the Prophet ﷺ censures a future people for treating them as permissible. Ibn Hajar and other major scholars understood *ma‘azif* here to mean musical instruments and used this hadith as evidence for prohibition.

Third, the narrations used by the other side do not establish general permissibility. The two girls singing in the house of ‘A’ishah occurred on Eid, and the Prophet ﷺ justified it by saying:

> “Every people has a festival, and this is our festival.”  
> **Bukhari and Muslim**

Likewise, the wedding narrations show the permissibility of the daff and innocent singing in wedding celebration. These are real allowances, but they are limited allowances. Exceptions do not abolish the rule. The fact that the Prophet ﷺ gave a specific reason—Eid, wedding, celebration—shows that this was not an open license for musical entertainment in general.

Fourth, the mainstream juristic tradition supports this reading. Across the four madhhabs, the dominant position was that musical instruments are prohibited, with exceptions such as the daff in recognized celebratory contexts. Scholars such as Ibn Qudamah, al-Nawawi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Taymiyyah, and Ibn Hajar all reflect this broader classical stance. Yes, some scholars differed, but disagreement does not make the permissive view stronger. When the Qur’anic warnings, the hadith of *ma‘azif*, and the dominant juristic understanding are weighed together, the safer and stronger position is clear.

My opponent’s case ultimately shifts the debate to a weaker claim: “Some forms of sound, singing, or daff are permitted in some contexts.” But that is not disputed. What is disputed is the proposition that Islam permits music generally. The evidence does not support that claim.

The balanced Islamic position is this:

Islam permits wholesome speech, poetry, chanting, and limited celebratory use of the daff. But instrumental music and entertainment music are not generally permitted, especially when they cultivate heedlessness, desire, and distraction from Allah.

For these reasons, the proposition “Islam permits music” should be rejected.

debates.topic: Islam promotes peace

steps.opening_for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

I rise to affirm the proposition: **Islam promotes peace**.

To debate this fairly, we must ask: *What does it mean for a faith to promote peace?* It cannot mean that every person who claims the faith has always acted peacefully. No major civilization or religion could pass that test. The fair standard is this: **What do the religion’s core teachings, moral ideals, and foundational examples encourage?** By that standard, Islam is a religion that promotes peace through justice, mercy, restraint, reconciliation, and the sanctity of human life.

First, Islam places the preservation of life at the heart of its moral vision. The Qur’an declares:

> “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely.”  
> — **Qur’an 5:32**

This is one of the strongest possible statements of the sacredness of human life. A religion that equates saving one life with saving all humanity is clearly not built on a celebration of violence.

Second, Islam rejects forced faith. The Qur’an states plainly:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:256**

Peace is impossible where conscience is coerced. Islam’s own scripture insists that belief must not be forced. This principle supports religious freedom and peaceful coexistence.

Third, Islam commands justice even toward enemies. The Qur’an says:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> — **Qur’an 5:8**

This is a profound ethic of peace. It does not say, “Be just only to your own group.” It says justice must remain intact even when dealing with those you dislike or fear. Peace without justice is fragile; Islam promotes peace by demanding justice as a moral duty.

Fourth, Islam encourages reconciliation over conflict. The Qur’an teaches:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and trust in God.”  
> — **Qur’an 8:61**

Even in the context of conflict, the Qur’anic instruction is to accept opportunities for peace. War is not presented as the ideal; reconciliation is.

Fifth, Islam limits warfare and forbids aggression. The Qur’an permits fighting only in response to aggression and immediately restricts it:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:190**

This is not a blank cheque for violence. It is a rule of restraint: no aggression, no transgression, no excess. The Prophet Muhammad also forbade the killing of noncombatants, including women and children. This is recorded in major hadith collections:

> The Prophet “forbade the killing of women and children.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**

That matters because it shows that Islamic teaching distinguishes between combatants and civilians and imposes moral limits even during war.

Sixth, the Prophet Muhammad’s mission is described in the Qur’an as mercy:

> “We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.”  
> — **Qur’an 21:107**

Mercy is not incidental to Islam; it is central. The Prophet also taught:

> “A Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40**

That definition is powerful. A true Muslim is not identified by violence, cruelty, or domination, but by the safety others feel from his words and actions.

Finally, Islam promotes peace at the everyday social level. Muslims greet one another with **“peace be upon you” — as-salamu alaykum**. The Prophet encouraged believers to “spread peace” among people:

> “You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I tell you something which, if you do, you will love one another? Spread peace among yourselves.”  
> — **Sahih Muslim 54**

This shows that peace in Islam is not merely a diplomatic goal; it is a daily habit, a greeting, a social ethic, and a spiritual practice.

So the case is clear. Islam promotes peace by sanctifying life, forbidding religious compulsion, commanding justice, encouraging reconciliation, restricting warfare, protecting civilians, and defining true faith through mercy and safety.

Yes, some people have committed violence in the name of Islam. But abuse of a teaching is not the same as the teaching itself. The question before us is not whether Muslims are always perfect; no community is. The question is whether Islam’s core principles promote peace. The evidence from the Qur’an, the Prophet’s teachings, and Islamic ethics shows that they do.

For these reasons, I strongly affirm: **Islam promotes peace.**
steps.opening_against:
Ladies and gentlemen, I oppose the proposition **“Islam promotes peace”** not because I claim that all Muslims are violent, or that Islam contains no peaceful teachings. Many Muslims are peaceful, and Islamic scripture includes passages urging mercy, restraint, and reconciliation. But the proposition before us is broader: it asks whether Islam, as a religious-legal system rooted in scripture, prophetic precedent, and classical jurisprudence, *promotes peace*. My argument is that this claim is too simplistic and ultimately false.

Islam does not merely contain a message of private spirituality or peaceful coexistence. It also contains explicit scriptural and legal material authorizing warfare, religious supremacy, coercion against dissent, and unequal treatment of non-Muslims under Islamic rule.

First, the Qur’an contains verses that command fighting not simply in immediate self-defense, but in pursuit of religious and political dominance. For example, Qur’an 9:29 instructs Muslims to fight “those who do not believe in Allah” among the People of the Book “until they pay the jizya with willing submission and feel themselves subdued.” That is not a neutral peace doctrine; it is a doctrine of subordination. Qur’an 8:39 says to fight “until there is no fitnah and the religion is entirely for Allah.” Qur’an 9:5, often called the “Sword Verse,” commands fighting against polytheists after the sacred months unless they repent, pray, and pay alms. Even allowing for historical context, these texts have been used by major jurists to construct a doctrine of expansionist jihad.

Second, the hadith literature reinforces this. In Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, Muhammad is reported to have said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…” This is difficult to square with the claim that Islam simply promotes peace. Another hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari states: “Whoever changes his religion, kill him,” which became a basis for classical apostasy laws. A religion that legally threatens death for leaving it cannot easily be described as promoting peace in the modern sense of freedom of conscience.

Third, classical Islamic jurisprudence did not generally develop as a pacifist tradition. Major legal schools treated jihad as a collective duty of the Muslim community. Classical jurists discussed rules for warfare, truces, treatment of captives, taxation of conquered non-Muslims, and the expansion of Islamic rule. Scholars of Islamic law such as Majid Khadduri and Rudolph Peters have documented that jihad in classical law was not merely inner spiritual struggle but included armed struggle to expand or defend the domain of Islam.

Fourth, history matters. The early Islamic caliphates expanded rapidly through military conquest across the Middle East, North Africa, Persia, and beyond. Of course, all empires used violence, including Christian, Persian, Mongol, and secular empires. But that is precisely the point: Islam was not historically just a peace movement. It developed as a religious-political order with armies, conquests, taxation of subject peoples, and laws regulating non-Muslim communities beneath Muslim sovereignty.

So my position is not that Islam contains no peaceful elements. It plainly does. Nor is my position that Muslims are inherently violent. They are not. My argument is that the proposition “Islam promotes peace” is misleading because it selectively emphasizes peaceful passages while ignoring equally authoritative texts and traditions that promote coercion, warfare, and religious supremacy.

A more honest statement would be: **Islam, like many major religious traditions, contains both peaceful and violent strands.** But if the proposition claims that Islam as a whole is essentially or consistently a religion of peace, the evidence from scripture, hadith, classical law, and history does not support it.

### Relevant citations

- Qur’an 9:29 — command to fight People of the Book until they pay jizya “with willing submission.”  
- Qur’an 8:39 — “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”  
- Qur’an 9:5 — the “Sword Verse,” commanding fighting against polytheists after the sacred months unless they repent.  
- Qur’an 2:216 — “Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you.”  
- Qur’an 47:4 — instructions concerning fighting unbelievers and captives.  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22 — “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify…”  
- Sahih al-Bukhari 6922 — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
- Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1955.  
- Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, Markus Wiener, 1996.  
- Bernard Lewis, *The Political Language of Islam*, University of Chicago Press, 1988.
steps.response_for:
Ladies and gentlemen,

The opposition’s case proves one thing: **Islam is not a pacifist religion**. I accept that. Islam does not teach that force is never permissible under any circumstance. But that is not the same as proving that Islam does not promote peace. A tradition can promote peace while still allowing limited, regulated force against aggression, persecution, or treaty-breaking.

The real question is: **Does Islam make violence the norm, or does it restrict violence in pursuit of justice, security, and reconciliation?** The evidence shows the latter.

## 1. The Qur’anic fighting verses are not blanket commands for violence

The opponent cited verses such as Qur’an 9:5, 9:29, and 8:39. But these cannot be read in isolation while ignoring the Qur’an’s own limits on fighting.

The general rule is stated clearly:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:190**

This is not unlimited warfare. It is restricted warfare: against those who fight you, without transgression.

Another verse explains why fighting was permitted in the first place:

> “Permission to fight has been given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged…”  
> — **Qur’an 22:39**

And the very next verse says that one purpose of resisting aggression is to protect religious freedom broadly:

> “Had God not repelled some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques, in which God’s name is much mentioned, would surely have been destroyed.”  
> — **Qur’an 22:40**

That is important: the Qur’an does not only mention mosques. It mentions monasteries, churches, and synagogues too. That is a peace-and-protection ethic, not a program of indiscriminate religious violence.

## 2. Qur’an 9:5 is about treaty-breakers, not all non-Muslims

The so-called “Sword Verse,” Qur’an 9:5, is often quoted without the surrounding verses. But the same passage explicitly exempts those who kept their treaties:

> “Except those polytheists with whom you made a treaty and who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term.”  
> — **Qur’an 9:4**

Then, immediately after the fighting verse, the Qur’an commands Muslims to grant asylum to a polytheist enemy who seeks protection:

> “And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of God, then escort him to his place of safety.”  
> — **Qur’an 9:6**

That completely undermines the idea that Qur’an 9:5 is a command to kill polytheists simply for being polytheists. If it were, Qur’an 9:6 would make no sense. The passage is dealing with hostile groups, broken treaties, and active conflict.

The Qur’an itself gives the reason:

> “Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, intended to expel the Messenger, and attacked you first?”  
> — **Qur’an 9:13**

So the context is not peaceful religious difference; it is aggression and treaty violation.

## 3. Qur’an 8:39 is about ending persecution, not forcing conversion

The opponent also cited:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is entirely for God.”  
> — **Qur’an 8:39**

But again, context matters. The previous verse says:

> “Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has previously occurred will be forgiven…”  
> — **Qur’an 8:38**

And later in the same chapter:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and trust in God.”  
> — **Qur’an 8:61**

So the command is not “fight forever until everyone converts.” It is fight until persecution, expulsion, and violent suppression of faith end. The Qur’an repeatedly uses **fitnah** in the sense of persecution and oppression. This fits with another verse:

> “If they withdraw from you and do not fight you and offer you peace, then God has not made for you a way against them.”  
> — **Qur’an 4:90**

That is a clear peace principle: if they stop fighting and offer peace, Muslims have no legitimate cause to continue fighting.

## 4. Qur’an 9:29 does not command forced conversion

The opponent cited Qur’an 9:29 regarding fighting some among the People of the Book until they pay jizya. But even this verse does not command forced conversion. In fact, the existence of jizya proves that non-Muslims were allowed to remain non-Muslim under Muslim rule.

We may debate whether premodern jizya fits modern ideals of equal citizenship. But the point in this debate is different: the verse does not say, “Fight them until they become Muslim.” It establishes a political settlement under which religious communities could retain their faith, property, and communal life.

This is consistent with the Qur’an’s broader principle:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:256**

And:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.”  
> — **Qur’an 60:8**

That verse is decisive. Islam does not command hostility toward non-Muslims as such. It commands justice and kindness toward peaceful non-Muslims.

## 5. The hadith about “fighting the people” cannot mean forced conversion of all humanity

The opponent cited the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**

But this hadith cannot be interpreted as a universal command to force every non-Muslim to convert, because that would contradict the Qur’an and the Prophet’s own practice.

The Prophet made treaties with non-Muslims. The Qur’an allowed People of the Book to remain People of the Book. Qur’an 9:6 even requires safe passage for a polytheist who does not convert. So the hadith must be read in its historical and legal context: it concerns hostile groups in the Prophet’s Arabian context, not peaceful non-Muslim civilians everywhere.

The Prophet also said:

> “Do not wish to meet the enemy; ask God for safety. But if you meet them, be patient.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3024; Sahih Muslim 1742**

That is not the language of someone glorifying war. It is the language of restraint.

He also forbade killing noncombatants:

> The Prophet “forbade the killing of women and children.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**

And in another narration:

> “Do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, and do not kill children.”  
> — **Sahih Muslim 1731**

These are not minor details. They show that Islamic teaching regulates war to protect life and prevent excess.

## 6. Apostasy law is more complex than the opponent suggests

The opponent cited:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 6922**

This hadith exists, and classical jurists did often discuss apostasy as a capital offense. But the matter is not as simple as saying Islam promotes killing people merely for private belief.

First, the Qur’an repeatedly mentions people who leave faith, but it does not prescribe a worldly death penalty for mere disbelief. For example:

> “Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief — God will not forgive them…”  
> — **Qur’an 4:137**

This verse describes repeated belief and disbelief. If the worldly rule were simply “kill anyone immediately upon apostasy,” this verse would be difficult to understand.

Second, another major hadith gives the legal category more specifically:

> “The blood of a Muslim is not lawful except in three cases: a married adulterer, life for life, and one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676**

The phrase **“separates from the community”** matters. In the Prophet’s context, apostasy was often tied to political rebellion, treason, or joining enemy forces in wartime. That is why many modern Muslim scholars distinguish between private change of belief and violent sedition.

So even on this difficult issue, the opponent’s presentation is selective. The Qur’anic principle remains:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> — **Qur’an 2:256**

## 7. Classical Islamic law was not pacifist, but it was deeply concerned with restraint

The opponent is correct that classical Islamic law developed rules for jihad, captives, truces, taxation, and relations with non-Muslim communities. But that actually supports part of my argument: Islam did not leave war unregulated. It placed war under law.

Islamic law forbade treachery, mutilation, killing children, killing women, and killing protected non-Muslims. The Prophet warned:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 3166**

That is an extremely severe warning. It means that the life of a protected non-Muslim is sacred under Islamic law.

The Prophet also taught:

> “A Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> — **Sahih al-Bukhari 10; Sahih Muslim 40**

That is the ethical ideal: safety from harm.

## 8. History shows political empires, not the absence of Islamic peace ethics
